stem: A 6-month-old, previously well male is brought to a metropolitan emergency department in late winter with 3 days of coryza and cough, now feeding about 60% of his usual volumes. He is alert and consolable in his mother's arms. On examination he has nasal flaring, tracheal tug, and mild subcostal recession. Bilateral fine inspiratory crackles and end-expiratory wheeze are audible throughout both lung fields. He has not received any prior treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158/min, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 56/min, SpO2 88% on room air, temperature 37.8°C
data_table.Examination: Alert, consolable; nasal flaring, tracheal tug, mild subcostal recession; bilateral crackles and wheeze; perfusion warm
data_table.Investigations: CXR not performed; viral PCR pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial respiratory support?

options.text: Heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min as the initial form of respiratory support.
Nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min titrated to maintain SpO2 at or above 90 percent.
Continuous positive airway pressure via a tight-fitting mask set initially at 7 cmH2O of pressure.
Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg via face mask repeated every 20 minutes for three doses.
Nebulised hypertonic 3 percent saline given with nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000.

stem: A 4-day-old term male (born at 40+2 weeks, birth weight 3.4 kg) is brought to the general practice for review because his mother thinks he is more yellow than yesterday. He is exclusively breastfed, latching well, with about 6 heavy wet nappies per day and yellow seedy stool. He is alert and not floppy. Jaundice is visible to his chest but not below the umbilicus. Maternal blood group is O Rh-positive; baby cord blood direct antiglobulin test was negative. He has no risk factors for severe hyperbilirubinaemia. Total serum bilirubin at 96 hours is 305 micromol/L with a direct fraction of 8 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138/min, respiratory rate 42/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9°C, weight 3.32 kg (2.4 percent below birth weight)
data_table.Examination: Alert; jaundice extends to chest but not below umbilicus; no hepatosplenomegaly; tone normal
data_table.Investigations: TSB 305 micromol/L; direct 8 micromol/L; phototherapy threshold for this risk profile at 96 hours is 350 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intensive phototherapy in hospital and recheck the bilirubin level after 6 hours.
Stop breastfeeding for 24 hours and switch to formula to reduce enterohepatic recirculation.
Give intravenous immunoglobulin while preparing the team for a double-volume exchange transfusion.
Continue established breastfeeding, reassure the mother, and repeat the bilirubin in 24 hours.
Send urgent G6PD assay and commence empirical IV ampicillin and gentamicin pending blood cultures.

stem: A 3-year-old boy weighing 14 kg presents to a regional emergency department with 14 hours of fever and an evolving non-blanching purpuric rash on his trunk and lower limbs. He is rousable but increasingly irritable. He looks mottled with cool peripheries. Two attempts at peripheral intravenous access by experienced staff have failed; an intraosseous kit is open and on the trolley. The on-call paediatric retrieval team has been notified.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 175/min, blood pressure 78/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 42/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 39.8°C
data_table.Examination: Rousable but irritable, capillary refill 5 seconds, mottled skin, spreading purpura on trunk; no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.22, lactate 5.6 mmol/L; bedside glucose 3.4 mmol/L; blood culture bottles primed

lead_in: What is the correct order of the next four interventions over the next 15 minutes?

options.text: Intraosseous access, 20 mL/kg saline bolus, blood cultures, then IV ceftriaxone afterwards.
Intraosseous access, IV ceftriaxone, 20 mL/kg saline bolus, then adrenaline infusion 0.1 mcg/kg/min.
Blood cultures peripherally, then IV ceftriaxone, then 20 mL/kg saline, intraosseous as backup.
Saline bolus 20 mL/kg via IO, blood cultures, IV ceftriaxone, then commence noradrenaline infusion.
Intraosseous access, blood cultures drawn, IV ceftriaxone given, then 20 mL/kg saline bolus.

stem:
A 9-year-old girl weighing 28 kg is in the paediatric high-dependency unit at hour 6 of a new-presentation diabetic ketoacidosis pathway. She received a 10 mL/kg saline bolus on arrival and is now on maintenance 0.9% saline with potassium and an insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hr. Initial pH was 6.92 with glucose 38 mmol/L and ketones 5.8 mmol/L; current glucose is 19 mmol/L. Over the last 30 minutes her mother says she became hard to rouse and complained of a headache.

On re-examination she opens her eyes to voice, says inappropriate words, and localises to pain. Her left pupil is 5 mm and sluggish; the right is 3 mm and reactive. The bedside nurse has just rechecked her observations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 70/min (down from 120/min an hour ago), blood pressure 138/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5); left pupil 5 mm sluggish, right pupil 3 mm reactive; chest clear; perfusion adequate
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.12; glucose 19 mmol/L; sodium 138, potassium 3.6, ketones 4.2 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: 0.9% saline 75 mL/hr with KCl 40 mmol/L; insulin infusion 0.05 units/kg/hr

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Give 3 percent hypertonic saline 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes and reduce maintenance fluid rate by one third.
Intubate and hyperventilate to PaCO2 25 mmHg until a CT brain has confirmed cerebral oedema.
Give mannitol 1 g/kg intravenously over 10 minutes and continue current fluid and insulin rates.
Stop the insulin infusion, give 2 mL/kg of 10 percent dextrose intravenously, and recheck the glucose level.
Give a 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus while arranging an urgent CT brain to exclude haemorrhage.

stem:
A 5-week-old first-born male presents with a 6-day history of vomiting that started as small post-feed possets and has become forceful after every feed over the last 48 hours. His mother describes the vomit as just looking like milk. He has been feeding hungrily between vomits. Today she noted his nappies are noticeably less wet. On a test feed in ED, a 1.5 cm firm mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant of his abdomen.

Blood results are now back from the ED point-of-care analyser and he is awaiting a paediatric surgical opinion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 165/min, blood pressure 78/45 mmHg, respiratory rate 38/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Sunken anterior fontanelle, dry mucous membranes; abdomen soft with palpable RUQ mass during test feed; visible gastric peristalsis
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 134 mmol/L; potassium 3.0 mmol/L; chloride 90 mmol/L; bicarbonate 32 mmol/L; pH 7.51; glucose 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Proceed directly to pyloromyotomy after a single 20 mL/kg saline bolus is delivered in the emergency department.
Trial a three day course of oral erythromycin ethylsuccinate 12.5 mg/kg given four times daily.
Commence 0.9 percent saline with added potassium and refer the infant for definitive surgical repair.
Recommend thickened feeds with ranitidine 1 mg/kg given three times daily and outpatient review next week.
Arrange an upper gastrointestinal contrast study before any fluid resuscitation to confirm the diagnosis.

stem:
An 8-day-old, previously well term breastfed male becomes acutely unwell at home with three vomits in the last 4 hours that his mother describes as bright green. He has not had a wet nappy in the last 6 hours and has not opened his bowels today. On arrival to the emergency department he is mottled, sleepy but rousable, and grunting intermittently. His abdomen is soft but slightly distended with reduced bowel sounds and no palpable mass.

Intravenous access has been secured and bloods are being processed; the surgical registrar has been paged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 180/min, blood pressure 65/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 50/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.4°C
data_table.Examination: Mottled, sleepy but rousable; capillary refill 4 seconds; abdomen soft, slightly distended; no palpable mass or hernia
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.27, lactate 3.8 mmol/L; bedside glucose 3.6 mmol/L; bloods pending

lead_in: After initial resuscitation, what is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Erect abdominal radiograph plus a left lateral decubitus film to look for free intra-abdominal air.
Ultrasound of the abdomen looking for the target sign of an ileocolic intussusception.
Stool culture with rotavirus PCR together with rehydration and observation in the short stay unit.
Upper gastrointestinal contrast study after a 10 mL/kg saline bolus and ongoing maintenance fluid.
Per rectal contrast enema to look for meconium ileus or another distal bowel obstruction.

subtopic_detail: Fever of three days with only two clinical criteria and no diagnostic threshold reached
stem: A previously well 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with three days of fever. He is alert, playing in the cubicle and drinking normally.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.9, HR 138, RR 28, BP 94/56, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis; polymorphous trunk rash; no mucosal, limb or node changes
data_table.Investigations: CRP 42 mg/L, platelets 310 x10^9/L, albumin 36 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange clinical review in 48 hours with repeat inflammatory markers
Admit now for intravenous immunoglobulin and high-dose aspirin
Start oral amoxicillin and review him in the community in a week
Arrange urgent echocardiography today and admit him under the cardiology team
Discharge with antipyretic advice and no planned medical review

stem: A four-month-old has been on humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with FiO2 0.40 for four hours for RSV bronchiolitis. Mother says he breastfed only briefly before tiring. On examination there is marked substernal recession, head bob, and audible grunting. Capillary blood gas: pH 7.28, pCO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation with no focal consolidation. The paediatric retrieval team has been contacted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178, BP 78/45 mmHg, RR 68, SpO2 89%, temperature 37.9°C
data_table.Examination: Substernal recession, head bob, grunting, lethargic but rousable
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.28, pCO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L; chest X-ray hyperinflated, no focal consolidation
data_table.Medications: Humidified HFNC 2 L/kg/min, FiO2 0.40 for 4 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Initiate CPAP at 6 cm H2O via retrieval team prior to PICU transfer
Endotracheal intubation and conventional ventilation immediately
Increase HFNC flow to 3 L/kg/min and reassess after one hour
Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with hypertonic saline 3% nebuliser
IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg empirically for bacterial co-infection

stem: A five-week-old boy presents with two weeks of forceful non-bilious vomiting after every feed. Mother describes the vomiting as 'shooting across the cot'. He looks sunken-eyed and his nappies have been very dry. Ultrasound shows pyloric muscle thickness 4.5 mm and channel length 18 mm. Surgical team plans pyloromyotomy. Venous gas: pH 7.52, pCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3 36 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 2.9 mmol/L, chloride 88 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168, BP 82/48 mmHg, RR 38, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Sunken anterior fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, weight 3.8 kg (was 4.4 kg)
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.52, pCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3 36 mmol/L, Na 132, K 2.9, Cl 88 mmol/L; ultrasound pylorus 4.5 mm thick, channel 18 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Resuscitate with 0.45% saline plus 5% dextrose plus 20 mmol/L KCl
Correct alkalosis and electrolytes with 0.9% saline plus 20 mmol/L KCl before theatre
Proceed directly to pyloromyotomy after one 20 mL/kg saline bolus
Start IV omeprazole and nasogastric feeding to bypass the pylorus
Give 4% albumin 20 mL/kg bolus then transfer urgently for theatre

subtopic_detail: Corticosteroid route in acute asthma after vomiting
stem: A 5-year-old girl with a moderate asthma exacerbation vomits her oral prednisolone twice, each time within 10 minutes of the dose. She has had salbutamol 6 puffs by spacer three times and remains wheezy. She weighs 18 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140, RR 32, SpO2 94 percent in room air
data_table.Examination: Speaking in short phrases, subcostal recession, widespread wheeze

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid now?

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 milligram per kilogram
Repeat oral prednisolone 1 milligram per kilogram
Nebulised budesonide 1 milligram with the next salbutamol
Intramuscular dexamethasone 0.6 milligrams per kilogram
Oral dexamethasone 0.6 milligrams per kilogram wafer

stem: A nine-week-old presents to ED with father who reports the baby 'rolled off the change table' onto carpet 90 minutes ago. The baby has not yet rolled developmentally and was 'a bit floppy' afterwards but is now feeding. Examination shows a torn upper lip frenulum, a 2 cm boggy left parietal swelling, and three small round bruises on the left cheek and right upper arm. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral pre-retinal haemorrhages. CT brain shows a thin left subdural haematoma and an associated parietal skull fracture. The father is distressed and asks to leave with the baby to return tomorrow.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158, BP 78/46 mmHg, RR 42, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Torn upper lip frenulum, left parietal boggy swelling 2 cm, three small round bruises (cheek and right upper arm), AF soft and flat
data_table.Investigations: CT brain: thin left subdural haematoma plus parietal skull fracture; bilateral pre-retinal haemorrhages on fundoscopy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Discharge home with parents after social work phone follow-up tomorrow
Arrange outpatient MRI brain and request a coagulation screen as priority
Allow father to leave with the baby pending paediatric review next week
Admit, notify child protection services, and complete a skeletal survey
Order a metabolic bone disease workup to exclude osteogenesis imperfecta

stem: A previously well 19-month-old has a single 90-second generalised tonic-clonic seizure during a febrile URTI. By the time you assess her she is alert, interactive, and feeding normally. She has no focal neurological signs and her anterior fontanelle is closed. Her older brother had two febrile seizures at two years of age. There is no family history of epilepsy. The mother asks whether her daughter needs admission, anti-seizure medication, or imaging.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 99%, temperature 39.1°C
data_table.Examination: Alert, no neck stiffness, no rash, ENT mildly inflamed tympanic membranes bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition and counselling?

options.text: Admit overnight and start prophylactic oral diazepam for the next febrile illness
Arrange outpatient EEG and brain MRI before allowing return home
Admit for 24 hours of paracetamol every 4 hours to prevent further fever spikes
Perform a lumbar puncture before any decision is taken on disposition
Discharge with parental advice on first aid and risk of one-in-three recurrence

stem: A 14-year-old presents with three weeks of fatigue, scleral icterus, and new tremor that the school noticed in handwriting class. She has not been on any new medications and there is no travel or paracetamol exposure. Her mother died of liver failure at 38. On examination she has hepatomegaly, dysarthria, and dark coloured urine. Bloods: haemoglobin 84 g/L (115-155), reticulocytes 6%, bilirubin 78 micromol/L (5-20), ALT 220 U/L (5-40), AST 290 U/L, ALP only 32 U/L (115-300), INR 1.6, ceruloplasmin 0.07 g/L (0.20-0.60), direct antiglobulin test negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 112/64 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Scleral icterus, hepatomegaly 3 cm, dysarthria, intention tremor on finger-nose; Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit lamp
data_table.Investigations: Hb 84 g/L, retics 6%, bilirubin 78 micromol/L, ALT 220 U/L, AST 290 U/L, ALP 32 U/L, INR 1.6, ceruloplasmin 0.07 g/L, DAT negative, 24-hour urinary copper pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Perform 24-hour urinary copper and arrange urgent percutaneous liver biopsy
Send peripheral blood film and direct antiglobulin testing for cold agglutinins
Repeat full blood count and reticulocyte count in 72 hours to confirm trend
Order MRI brain with susceptibility imaging for basal ganglia copper deposits
Send paracetamol level, alpha-1 antitrypsin, and autoimmune hepatitis panel

stem: A six-year-old boy presents with two days of refusal to weight bear on his right leg following a viral URTI last week. He has had a low-grade fever overnight. He holds the right hip flexed, abducted, and externally rotated, and resists log-roll on the right. Pulse rate 116, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99%, temperature 38.7°C. Bloods: WCC 14.5 x10^9/L, CRP 64 mg/L, ESR 48 mm/hr. Ultrasound shows a moderate right hip joint effusion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 99%, temperature 38.7°C
data_table.Examination: Right hip held in flexion, abduction, external rotation; refuses weight bearing; log-roll resisted
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.5 x10^9/L, neutrophils 11.0, CRP 64 mg/L, ESR 48 mm/hr; ultrasound right hip moderate effusion; blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with rest and ibuprofen and review in 48 hours for transient synovitis
Refer for theatre aspiration and washout with IV flucloxacillin after cultures
Arrange MRI hip with contrast before any decision on aspiration is taken
Admit for serial examination and repeat inflammatory markers in 24 hours
Start oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg q6h and arrange outpatient orthopaedic review

stem:
A 7-year-old (weight 26 kg) presents with two days of polyuria, weight loss, and vomiting today. Mother reports rapid deep breathing for six hours. He responds to voice and is orientated but mildly drowsy. He has not received any insulin previously. Capillary glucose is 28 mmol/L (3.5-7.8 fasting), venous pH 7.10, HCO3 8 mmol/L (22-32), ketones 5.6 mmol/L. Sodium is 134 mmol/L (135-145) and potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0). He is alert but lethargic with capillary refill 3 seconds and dry mucous membranes. He weighs 26 kg.

The registrar is preparing the first hour of management.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 98/60 mmHg, RR 38, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, Kussmaul breathing, capillary refill 3 seconds, dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 28 mmol/L, venous pH 7.10, HCO3 8 mmol/L, ketones 5.6 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-hour fluid plan?

options.text: 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus, then maintenance plus deficit over 48 hours
20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus over 15 minutes, repeated to 60 mL/kg if needed
Commence IV insulin 0.1 unit/kg/hour immediately before any fluid resuscitation
8.4% sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 30 minutes to correct acidosis
0.45% sodium chloride 5 mL/kg/hour with no initial bolus and no potassium

stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought in because he started coughing and choking suddenly two days ago while eating peanuts. The episode settled within a minute and he resumed playing. Since then his parents have noticed intermittent cough and some breathlessness on running. He has no fever. On auscultation there is reduced air entry over the left lower zone and a localised expiratory wheeze on the left only. Chest X-ray with expiratory phase shows left-sided hyperinflation that does not deflate.

He is comfortable at rest with no stridor.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 110, BP 96/62 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 97%, temperature 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Reduced left lower zone air entry, localised left expiratory wheeze, no stridor
data_table.Investigations: Chest X-ray: left-sided hyperinflation persisting on expiratory film, mediastinal shift to the right on expiration

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent rigid bronchoscopy in theatre with paediatric ENT and anaesthetics
Trial of inhaled salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer and reassess in one hour
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg for five days and review in clinic
Five back blows then five chest thrusts performed in the emergency department
Discharge with safety netting and review in 48 hours by general practice

stem:
A 3-year-old girl was admitted three days ago with confirmed Kawasaki disease (fever for six days, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, right cervical lymphadenopathy 1.8 cm, and peripheral oedema). She received IVIG 2 g/kg over 12 hours plus aspirin 30 mg/kg/day on day 2 of admission. Her fever defervesced within 24 hours of IVIG. Today, 48 hours after the IVIG infusion completed, she has a temperature of 39.1°C, irritability, and recurrence of conjunctivitis. CRP has risen from 35 to 168 mg/L (0-5). The echocardiogram shows normal coronary arteries.

The paediatric cardiology team has been called.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 96/56 mmHg, RR 30, SpO2 98%, temperature 39.1°C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, irritable
data_table.Investigations: CRP 168 mg/L (rose from 35), ESR 78 mm/h, WCC 18.4 x10^9/L, platelets 612 x10^9/L; echocardiogram coronary arteries normal
data_table.Medications: IVIG 2 g/kg completed 48 h ago; aspirin 30 mg/kg/day

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Second IVIG 2 g/kg infusion over 12 hours plus continued aspirin
Switch aspirin to clopidogrel and observe without further immunotherapy
Initiate infliximab 5 mg/kg as first-line second therapy
Empiric IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg for occult bacterial co-infection
Cease aspirin and start oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day monotherapy

stem:
A 14-month-old boy presents with eight hours of intermittent episodes where he suddenly starts crying, draws his legs up, and then settles. He has vomited twice but is not bilious. His mother saw dark red jelly-like material in his nappy this morning. On examination he is pale, mottled, with capillary refill 4 seconds and a palpable long thin lump in his right upper tummy. Ultrasound confirms an ileocolic target sign. Venous lactate is 4.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.0) and pH 7.31.

IV access has been obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168, BP 78/42 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.4°C
data_table.Examination: Pale, mottled, capillary refill 4 seconds, palpable right upper quadrant mass, dark red jelly stool
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: ileocolic target sign; lactate 4.2 mmol/L; pH 7.31

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus and urgent surgical reduction in theatre
Proceed directly to air enema reduction under fluoroscopy
Trial of oral rehydration with frequent small volumes and observe four hours
Insert nasogastric tube and admit for serial abdominal examinations
Glycerol suppository to assist spontaneous reduction with bowel evacuation

subtopic_detail: ALL presentation with tumour lysis prevention
stem:
A 5-year-old presents with three weeks of fatigue, bruising, and bilateral knee pain. His mother noted pallor. On examination he has petechiae, hepatomegaly 3 cm and splenomegaly 4 cm below the costal margin. The full blood count shows haemoglobin 64 g/L (115-155), white cells 96 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0) with 84% blasts on film, and platelets 24 x10^9/L (150-450). Urate is 0.62 mmol/L (0.20-0.42), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), phosphate 2.1 mmol/L (1.2-1.8), and creatinine 56 micromol/L (30-50). Lactate dehydrogenase is 4800 U/L.

The paediatric haematology team is en route.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 99%, temperature 37.5°C
data_table.Examination: Pallor, petechiae, hepatomegaly 3 cm, splenomegaly 4 cm
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 64 g/L, white cells 96 x10^9/L (84% blasts), platelets 24 x10^9/L, urate 0.62 mmol/L, potassium 5.4 mmol/L, phosphate 2.1 mmol/L, creatinine 56 micromol/L, LDH 4800 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line tumour lysis prevention?

options.text: IV hyperhydration 3 L/m^2/day without potassium and rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg
Allopurinol 10 mg/kg/day orally with normal maintenance fluids
IV sodium bicarbonate infusion targeting urine pH 7.5 plus allopurinol
Furosemide 1 mg/kg IV every 6 hours to force diuresis with normal saline
Withhold all fluids and chemotherapy until urate normalises spontaneously

subtopic_detail: Urea cycle disorder vs Reye in encephalopathy
stem:
A previously well 3-year-old presents with three days of vomiting after a viral illness, now confused and agitated with intermittent posturing. He has received paracetamol 15 mg/kg every six hours but no aspirin or other medications. Glucose is 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-7.8). Liver function shows ALT 220 U/L (0-40), AST 240 U/L (0-40), bilirubin 12 micromol/L (3-21), INR 1.2 (0.9-1.2). Ammonia is 380 micromol/L (less than 50). Venous gas shows pH 7.51, pCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L. Lactate is 1.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.0). Urine ketones are negative.

Metabolic and intensive care teams have been notified.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 99%, temperature 37.0°C
data_table.Examination: Confused, intermittent decorticate posturing, no rash, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Ammonia 380 micromol/L, ALT 220 U/L, AST 240 U/L, bilirubin 12 micromol/L, INR 1.2, glucose 4.6 mmol/L, venous pH 7.51, pCO2 28 mmHg, lactate 1.8 mmol/L, urine ketones negative
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg six-hourly for three days

lead_in: Which is the most likely underlying disorder?

options.text: Late-onset ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency
Reye syndrome related to viral illness and aspirin exposure
Paracetamol-induced acute fulminant liver failure
Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency
Acute viral hepatitis A with hepatic encephalopathy

stem:
A 7-month-old presents in early winter on day 3 of coryza followed by cough, wheeze and poor feeding. He has had no apnoeas. His mother says he is taking about half his usual feeds and is drowsier than usual but still rousable. He is on no regular medications and has no significant past history.

Nasopharyngeal aspirate is positive for RSV. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation without focal consolidation. He has just been transferred to the paediatric ward.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 160, BP 88/54 mmHg, RR 62, SpO2 89% in room air, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Mild intercostal recession, scattered fine inspiratory crackles, no grunting, alert when handled
data_table.Investigations: RSV positive, chest X-ray hyperinflation only, capillary blood gas pH 7.38 pCO2 42 mmHg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial respiratory support?

options.text: Trial of nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with reassessment in 20 minutes
Heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min as first-line support
Continuous positive airway pressure via paediatric mask at 6 cmH2O
Low-flow oxygen via nasal prongs at 1-2 L/min titrated to SpO2 ≥90%
Nebulised hypertonic saline 3% every 6 hours for airway clearance

stem:
A previously well 4-year-old girl is at a birthday party. About 10 minutes after eating a slice of cake she develops urticaria over her trunk and limbs and starts to cough. Her father, who is a paramedic, places her on the floor and notes her colour and breathing are worsening. He has called an ambulance and is on the phone to you.

Her weight at her last GP visit was 18 kg. She has no known regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 150, BP not measured (no cuff), RR 40 with audible wheeze, SpO2 not measured, temperature not measured
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria, perioral swelling, wheeze on auscultation, no stridor, alert and crying
data_table.Investigations: Bedside only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first dose of intramuscular adrenaline?

options.text: Adrenaline 1:10 000 0.18 mg IV (180 mcg) over 5 minutes by ambulance
Adrenaline 1:1000 0.30 mg IM (300 mcg) to the mid-anterolateral thigh
Adrenaline 1:1000 0.15 mg IM (150 mcg) to the mid-anterolateral thigh
Adrenaline 1:1000 0.18 mg IM (180 mcg) by calculated mg/kg arithmetic
Adrenaline 1:1000 0.15 mg IM (150 mcg) into the deltoid muscle

stem:
A 5-week-old boy is brought in by his mother who says he has been more sleepy than usual and is feeding poorly today. She last fed him 6 hours ago and he took only a few sucks. His older sister had a cold last week. He was born at term by normal vaginal delivery without complications, and has been gaining weight along the 50th centile.

On arrival to the emergency department he is irritable when handled but settles in mother's arms. There is no rash. He has had no recent overseas travel.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 180, BP 78/46 mmHg, RR 56, SpO2 97% in air, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Anterior fontanelle soft and flat, mildly irritable but consolable, capillary refill 3 seconds, no rash, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 4.2 mmol/L, urinalysis pending, FBC and blood cultures not yet drawn

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urine, FBC and blood cultures only, then admit for observation off antibiotics
Full septic workup including lumbar puncture, then empirical IV cefotaxime
Trial of oral fluids and discharge to GP review in 24 hours if improved
Intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg and reassess in 12 hours at the GP
Computed tomography of the head before any lumbar puncture

stem:
A 2-year-old girl presents with a 2-day history of watery diarrhoea and intermittent vomiting. Her mother estimates she has had around 10 loose stools and 5 vomits in 24 hours, and she has not tolerated oral rehydration solution at home because she vomits within minutes of each cup. Her urine output is reduced - she has had only one wet nappy this morning. She weighs 13 kg.

She has no other significant past history and has had no overseas travel.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 150, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 30, SpO2 99% in air, temperature 37.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, capillary refill 2 seconds, abdomen soft non-tender, alert and irritable but consolable
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 4.6 mmol/L, ketones 1.2 mmol/L, no electrolytes drawn yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Single oral ondansetron 4 mg, then oral cup-by-cup rehydration for 4 hours
Intravenous 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus then ongoing IV maintenance fluids
Continue oral rehydration solution at home and review with GP in 12 hours
Single oral ondansetron 2 mg, then nasogastric ORS at 25 mL/kg/h for 4 hours
Loperamide single oral dose with oral rehydration solution given by syringe

stem:
A 4-year-old boy with no past medical history is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with a 12-hour history of fever and lethargy. His parents say he 'just wants to lie on the couch' and has not opened his eyes for them for the last hour. There is no rash. He weighs approximately 17 kg.

On arrival he is mottled to the knees, peripherally cool, and only briefly opens his eyes to painful stimuli. You have a paediatric registrar and a senior nurse with you, and have just called the consultant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 180, BP 78/40 mmHg, RR 44, SpO2 96% in air, temperature 39.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Mottled lower limbs, capillary refill 5 seconds, no rash, chest clear, abdomen soft, GCS 12
data_table.Investigations: Capillary lactate 4.8 mmol/L, capillary glucose 4.4 mmol/L, no other results yet

lead_in: After confirming IV access and drawing blood cultures, what is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Start IV peripheral adrenaline infusion at 0.1 mcg/kg/min before any fluid bolus
IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg, then 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus over 5-10 minutes
Administer IV dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as the first medication for septic shock
Give 40 mL/kg colloid (4% albumin) over 30 minutes before any antibiotic
Place a central venous line before any fluid or antibiotic administration

stem:
An 18-month-old girl had her first episode of urinary tract infection 5 days ago. Her urine culture grew Escherichia coli sensitive to cefalexin. She defervesced within 24 hours of starting oral cefalexin and finished her course yesterday. She is otherwise well, fully immunised, and was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy with antenatal scans documenting normal renal tracts.

She is meeting all developmental milestones. The family asks the practice nurse about follow-up imaging and you are asked to advise.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 110, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 100% in air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Well-grown along the 50th centile, abdomen soft non-tender, no palpable mass, genitalia normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine culture E. coli sensitive to cefalexin, FBC and UEC within normal limits, no abnormal antenatal renal scans

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for renal-tract imaging?

options.text: No routine imaging now; re-image only if a further UTI or atypical features develop
Renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks for all children under 2 with a first UTI
DMSA scan at 6 months to detect cortical scarring after the first febrile UTI
Micturating cystourethrogram now to exclude vesicoureteric reflux scarring
Indirect cystography with technetium tracer to look at reflux without catheterisation

subtopic_detail: DKA fluid plan with cerebral oedema risk
stem:
A 9-year-old girl with no past history presents with 2 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, and 24 hours of vomiting and headache. Her parents say she has been increasingly drowsy on the drive in and has not been able to give clear answers to their questions. She weighs 30 kg.

Venous blood gas shows pH 7.05, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L. Capillary glucose is 32 mmol/L and capillary ketones are 6.2 mmol/L. Sodium (corrected for glucose) is 140 mmol/L. Her GCS is 12 (E3 V4 M5). Pupils are equal and reactive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140, BP 110/70 mmHg, RR 36 Kussmaul, SpO2 99% in air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, drowsy but rousable, fundoscopy not yet performed, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.05, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L (22-32), glucose 32 mmol/L, ketones 6.2 mmol/L, corrected sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid and insulin plan?

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 1 hour to correct acidosis before any fluid bolus
20 mL/kg saline bolus repeated to 60 mL/kg, then immediate insulin at 0.1 units/kg/h
10 mL/kg saline once, deficit plus maintenance over 48 hours, insulin 0.05 units/kg/h after 1 hour
Subcutaneous insulin glargine 0.3 units/kg plus oral rehydration with sugar-free fluids
Immediate intubation, hyperventilation to pCO2 30 mmHg, plus 3% saline 5 mL/kg bolus

subtopic_detail: Pertussis with apnoea in young infant
stem:
A 4-week-old girl is brought in by her mother on day 7 of what was initially a coryzal illness. Today she has had three coughing fits, each ending with brief cyanosis and a 10 to 15 second pause in breathing that resolved with stimulation. Between fits she has fed about half her usual volume and appears alert. Her mother had several weeks of a paroxysmal night cough that has since settled; she received Boostrix at 26 weeks gestation. The infant has had no fever and no vomiting between coughing fits.

She is now in the resuscitation cubicle on continuous monitoring.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 162, BP 78/52 mmHg, RR 56, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Pink and alert between fits, mild bilateral fine crackles, no recessions or grunting, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 28 x10^9/L (5-19), lymphocytes 70%, neutrophils 18%; CRP 6 mg/L (<5); chest X-ray non-specific peribronchial markings; NPA PCR pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and reassess respiratory effort in 20 minutes
Admit and start oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily on cardiorespiratory monitoring
Admit for low-flow oxygen 1 L/min via nasal prongs without antibiotics
Commence cefotaxime 50 mg/kg intravenously and perform a lumbar puncture
Arrange discharge home with red-flag advice and review in 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Moderate croup steroid dose and disposition
stem:
A 2-year-old presents at 2300 with a 1-day barking cough and stridor that is now audible at rest. His mother says he sounded "like a dog" all evening and is now "breathing harder". He is alert, engages with his parents, and tolerates examination.

He has been previously well and is fully immunised.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 142, BP 96/62 mmHg, RR 38, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 38.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Audible inspiratory stridor at rest, moderate intercostal recession, no cyanosis, soft barking cough, no drool, no tripod posture
data_table.Investigations: Nil performed

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management plan in ED?

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 plus dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg, observe 3 hours
Intramuscular dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg with admission to short-stay unit
Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally with admission and 4-hourly review
Humidified air via face mask and reassess respiratory effort in 30 minutes
Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally, observe 30 minutes, then plan disposition

subtopic_detail: Severe paediatric asthma escalation past back-to-back salbutamol
stem:
A 12-year-old girl with known asthma is brought to ED at 0200 by her parents. She has had a viral coryza for 3 days and a worsening cough; she used her salbutamol inhaler eight times over the past 6 hours with limited relief. Her usual preventer is fluticasone 100 micrograms twice daily but she has been non-adherent. She has previously had one ICU admission for asthma at age 9.

She has been given continuous nebulised salbutamol 10 mg, nebulised ipratropium 250 micrograms three times, and a single dose of oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg in the last hour. She remains in significant distress and is now sitting forward in tripod posture and answering only in single words. The senior decision-maker has reviewed her in person.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 152, BP 132/76 mmHg, RR 38, SpO2 91% on 8 L/min via Hudson mask, temperature 37.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Tripod posture, marked intercostal and subcostal recession, widespread polyphonic wheeze with prolonged expiratory phase, mild drowsiness on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.30, pCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L, lactate 3.2; peak flow not obtainable
data_table.Medications: Continuous nebulised salbutamol, nebulised ipratropium, oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg given 1 hour ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate rapid sequence intubation with ketamine and rocuronium
Loading dose intravenous aminophylline 5 mg/kg over 60 minutes
Nebulised hypertonic saline 7% and chest physiotherapy
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes
Intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg into the lateral thigh

stem: A 6-year-old girl with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, on day 12 post-induction chemotherapy, presents with a single temperature of 38.4 °C recorded by her parents 90 minutes ago. She has had no rigors, no localising symptoms, and no antibiotics in the last 7 days. She has a tunnelled central venous catheter that looks clean and non-tender. Her oncology unit has a written febrile neutropenia pathway and the on-call oncologist has been notified.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 102/68 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 38.1 °C on arrival
data_table.Examination: Pale but well-perfused, capillary refill 2 seconds, no mucositis, central line site clean, no rash, chest clear, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: FBC neutrophils 0.3 x10^9/L (1.5-8.0), Hb 92 g/L (115-160), platelets 88 x10^9/L (150-400); CRP 28 mg/L (<5); urinalysis nil; blood cultures from line and peripherally just drawn
data_table.Medications: Tunnelled CVC, on maintenance phase intravenous chemotherapy due in 7 days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Wait for repeat temperature to confirm a true fever before starting antibiotics
Give oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and ciprofloxacin and discharge for outpatient follow-up
Withhold antibiotics pending the chest X-ray result and abdominal examination by the oncology registrar
Commence intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg as soon as the cultures have been taken
Add intravenous vancomycin to piperacillin-tazobactam empirically due to the central line

subtopic_detail: Intussusception lay-language presentation and air enema vs surgery
stem:
An 11-month-old previously well boy is brought in by his mother. Over the past 6 hours she describes him as repeatedly "starting to cry, drawing both his legs up, then settling for 20 minutes" before another episode begins. Earlier today he passed a stool that she describes as "slimy and dark, a bit like jelly". He has vomited twice; the most recent vomit looked yellow-green. He has had no fever and no diarrhoea.

He was alert on triage and is now sleepy between episodes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158, BP 88/56 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Pale, capillary refill 2.5 seconds, soft abdomen with a vague long thin lump felt in the right upper quadrant, normal genitalia, no peritonism, no abdominal distension
data_table.Investigations: FBC unremarkable; UEC normal; abdominal ultrasound just performed shows a target-sign lesion in the right upper quadrant with peristalsis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Observe for 4 hours and reassess if any new symptoms develop
Proceed to air enema reduction under fluoroscopy after fluid resuscitation
Give barium contrast enema for both diagnosis and therapeutic reduction
Give a single dose of nasogastric polyethylene glycol and reassess in 6 hours
Proceed straight to laparotomy and manual reduction after induction

subtopic_detail: First UTI in infant under 6 months - RCH imaging cascade
stem:
A 4-month-old boy is admitted with his first urinary tract infection. Suprapubic-aspirate culture grows Escherichia coli 100 sensitive to oral cefalexin. He responded clinically to 48 hours of IV gentamicin and benzylpenicillin and is now afebrile, feeding well, and ready to transition to oral antibiotics for 7 days total.

He was born at term with no antenatal renal abnormalities documented on the routine 20-week scan. He has had no other infections.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 78/52 mmHg, RR 34, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Active, well-hydrated, abdomen soft, no flank tenderness, normal genitalia, circumcised
data_table.Investigations: Suprapubic urine culture: E. coli >10^8 CFU/L, sensitive to cefalexin; UEC normal; inflammatory markers improving
data_table.Medications: IV gentamicin and benzylpenicillin (last dose 6 hours ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate post-discharge imaging plan?

options.text: Renal ultrasound during the current inpatient admission
No imaging - documented antenatal scan is sufficient
DMSA scan in 4 to 6 months to assess for renal scarring
Repeat urine microscopy and culture in 1 week to confirm clearance
Micturating cystourethrogram performed before discharge

subtopic_detail: Paediatric DKA fluid plan with cerebral oedema risk
stem:
A 6-year-old girl, body weight 20 kg, presents with a 1-week history of polyuria, polydipsia and 3 kg weight loss. She vomited three times today and is now drowsy.

The paediatric registrar has confirmed new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus with DKA. She is clinically about 7% dehydrated. There has been one fluid bolus of 10 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride given over 30 minutes for poor peripheral perfusion. Her conscious state is now stable with GCS 13.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140, BP 90/60 mmHg, RR 32 (Kussmaul pattern), SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, capillary refill 3 seconds, no focal neurology, no headache
data_table.Investigations: BSL 28 mmol/L, blood ketones 5.6, VBG pH 7.10 pCO2 18 mmHg HCO3 8 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), corrected sodium 138 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next fluid and insulin plan?

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol over 30 minutes to correct the metabolic acidosis
Commence 0.9% sodium chloride at maintenance with 7% deficit over 48 hours and insulin after 1 hour
Commence 5% dextrose / 0.45% sodium chloride immediately with insulin 0.1 unit/kg/hour bolus
Start subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin 0.1 unit/kg and intravenous fluids at maintenance only
Repeat 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus then commence insulin 0.1 unit/kg/hour immediately

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease diagnosis and IVIG decision
stem:
A 14-month-old boy of Korean heritage has had 7 days of fever, peaking at 39.6 °C, unresponsive to paracetamol and ibuprofen. He is irritable but consolable. His mother reports he had a rash for 24 hours on day 3 that has now resolved and one episode of conjunctival redness without discharge that also resolved. He has had no cervical lymphadenopathy and no mucosal changes.

The paediatric registrar has reviewed and the AHA "incomplete Kawasaki" supplementary criteria have been considered. An echocardiogram has been ordered.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 39.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Irritable, mild peri-anal desquamation, no oral mucosal changes today, no cervical lymphadenopathy, no rash visible, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: WCC 19 x10^9/L (5-15), neutrophils 14 x10^9/L (1.5-8), platelets 612 x10^9/L (150-400) on day 7, CRP 156 mg/L (<5), ESR 78 mm/hr (<20), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), ALT 96 U/L (<45), Na 132 mmol/L (135-145), urinalysis 25 leukocytes/HPF with sterile culture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg for occult bacteraemia and reassess in 24 hours
Await echocardiogram and treat only if coronary artery dilatation is documented
Commence intravenous flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Commence intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse for 3 days as primary therapy
Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with high-dose aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg in four divided doses

stem:
A 15-year-old previously well girl is brought in by her parents with a 10-day history of progressive personality change. They report new agitation, paranoid statements that strangers are stealing from her, and a 4 kg weight loss. Yesterday she had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds with full recovery, and this morning she developed orofacial dyskinesias and rhythmic limb posturing. There has been no fever, no recent infection, no overseas travel, and no drug use.

The family history is unremarkable. Toxicology screen on arrival is negative. She is currently being investigated as part of a paediatric neurology workup.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Fluctuant agitation alternating with mutism, intermittent orofacial dyskinesia, mild autonomic instability with episodic BP swings, no focal weakness, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: FBC and UEC within normal limits, CRP 4 mg/L (<5), MRI brain normal, EEG generalised slowing without focal epileptiform activity, CSF protein 0.42 g/L (0.15-0.45) lymphocytes 18 x10^6/L (<5) glucose 3.6 mmol/L (paired BSL 5.2), HSV PCR negative, serum and CSF anti-NMDA receptor antibodies pending
data_table.Medications: Lorazepam 2 mg IV given for dyskinesia 1 hour ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to mental health for first-episode psychosis and start olanzapine 10 mg orally daily
Arrange routine MRI brain with contrast on the next available outpatient slot and review in clinic
Commence high-dose methylprednisolone and IVIG and arrange pelvic ultrasound for ovarian teratoma
Commence intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg three times daily and complete a 14-day course pending HSV PCR
Commence levetiracetam 60 mg/kg/day for seizure prophylaxis without other intervention

subtopic_detail: Methaemoglobinaemia in infant from topical anaesthetic
stem:
A 5-month-old boy is brought to ED 90 minutes after his mother applied a generous layer of an over-the-counter teething gel containing benzocaine to his gums every 30 minutes for the past 3 hours. She thought he was teething because of poor sleep. He has become progressively pale and dusky around the lips despite warming and looks slate-grey on inspection.

Nasal cannula oxygen at 4 L/min has not changed his appearance. He is alert.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168, BP 84/52 mmHg, RR 56, SpO2 86% on 4 L/min nasal-prong oxygen (unchanged on 8 L/min), temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Slate-grey central cyanosis, no respiratory distress beyond tachypnoea, chest clear, capillary refill 2 seconds, alert with normal tone
data_table.Investigations: Arterial blood gas pH 7.36 pCO2 36 mmHg pO2 198 mmHg on 8 L/min, lactate 1.8; co-oximetry methaemoglobin level 32% (<2%), Hb 110 g/L (95-130); chest X-ray clear
data_table.Medications: Benzocaine teething gel (frequent application in last 3 hours)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence broad-spectrum antibiotics for sepsis with cyanosis
Administer methylene blue 1 mg/kg intravenously over 5 minutes
Administer ascorbic acid 200 mg intravenously and observe
Increase oxygen to 15 L/min via non-rebreather and observe
Arrange transfusion of one unit of packed red blood cells

stem:
A 4-month-old boy is brought to the paediatric emergency department by his parents in winter with 3 days of runny nose, cough and noisy breathing. He has been feeding only half his usual volumes for 24 hours and his nappies are drier. He was born at 38 weeks and has had no previous admissions. His parents are non-smokers and he is up to date with immunisations.

He has been on nasal prong oxygen 1.5 L/min for 2 hours since arrival. The bedside nurse asks you to review him because his work of breathing has worsened over the last 20 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 72, SpO2 89% on nasal prong 1.5 L/min, temperature 37.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert but tiring, marked subcostal and intercostal recession, head bobbing, widespread fine inspiratory crackles and expiratory wheeze, capillary refill 2 seconds, no apnoeas observed
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.30, pCO2 56 mmHg, HCO3 26, lactate 1.6; nasopharyngeal viral PCR pending; chest X-ray hyperinflation with no focal consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Commence humidified high-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min
Start nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back-to-back for three doses
Give a single intramuscular dose of dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg
Intubate and commence pressure-controlled ventilation
Trial nebulised hypertonic saline 3% with chest physiotherapy

stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the paediatric emergency department at 2 am by his parents with a 12-hour history of barking cough and 2 hours of noisy breathing. He has had a coryzal illness for 3 days. He is not immunised against any disease because his parents have not yet engaged with their GP. He has no previous admissions and no known allergies.

On the way to the ambulance bay he became increasingly distressed. The triage nurse has placed him in his mother's lap in the resuscitation cubicle and called you.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 38, SpO2 93% in room air, temperature 38.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Loud biphasic stridor at rest, marked tracheal tug and intercostal recession, agitated and clinging to mother, barking cough, no drooling, no trismus, no neck swelling
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed - imaging or bloods would distress the child further

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose and discharge home after 1 hour observation
Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as monotherapy and admit for observation
Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg with concurrent nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000
Intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg empirically with airway preparation in theatre
Intubate in theatre with an anaesthetist and ENT surgeon present

stem:
A 6-week-old girl is brought to the children's hospital ED by her mother with a 9-day history of cough. She was born at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery and has been well otherwise. Her mother declined the pertussis vaccine in pregnancy. Her older brother (age 4) has had a runny nose and cough for 3 weeks.

Her cough comes in clusters and she goes red and then briefly blue with the spells, followed by exhausted feeding. Between spells she looks well. She has had two brief pauses in breathing during spells today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 144, BP 78/46 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 96% in room air between spells (drops to 88% during spells), temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Well-perfused between spells, chest clear, no recession at rest, paroxysmal coughing fits with brief facial cyanosis observed
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 32 x10^9/L with marked lymphocytosis 22 x10^9/L (1.5-8.5), CRP 6 mg/L, chest X-ray clear, nasopharyngeal PCR pertussis pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with safety-netting advice and outpatient follow-up review in 3 days
Admit for inpatient cardiorespiratory observation alone while awaiting PCR confirmation
Admit and start intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily for community-acquired pneumonia
Admit and start oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily for 5 days plus contact prophylaxis
Admit and start oral erythromycin 10 mg/kg four times daily for 7 days with monitoring

subtopic_detail: Acute otitis media in young child
stem:
A 19-month-old Aboriginal boy presents with his mother to the remote area clinic with 36 hours of ear pulling and fever to 39.0 °C. He was treated for an acute otitis media in the same ear 6 weeks ago with a 5-day course of amoxicillin. He has been drinking less but is still wetting nappies normally. He has had two previous courses of antibiotics for ear infections this year.

Today he is irritable but consolable. His mother says he has been pulling at the same ear and crying with feeds.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Right tympanic membrane bulging, opaque and erythematous with no perforation; left tympanic membrane normal; no mastoid tenderness or post-auricular swelling; alert and consolable
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Watchful waiting for 48 to 72 hours with paracetamol cover and clinical review
Oral cefuroxime 15 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days as second-line cover
Oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 3 days as second-line cover
Intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin 50 mg/kg as a single one-off dose
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days as second-line

stem:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to the paediatric outpatient clinic by her parents with an 18-month history of infrequent stools. She passes hard pebble-like stools every 4 to 6 days with abdominal pain and occasional soiling of her underwear between motions. She has tried lactulose and dietary fibre for 8 weeks without improvement. She is otherwise developmentally normal, has been growing along the 50th centile and has no red flags.

Her parents report she now actively withholds stool because passing them is painful.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen with a palpable faecal mass in the left lower quadrant; perianal inspection unremarkable; spine and lower limb neurology unremarkable; growth on the 50th centile for weight and height
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated - functional constipation is a clinical diagnosis
data_table.Medications: Lactulose 10 mL twice daily for 8 weeks (poor response)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Oral macrogol 3350 disimpaction for 3 days then maintenance dose for 6 months
Increase the lactulose dose and add senna stimulant at bedtime for 8 weeks
Refer for a contrast enema study to exclude Hirschsprung disease this week
Admit for a phosphate enema and digital rectal examination under anaesthetic
Refer to paediatric gastroenterology for anorectal manometry under sedation

stem:
A term male newborn weighing 4.6 kg (above 97th centile) is admitted to the neonatal unit on day 1 with recurrent symptomatic hypoglycaemia. He was born at 39 weeks by emergency caesarean section for failure to progress to a 32-year-old G2P1 woman whose pregnancy was complicated by gestational diabetes treated with insulin from 28 weeks. The baby developed jitteriness and a low blood glucose of 1.4 mmol/L at 90 minutes after birth, treated with feeds and IV dextrose.

He has now required escalating dextrose infusions. Despite a glucose infusion rate of 14 mg/kg/min he has had two further symptomatic episodes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 162, BP 64/38 mmHg, RR 52, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Macrosomic, mild plethora, no obvious dysmorphism, no organomegaly, no umbilical defect, tone slightly reduced when hypoglycaemic, normal between episodes; cardiac and respiratory examinations within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: BSL during episode 1.6 mmol/L (>2.6); insulin 18 mIU/L (suppressed when normoglycaemic), C-peptide elevated, beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.1 mmol/L (low), free fatty acids low, ammonia 38 micromol/L (<50), cortisol 380 nmol/L, growth hormone 14 mIU/L, lactate 1.1; karyotype 46XY pending; abdominal ultrasound and brain MRI unremarkable; ear examination normal pinnae
data_table.Medications: Intravenous 10% dextrose at 12.5 mg/kg/min glucose infusion rate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase glucose infusion rate to 18 mg/kg/min through a central venous line
Commence oral diazoxide 5 mg/kg per day in divided doses plus chlorothiazide
Start hydrocortisone 5 mg/kg per day for possibly inadequate stress cortisol
Refer urgently for partial pancreatectomy without medical trial of diazoxide
Continue current management as macrosomic infants typically resolve by 72 hours

stem:
A term male newborn becomes cyanotic in the postnatal ward at 6 hours of age. He was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal delivery to a 28-year-old G1P0 woman with no antenatal concerns; her 20-week anomaly scan was reported as normal. Apgars were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. He fed once at the breast and pinked up initially.

On nursing review for cyanosis he has central blue discolouration but is not in respiratory distress. The paediatric registrar is at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 162, BP 64/40 mmHg in right arm and 62/38 mmHg in right calf, RR 48, SpO2 65% pre-ductal (right hand) and 64% post-ductal (right foot), temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Centrally cyanosed, well perfused, no respiratory distress, single S2 with no murmur, femoral pulses palpable and equal, liver not enlarged, no facial features of trisomy 21 or DiGeorge phenotype
data_table.Investigations: Hyperoxia test SpO2 rose to 69% after 10 minutes in 100% O2 face mask; chest X-ray shows narrow superior mediastinum with "egg on side" cardiac silhouette and pulmonary plethora; ECG normal neonatal axis; capillary blood gas pH 7.32, pCO2 38, lactate 2.6

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase inspired oxygen to FiO2 1.0 by head box and reassess in 20 minutes
Intubate, ventilate and administer surfactant via the endotracheal tube immediately
Commence intravenous prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) 10 ng/kg/min and urgent echo
Administer intramuscular vitamin K plus intravenous furosemide for cardiac failure
Perform four-limb blood pressure measurement and arrange aortic CT angiogram

stem:
A 9-month-old boy is brought to the children's hospital emergency department by his mother. Over the past 18 hours he has had episodes of inconsolable crying lasting 10 to 15 minutes during which he draws his legs up to his tummy, then falls asleep exhausted between episodes. He had a single episode of redcurrant jelly nappy this morning and his mother says he has been pale and very tired. He had a runny nose a week ago.

He last fed 6 hours ago and has vomited twice. The paediatric surgical registrar has been called.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 156, BP 92/56 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 37.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Sleepy but rousable, slightly pale, soft abdomen with a palpable long thin lump in the right upper quadrant during a quiet period; no peritonism, no abdominal distension; capillary refill 2 seconds; rectal inspection shows red mucoid stool on the gloved finger
data_table.Investigations: FBC haemoglobin 108 g/L (105-135), WCC 14 x10^9/L; UEC within normal limits; venous blood gas pH 7.36, lactate 2.0; abdominal ultrasound shows a target sign in the right upper quadrant consistent with ileocolic intussusception, no free fluid, no pneumatosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial of bowel rest with intravenous fluid resuscitation and reassess in 6 hours
Proceed immediately to open laparotomy for manual reduction without enema trial
Diagnostic laparoscopy to look for a pathological lead point before reduction
Resuscitate with intravenous fluids then proceed to air enema with surgical standby
Insert nasogastric tube and give intravenous antibiotics with observation only

subtopic_detail: Acute otitis media in Aboriginal child
stem:
A 22-month-old Aboriginal girl is brought to your remote clinic by her mother with 2 days of fever and pulling at her right ear. Her mother reports she has been waking and crying at night and is feeding less. She is fully immunised, attends day care, and has had two previous similar episodes in the last six months. There is no ear discharge.

On examination she is irritable but consolable, and there is no neck stiffness or rash. The right tympanic membrane is bulging and opaque with no perforation; the left tympanic membrane appears normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Right ear: bulging opaque tympanic membrane, no discharge. Left ear normal. Throat injected without exudate. No cervical lymphadenopathy. Chest clear.
data_table.Investigations: Not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics and review in 48 hours with safety-net advice
Prescribe oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg twice daily for five days for this patient
Prescribe oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily for seven days
Refer urgently to ENT for myringotomy and grommet insertion as the proposed approach
Prescribe intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin 50 mg/kg as a single dose

stem:
An 18-month-old girl is brought to your GP clinic by her father for a routine check. He reports she is well, walks confidently and has a vocabulary of about 30 words. She has been drinking around 1 litre of cow's milk daily since 12 months and is a fussy eater who refuses red meat. She was breastfed exclusively until six months.

On examination she is pale around the mouth and conjunctivae but otherwise well, with normal growth percentiles. There is no organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or rash. Routine FBC is sent at the father's request.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 110, BP 92/56 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival pallor, no glossitis, no koilonychia, no organomegaly. Tone and tendon reflexes normal. Heart sounds dual with no murmur. Chest clear.
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (110-140), MCV 64 fL (70-86), MCH 22 pg (24-30), platelets 460 x10^9/L (150-450), white cell count 9.2 x10^9/L (5-15), reticulocytes 0.6%; ferritin pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence oral elemental iron 3 mg/kg daily, reduce cow's milk to 500 mL daily, repeat FBC in 4 weeks
Refer for upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and faecal occult blood testing as the proposed approach
Arrange haemoglobin electrophoresis and send blood film before commencing any therapy
Arrange intravenous iron carboxymaltose infusion as a single dose as the proposed approach
Recommend dietary modification alone and review with repeat FBC in 12 weeks as the proposed approach

stem:
A 7-month-old girl has been an inpatient for 30 hours with RSV bronchiolitis. She required nasal prong oxygen 1 L/min for the first 12 hours, weaning to room air overnight. She is taking 70% of her usual feed volumes by bottle, with normal wet nappies. Her parents are reliable and live a 15-minute drive from the hospital.

On morning round she is alert and playful between feeds. There is mild subcostal recession but no head bobbing, grunting or nasal flaring. Her parents ask when she can go home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 142, BP 92/54 mmHg, RR 44, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recession, scattered fine crackles bilaterally, no wheeze, hydration adequate, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Not repeated overnight

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange overnight pulse oximetry monitoring at home through community paediatric outreach
Continue inpatient observation until respiratory rate is below 40 breaths/min
Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days before discharge as the proposed approach
Discharge home now with safety-net advice and routine GP review in 1-2 days
Repeat chest X-ray and capillary blood gas before deciding on discharge

stem:
A 5-month-old boy presents to your paediatric assessment unit with 24 hours of fever to 39 °C, irritability and reduced feeds. A clean-catch urine grows pure Escherichia coli at greater than 10^8 cfu/L sensitive to all tested agents. He responds well to IV gentamicin and benzylpenicillin within 24 hours and is afebrile by hour 36. His antenatal scans were reported as normal at his birth hospital in regional NSW.

On examination today he is well-perfused, feeding fully and playful. There is no abdominal mass, no spinal anomalies, and his external genitalia are normal. Renal function and electrolytes have normalised.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, no palpable bladder, normal external genitalia, no spinal dimple or hair tuft
data_table.Investigations: Urine MC&S Escherichia coli >10^8 cfu/L pansusceptible; sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 28 micromol/L, CRP peak 88 mg/L now 22 mg/L, blood cultures negative
data_table.Medications: IV gentamicin, IV benzylpenicillin (now switching to oral cefalexin to complete 7 days)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging plan?

options.text: No imaging required as the UTI was typical with a good antibiotic response
DMSA scan in 4-6 months to assess for renal scarring as the proposed approach
Micturating cystourethrogram to exclude vesicoureteric reflux
Renal tract ultrasound during this admission as the proposed approach
Cystoscopy and posterior urethral valve assessment under urology

stem:
A 6-year-old boy is reviewed in the paediatric clinic 3 weeks after diagnosis of IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura). At diagnosis he had palpable purpura on the buttocks and lower limbs, arthralgia of the ankles, and one episode of colicky abdominal pain that settled with paracetamol. His baseline urinalysis was clear and renal function normal.

Today his rash has faded, the arthralgia has resolved, and he is back at school. On routine follow-up urinalysis he has 2+ protein and 1+ blood. His blood pressure today is 116/76 mmHg, on the 95th centile for age and height.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 116/76 mmHg (95th centile for age/height), RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Fading purpura over lower limbs, no joint swelling, no abdominal tenderness, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis protein 2+, blood 1+; urine protein:creatinine ratio 88 mg/mmol (<25); creatinine 42 micromol/L (28-66), albumin 36 g/L (35-50), urine MC&S no growth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure and continue weekly urinalysis with routine GP follow-up
Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 4 weeks as the proposed approach
Refer to paediatric nephrology for assessment within 1-2 weeks
Start oral perindopril 1 mg daily and review BP in 4 weeks
Arrange 24-hour urinary protein collection before any specialist referral

stem:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to your GP clinic by her mother with 3 weeks of perianal and vulval itch worse at night, with occasional white-yellow vaginal discharge. Her mother has noted small white worms on the perianal skin when applying nappy cream. Her 3-year-old brother has been scratching his bottom for the last week. The girl is otherwise well, fully immunised, and attends preschool.

On examination there is mild erythema around the perianal area and vulva, with a small amount of non-offensive discharge. Bedside microscopy of a perianal tape sample shows oval eggs flattened on one side.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 94/58 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Mild perianal and vulval erythema, scant non-offensive discharge, no excoriation breaks, no anal fissure, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Perianal tape: oval eggs flattened on one side. Vulval swab: mixed normal flora, no Candida, no STI organisms.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Single dose oral mebendazole 100 mg now to the girl only, with a repeat dose in 2 weeks as the proposed approach
Refer to paediatric gynaecology for assessment of vulvovaginitis and possible sexual abuse as the proposed approach
Topical clotrimazole cream twice daily to the vulva and perianal area for 7 days as the proposed approach
Single dose oral mebendazole 100 mg now and repeated at 2 weeks for all household members aged 6 months and over, with hygiene advice
Single dose oral albendazole 400 mg once with no repeat and no household treatment as the proposed approach

stem:
A 13-year-old girl with established type 1 diabetes is brought in by ambulance with 18 hours of vomiting and abdominal pain. She has been managing on a basal-bolus regimen with continuous glucose monitoring. Her usual home blood sugar logs have been stable until 3 days ago when she stopped eating and self-reduced her insulin.

In the resuscitation bay she is drowsy with Kussmaul respiration. Her abdomen is tender in the right iliac fossa with rebound and guarding. Bedside glucose 24 mmol/L, blood ketones 6.2 mmol/L. She is started on the RCH DKA pathway with 10 mL/kg saline bolus, fluid replacement, and an insulin infusion at 0.05 unit/kg/hour after 1 hour. Two hours into therapy her ketones are 4.8 mmol/L and her abdominal tenderness has not improved.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 102/68 mmHg, RR 36 Kussmaul, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 13, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, right iliac fossa tenderness with rebound and guarding, bowel sounds reduced
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 24 mmol/L, ketones 6.2 mmol/L; venous gas pH 7.10, HCO3 6 mmol/L, base deficit -22, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L; lipase 38 U/L (<60); white cell count 22 x10^9/L (5-15); abdominal ultrasound: dilated non-compressible appendix 9 mm with surrounding fluid
data_table.Medications: DKA pathway: maintenance + deficit replacement saline with KCl, insulin infusion 0.05 unit/kg/hour

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discuss urgent surgical review and theatre once initial fluid and potassium resuscitation is established, continuing the insulin infusion intraoperatively
Continue DKA pathway and reassess the abdomen once acidosis fully resolves before any surgical decision as the proposed approach
Stop the insulin infusion to allow ketones to clear before surgical review as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action
Give intravenous tramadol and morphine and trial conservative management with intravenous antibiotics alone as the proposed approach
Arrange immediate CT abdomen with contrast to confirm appendicitis before any surgical referral as the proposed approach

stem:
A 4-week-old infant presents to your emergency department with a 5-day history of progressive coughing fits. His mother describes bouts in which 'he goes red, then blue around the lips, then takes a deep noisy breath in and is exhausted'. He has fed poorly during these bouts. His sister had a cough 3 weeks ago and was told she had a viral chest infection. His mother did not receive the antenatal pertussis booster.

On examination he is afebrile and settled between paroxysms. There are bilateral subconjunctival haemorrhages and an audible inspiratory whoop is observed after one cough cluster in the department. The chest is clear on auscultation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168, BP 78/46 mmHg, RR 56 (paroxysmal bursts to 80), SpO2 nadir 84% during paroxysm and 96% at rest, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Subconjunctival haemorrhages bilaterally, inspiratory whoop, chest clear to auscultation, fontanelle soft, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Total white cell count 32 x10^9/L (5.0-19.5), lymphocyte 22 x10^9/L (3.0-9.5), CRP 6 mg/L (<5), chest X-ray clear, nasopharyngeal swab PCR pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family, give paracetamol for comfort, and discharge home with cough safety-net advice
Admit for cardiorespiratory monitoring, commence azithromycin orally for 5 days, and apply droplet precautions
Discharge on oral amoxicillin and arrange general practitioner review for an audible wheeze in 48 hours
Trial nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium and admit to the short-stay observation unit overnight
Commence empirical intravenous ceftriaxone for unrecognised early-onset neonatal bacterial sepsis

stem:
A previously well 22-month-old boy presents 90 minutes after a sudden coughing and choking episode at his grandmother's house. He had been eating a handful of peanuts on the lounge floor. His mother says 'he turned bright red, coughed for a few minutes, and now seems alright but is breathing a bit oddly'. He has no fever, no preceding cough, and no asthma history.

On examination he is alert, mildly tachypnoeic, and speaks in full short sentences. The trachea is central. There is reduced air entry over the right lower zone with a localised monophonic wheeze; the left chest is clear. A chest X-ray in inspiration looks essentially normal; expiratory and right lateral decubitus films show hyperinflation of the right lower lobe and mediastinal shift away from that side.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 38, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, no stridor, central trachea, reduced air entry right lower zone, localised monophonic right-sided wheeze, no drooling
data_table.Investigations: Inspiratory chest X-ray reported normal; expiratory and right lateral decubitus views show right lower lobe hyperinflation with mediastinal shift away from the affected side

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol and a short course of oral prednisolone, with respiratory clinic review in two weeks
Five back blows and five chest thrusts in head-down position, then admit for overnight observation
Refer urgently for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthetic for retrieval of the foreign body
Order a computed tomography scan of the chest before deciding on further airway management
Empirical oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and outpatient chest physiotherapy with review in three days

stem:
A 14-year-old boy presents to your emergency department with 2 hours of sudden severe left-sided scrotal pain that woke him at 5 am. He has vomited twice. He says 'it started straight away, not a slow build, and it hurts down to my belly button'. There is no dysuria, no urethral discharge, no recent trauma, and he denies sexual activity.

On examination he is in obvious distress. The left hemiscrotum is swollen and erythematous. The left testis is exquisitely tender, lies higher than the right, and is held horizontally. The cremasteric reflex is absent on the left and present on the right. There is no penile discharge. A bedside scrotal ultrasound is available but would take 90 minutes to arrange with formal Doppler reporting.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Left testis tender, high-riding, horizontal lie, absent cremasteric reflex; right side normal; no penile discharge; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis blood and leukocytes negative; FBC and inflammatory markers not yet returned

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed directly to surgical scrotal exploration without waiting for ultrasound imaging
Arrange formal scrotal colour Doppler ultrasound before any decision about operative exploration
Commence empirical intravenous ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline for presumed epididymo-orchitis
Attempt outward manual detorsion at the bedside as definitive treatment with discharge afterwards
