Administer intramuscular morphine and observe for 6 hours with repeat examination at intervals

stem:
A 5-day-old, term, exclusively breastfed boy is brought to the early-discharge clinic by his mother who says 'he looks more yellow today and is bringing his feeds up'. Birth weight 3.4 kg, now 3.05 kg (10% below birth weight). He was discharged at 28 hours of age with normal newborn screening swab pending and a normal transcutaneous bilirubin at 24 hours. His mother is blood group O Rhesus positive; baby's blood group is not yet known. Latch has been variable and feeds are short.

On examination he is sleepy but rousable, with jaundice extending to mid-thigh. There is no hepatosplenomegaly and the neurological exam is normal. Total serum bilirubin is 360 micromol/L with a conjugated fraction of 8 micromol/L. The phototherapy nomogram threshold for a well term infant at this postnatal age and risk profile is 340 micromol/L; the exchange transfusion threshold is 480 micromol/L. Direct antiglobulin test, baby's blood group, FBC, and reticulocyte count have been sent and remain pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, BP 72/44 mmHg, RR 44, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Visible jaundice to mid-thigh, sleepy but rousable, soft fontanelle, normal tone, no hepatosplenomegaly, mild dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bilirubin 360 micromol/L, conjugated bilirubin 8 micromol/L; phototherapy threshold 340 micromol/L; exchange threshold 480 micromol/L; DAT, blood group, FBC, reticulocyte count pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the mother, advise more frequent feeds, and review with repeat bilirubin in 24 hours
Arrange immediate exchange transfusion in a neonatal intensive care unit setting today
Discontinue breastfeeding for 48 hours and switch to a standard infant formula by bottle
Admit for intensive phototherapy and continue breastfeeding with lactation support and feed top-ups
Commence intravenous immunoglobulin empirically before the direct antiglobulin test result returns

stem:
A 6-year-old girl is reviewed in your general paediatric outpatient clinic after a 3-day history of a non-blanching rash on her buttocks and lower legs. Two days before the rash she had bilateral ankle swelling and pain. Her mother says 'she's been gripping her tummy when it cramps, but it goes off after a minute and she's eating'. There is no haematemesis, melaena, or testicular pain. She had a sore throat 10 days ago that settled without antibiotics.

On examination she is well and afebrile, with palpable purpura on the buttocks, posterior thighs, and shins. Joints are not warm and ranges are full. The abdomen is soft with mild central tenderness, no peritonism, and audible bowel sounds. Blood pressure is normal. Urinalysis shows 1+ blood and trace protein; spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 18 mg/mmol (normal <20). Renal function, FBC, and coagulation are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura buttocks and lower limbs, joints non-swollen, abdomen soft, mild central tenderness, no peritonism, no testicular involvement
data_table.Investigations: FBC and platelet count within normal limits, coagulation profile normal, creatinine 38 micromol/L, urinalysis blood 1+ trace protein, urine protein:creatinine ratio 18 mg/mmol (<20)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for intravenous methylprednisolone pulses and renal biopsy within the next 48 hours
Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for the cutaneous purpura and review in one week
Commence empirical oral amoxicillin for 10 days given the recent sore throat as a presumed trigger
Refer urgently to paediatric nephrology for an immediate inpatient renal biopsy this admission
Discharge home with analgesia, written safety-net advice, and weekly urinalysis and BP checks for 6 months

stem:
An 18-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department after a 90-second generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home. She had been febrile to 39.4 °C since waking that morning with a runny nose. The seizure stopped before paramedics arrived; she is now alert, taking fluids, and back to her usual play. Her mother says 'she had one of these six months ago when she had tonsillitis and we were told it was a febrile fit, but I'm worried it's becoming a habit'.

Family history is unremarkable; there is no family history of epilepsy. Development is age-appropriate, immunisations are up to date, and the most recent seizure description matches a typical simple febrile seizure. Neurological examination is normal. The chest is clear, tympanic membranes are pink without effusion, and the throat is mildly erythematous without exudate.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, playful, soft fontanelle closed, normal tone, brisk symmetrical reflexes, plantars downgoing, no neck stiffness, mildly erythematous oropharynx
data_table.Investigations: Bedside blood glucose 5.2 mmol/L, no other tests indicated by guideline; viral upper respiratory tract infection clinically
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg given at home 90 minutes ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management for this child and her family?

options.text: Admit for inpatient electroencephalogram and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain this admission
Discharge with parental seizure education, antipyretic-as-needed advice, and rectal diazepam only for prolonged events
Commence regular oral sodium valproate prophylaxis until age five for the recurrent febrile seizures
Prescribe alternating paracetamol and ibuprofen at the first sign of fever to prevent further events
Refer for routine outpatient paediatric neurology review and consider rectal diazepam prophylaxis daily

stem:
A 5-year-old boy is brought to your general practice clinic with daily soiling for the past 3 months. His father says 'he poos into his underpants without realising, and he hasn't sat on the toilet for a proper poo for at least 6 weeks'. Hard stools have been infrequent. He started school recently and avoids the school toilets. Diet is variable, fluid intake adequate, and growth has tracked the 50th centile throughout.

There is no blood per rectum, no vomiting, no abdominal distension at infancy, and meconium passed within 24 hours of birth. On examination he is afebrile with a soft, non-tender, palpably loaded left iliac fossa and faecal mass extending across to the right. Spine, anal position, sacral and lower limb neurological examination are normal. Recent abdominal X-ray taken at the emergency department demonstrates heavy faecal loading throughout the colon without evidence of obstruction.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 100/62 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, palpable faecal mass left iliac fossa extending to right, normal perianal exam, normal anal position, normal lower limb tone and reflexes, normal sacral skin
data_table.Investigations: Abdominal X-ray heavy faecal loading throughout colon, no air-fluid levels, no obstruction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for paediatric surgical opinion regarding suspected Hirschsprung disease and contrast enema studies
Recommend dietary fibre and fluid changes alone with general practitioner review in four weeks
Commence high-dose oral macrogol disimpaction over three days then a maintenance dose, plus toilet sit routine
Commence regular daily phosphate enemas as outpatient treatment for the next two weeks at home
Investigate with thyroid function tests, coeliac serology, and serum calcium before any treatment is started

stem:
You are the paediatric surgical registrar called to assess a term 40-hour-old boy born to non-consanguineous parents. The midwife reports 'he hasn't passed meconium yet and his tummy looks puffier this afternoon'. He has had two non-bilious vomits but is feeding poorly. There is no family history of cystic fibrosis. Antenatal scans were unremarkable; karyotype not performed.

On examination he has visible abdominal distension and reduced bowel sounds. Anal position is normal and the anocutaneous reflex is present, but per-rectal examination yields a snug rectum and an explosive passage of meconium after gentle finger withdrawal. He has no obvious dysmorphism. Abdominal X-ray shows distended gas-filled small and large bowel loops to a transition point at the rectosigmoid level with collapsed distal rectum. Newborn screening swab is pending. He is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, BP 64/40 mmHg, RR 50, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Abdominal distension, reduced bowel sounds, snug rectum with explosive passage of meconium after rectal examination, normal anal position, no dysmorphism
data_table.Investigations: Abdominal X-ray with multiple distended bowel loops, rectosigmoid transition zone, collapsed distal rectum; FBC, electrolytes, blood gas pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Rectal suction biopsy with histological assessment for ganglion cells and acetylcholinesterase staining
Water-soluble contrast enema looking for a string sign and microcolon in the descending colon
Urgent anorectal manometry to assess the rectoanal inhibitory reflex in the neonatal intensive care unit
Plain abdominal ultrasound to characterise bowel wall thickness at the suspected transition zone level
Sweat chloride testing on a properly weighted sample collected in the second week of life as next step

stem:
A 9-year-old boy is brought to your emergency department after 3 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and 4 kg weight loss. His mother says 'he's been drinking from the tap at night and wet the bed twice last week, which he never does'. He has had no vomiting, no abdominal pain, and is eating normally. He has had no recent viral illness and no family history of autoimmune disease.

On examination he is alert, well-perfused, with moist mucous membranes and a capillary refill under 2 seconds. There is no Kussmaul breathing and his breath is not ketotic. Bedside finger-prick glucose is 22 mmol/L. Capillary blood ketones measure 0.6 mmol/L (under 0.6 normal). Venous blood gas shows pH 7.36 (7.35-7.45) and bicarbonate 22 mmol/L (22-26). Urine dipstick shows glucose 3+, ketones trace, no nitrites or leukocytes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 108/68 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-perfused, mucous membranes moist, no Kussmaul breathing, no abdominal tenderness, weight tracking 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 22 mmol/L, capillary ketones 0.6 mmol/L, venous pH 7.36, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, urine glucose 3+ ketones trace

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride bolus and commence a fixed-rate insulin infusion
Admit under the paediatric endocrinology team for subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin and structured education
Arrange outpatient oral glucose tolerance testing and dietary review with the general practitioner in 1 week
Commence empirical oral metformin and lifestyle measures pending islet autoantibody and C-peptide results
Discharge with a glucose meter, finger-prick instructions, and a written safety-net to return if vomiting

stem:
A 7-year-old girl with known asthma is brought to your emergency department with 6 hours of worsening shortness of breath and wheeze. Her mother says 'she usually uses her blue puffer twice a week, but today she's needed it every 20 minutes and it's not really helping'. She has had a runny nose for 3 days. She is on a daily preventer (low-dose inhaled corticosteroid).

On arrival she is talking in short phrases, sitting upright, with audible wheeze and visible accessory muscle use. There is no cyanosis and she remains alert. She is given salbutamol 12 puffs by spacer and oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg. After three back-to-back salbutamol cycles, her tachypnoea has improved partially but the work of breathing remains moderate. There is good air entry bilaterally with persistent expiratory wheeze. Mum reports she had one prior admission for asthma 2 years ago and no history of intubation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 92% on room air rising to 96% on supplemental oxygen, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Sitting upright, talking in short phrases, suprasternal and subcostal recession, widespread expiratory wheeze with good air entry, no silent chest, alert
data_table.Investigations: Bedside finger-prick glucose 5.4 mmol/L, capillary blood gas not yet performed; chest X-ray clear
data_table.Medications: Daily inhaled corticosteroid (preventer); salbutamol 12 puffs by spacer x 3 cycles and oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg given so far

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intubate immediately and ventilate for impending respiratory failure with permissive hypercapnia
Add nebulised ipratropium bromide 250 mcg with the next two salbutamol doses given back-to-back
Commence an intravenous aminophylline loading dose with cardiac monitoring on the resuscitation bay
Discontinue inhaled salbutamol and start a subcutaneous adrenaline 1:1000 0.01 mg/kg injection
Discharge home with a written asthma action plan and review by general practitioner in 24 hours

stem:
A 13-year-old boy is brought to your general practice clinic with 6 weeks of right knee and thigh pain and a limp that has worsened over the past week. His mother says 'he stopped running around because his leg hurts and he keeps turning his foot out when he walks'. He has had no fever, no trauma, and no recent illness. He is at the 95th centile for weight and 50th for height.

On examination he is afebrile. He prefers to lie with the right leg externally rotated. Passive flexion of the right hip causes obligate external rotation and produces pain. Internal rotation of the right hip is limited to 5 degrees. Knee examination is unremarkable. He can weight-bear but limps with an out-toed gait. Lower limb neurovascular examination is normal. Plain frog-lateral pelvic X-ray shows a posterior and medial slip of the right capital femoral epiphysis on the metaphysis; the contralateral side is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 116/68 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Obligate external rotation on passive hip flexion, restricted internal rotation right hip, knee unremarkable, neurovascular intact
data_table.Investigations: Plain pelvis X-ray with frog-lateral views: posterior and medial slip of right capital femoral epiphysis; left hip normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Strict non-weight-bearing with crutches and urgent paediatric orthopaedic referral for surgical pinning
Outpatient referral to physiotherapy for hip range of motion strengthening and a 6-week activity plan
Magnetic resonance imaging of the right hip before discussing definitive orthopaedic management options
Prescribe oral ibuprofen analgesia for activity-related pain and routine review by general practitioner in 1 week
Investigate for transient synovitis with hip ultrasound and a course of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory cover

subtopic_detail: Brief resolved unexplained event risk stratification
stem:
A 5-week-old, term, exclusively breastfed boy is brought to your emergency department after a 30-second episode during feeding in which his mother says 'he went floppy and his face turned a bit blue around the lips, then he came right after I patted his back'. He is now alert and feeding normally. He was born at 39+5 weeks gestation by uncomplicated vaginal birth, with no neonatal nursery admission.

There have been no other episodes and no recent illness. He has no fever and no cough. There is no family history of sudden unexpected death in infancy. Examination is entirely normal: tone, fontanelle, chest auscultation, abdominal examination, hip examination, oxygen saturation in room air, and capillary refill are all normal. Bedside finger-prick glucose is 4.8 mmol/L. He has fed twice in the department and remained well-perfused with stable observations. His mother asks 'do we get to go home?'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140, BP 78/48 mmHg, RR 42, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-perfused, tone normal, fontanelle soft, chest clear, abdomen soft, hips stable, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Finger-prick glucose 4.8 mmol/L; no other tests indicated by guideline at this point

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for cardiorespiratory monitoring, send pertussis PCR, electrocardiogram, and electroencephalogram during admission
Discharge after shared decision-making with safety-net advice and early review by general practitioner
Observe in a short-stay unit for at least 4 hours with continuous saturation and cardiorespiratory monitoring
Refer to gastroenterology for upper endoscopy for suspected gastro-oesophageal reflux disease workup
Order a metabolic screen, ammonia, lactate, and a head magnetic resonance imaging study urgently

subtopic_detail: Timing of live attenuated vaccines after high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin
stem: A 13-month-old boy who received intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg for Kawasaki disease four weeks ago attends your clinic with his mother for his overdue 12-month immunisations.

data_table.Examination: Afebrile, thriving, cardiovascular examination normal
data_table.Immunisations: Due measles-mumps-rubella and meningococcal C conjugate vaccines

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about today's vaccines?

options.text: Give the inactivated vaccine now and defer the live vaccine 11 months
Give every one of the scheduled vaccines today because he has recovered well
Defer every scheduled vaccine until 11 months after the infusion
Give the live vaccine now and check measles serology in six weeks
Defer the live vaccine for three months and give the rest today

stem:
A 3-year-old girl is brought to your emergency department 90 minutes after falling from a sofa onto a carpeted floor. Her mother says 'she cried straight away, didn't pass out, vomited once on the way in, and now she just wants to sleep on me'. The fall height was about 80 cm. She has had no further vomiting and is consolable when alert. She has had no fever or recent illness.

On examination she is GCS 15 when stimulated, drowsy at rest but easily roused with appropriate interaction. There is a 3 cm boggy parietal haematoma on the right and no other scalp injury. Fontanelles are closed. Pupils are equal and reactive at 3 mm bilaterally. Tympanic membranes are intact, no haemotympanum, and no CSF rhinorrhoea. No focal neurological deficit on screening. The remaining systemic examination is unremarkable. She has not had any anti-emetic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: GCS 15, drowsy at rest, easily roused, right parietal 3 cm boggy haematoma, pupils 3 mm bilaterally reactive, no focal deficit, tympanic membranes intact
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.1 mmol/L, no other investigations performed yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with written head injury safety-net advice and review by general practitioner in 48 hours
Observe in the emergency department for at least 4-6 hours with serial neurological examinations
Order a non-contrast computed tomography head scan immediately for the high-risk features described
Arrange skull X-ray series to look for a linear or depressed fracture before further decision-making
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain on the next available outpatient slot to avoid radiation exposure

subtopic_detail: Pulse oximetry screening for critical congenital heart disease
stem:
You are the resident on the postnatal ward. A term newborn boy at 28 hours of age is screened with the routine pulse oximetry protocol. The midwife reports the readings to you. He is feeding, has had a wet nappy, and his mother says 'he looks pink to me'. His mother had unremarkable antenatal scans including a 20-week morphology scan. There is no family history of congenital heart disease.

On examination he is pink centrally and well-perfused, with normal tone. Cardiac auscultation reveals normal first and second heart sounds, no murmur, and femoral pulses are present and synchronous. Chest auscultation is clear. Capillary refill is under 2 seconds and the abdomen is soft. The four-limb blood pressure is unremarkable. Pre-ductal (right hand) SpO2 is 95% and post-ductal (right foot) SpO2 is 92% on three readings each, separated by 2 minutes; the difference is consistent across readings.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 142, BP 72/44 mmHg, RR 44, pre-ductal SpO2 95%, post-ductal SpO2 92%, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Pink centrally, well-perfused, soft fontanelle, no murmur, normal heart sounds, synchronous femoral pulses, clear chest, soft abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Pulse oximetry protocol over 6 minutes shows persistent pre-post differential 3% with both feet under 95%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the mother, repeat pulse oximetry in 24 hours, and continue routine ward observations meanwhile
Refer urgently for echocardiography and discuss with the on-call paediatric cardiology service today
Commence empirical prostaglandin E1 infusion immediately before any further imaging investigation
Discharge home with general practitioner follow-up and a 1-week outpatient cardiology clinic appointment
Order arterial blood gas first and only proceed to echocardiography if metabolic acidosis is documented

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to assess a previously well 4-year-old boy of Mediterranean heritage who has presented with 24 hours of fatigue, pallor, and dark coloured urine. His mother says 'his wee looks like Coca-Cola and the whites of his eyes have gone yellow today'. Three days ago he ate fresh fava beans at a relative's gathering and was started on oral co-trimoxazole for an ear infection. He has no fever now and no abdominal pain.

On examination he is alert, pale, with scleral icterus. Cardiovascular examination shows a quiet flow murmur at the left sternal edge; the spleen tip is palpable but not enlarged. There is no lymphadenopathy and no petechiae. Bloods show haemoglobin 72 g/L (115-150), reticulocytes 240 x10^9/L (50-100), unconjugated bilirubin 68 micromol/L (under 17), LDH 1480 U/L (under 250), haptoglobin under 0.1 g/L (0.3-2.0), direct antiglobulin test negative. A blood film reports bite cells and Heinz bodies. He has no known prior haemolytic episodes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 26, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, pale, scleral icterus, soft systolic flow murmur, spleen tip just palpable, no lymphadenopathy, no purpura
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 72 g/L (115-150), reticulocytes 240 x10^9/L (50-100), unconjugated bilirubin 68 micromol/L (under 17), LDH 1480 U/L (under 250), haptoglobin under 0.1 g/L (0.3-2.0), DAT negative, blood film bite cells and Heinz bodies
data_table.Medications: Oral co-trimoxazole started 3 days ago for otitis media

lead_in: What is the single best initial management step?

options.text: Withdraw co-trimoxazole, treat any persistent infection with an alternative agent, and supportive transfusion if symptomatic
Empirical intravenous methylprednisolone pulses for warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia presumption
Urgent splenectomy referral for management of compensated chronic haemolysis with hyperbilirubinaemia
Administer rasburicase prophylactically for tumour lysis prevention before chemotherapy assessment
Commence methylene blue infusion for any associated methaemoglobinaemia before haematology review

stem:
A 5-month-old, term, previously well boy is admitted to your general paediatric ward with 3 days of coryza, cough, and progressive work of breathing. His mother says 'he just won't take the bottle anymore and his ribs are sucking in when he breathes'. He is breastfed with some formula top-ups and is wet nappies five times per day.

On arrival 90 minutes ago he was started on nasal prong oxygen 1 L/min for SpO2 88% on room air; his saturation rose to 93% within 10 minutes. He is afebrile, alert, and well-perfused. Auscultation shows widespread fine crepitations and a few expiratory wheezes with good air entry. His subcostal recession has not improved despite the low-flow oxygen and his oral intake is now under 50% of normal volume. Capillary blood gas shows pH 7.34 (7.35-7.45), pCO2 50 mmHg (35-45), and bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22-26). His nasopharyngeal swab is positive for respiratory syncytial virus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168, BP 88/52 mmHg, RR 64, SpO2 93% on 1 L/min nasal prongs, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-perfused, marked subcostal recession, fine widespread crepitations, scattered expiratory wheeze, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Capillary pH 7.34, pCO2 50 mmHg (35-45), bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22-26), NPA positive for RSV
data_table.Medications: Nasal prong oxygen 1 L/min for the past 90 minutes; no bronchodilators given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min and reassess work of breathing again in another 2 hours
Commence high-flow nasal cannula therapy at 2 L/kg/min titrated to a target oxygen saturation of 90% or above
Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back-to-back with nebulised 3% hypertonic saline as a respiratory adjunct
Administer a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg with airway clearance physiotherapy added concurrently
Intubate and ventilate now for the rising carbon dioxide of 50 mmHg and the persistent increased work of breathing

stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to your emergency department at 0200 with a barking cough and noisy breathing. His mother says 'he sounded like a seal barking and now he's making this loud noise when he breathes in, even when he's just lying still'. He has had 2 days of coryza. He has had no contact with anyone unwell at home.

On examination he is alert but anxious, sitting on his mother's lap. He has audible stridor at rest with marked suprasternal and intercostal recession. He is moving air symmetrically with no wheeze. Oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. Capillary refill is under 2 seconds. He has not been febrile and he is well-hydrated. He has had no medication so far. The croup score (Westley) is calculated at 7, with stridor at rest, marked recession, and decreased air entry without cyanosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert anxious, sitting on mother's lap, stridor at rest, marked suprasternal and intercostal recession, no wheeze, symmetrical air entry
data_table.Investigations: Westley croup score 7 (severe); no blood tests indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg only and review the work of breathing in 30 minutes time
Give nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 plus oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg and observe for at least 3 hours
Intubate now for impending respiratory failure with persistent stridor and intercostal recession at rest
Administer nebulised budesonide 2 mg as the sole steroid agent and arrange admission for observation
Discharge home with a written information sheet on humidified air and a paracetamol dosing schedule

stem:
A 4-month-old boy is admitted to your paediatric ward with fever to 39.2 °C and irritability. His mother says 'he just goes red and screams when he wees and his nappies have been really smelly for two days'. He has had no cough, no diarrhoea, and no rash. He was born at term and was not screened on antenatal ultrasound for renal anomalies because his mother had no antenatal care.

On examination he is alert but unsettled, with a soft abdomen and no flank mass. Urinalysis from a clean catch sample shows leukocytes 3+ and nitrites positive; microscopy reports more than 100 white cells per high-power field. Empirical intravenous gentamicin plus benzylpenicillin was started 48 hours ago. He remains febrile to 38.6 °C and is still feeding poorly. Urine culture has now returned showing Klebsiella pneumoniae at 10^8 CFU/mL with the gentamicin being the only sensitive listed antibiotic; the sensitivity strip confirms susceptibility.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 42, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, unsettled, soft abdomen, no flank mass, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis leukocytes 3+ nitrites positive, microscopy WCC >100/HPF, urine culture Klebsiella pneumoniae 10^8 CFU/mL gentamicin-sensitive, CRP 96 mg/L (under 5), creatinine 36 micromol/L (15-37)
data_table.Medications: Intravenous gentamicin once daily plus benzylpenicillin for 48 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue current intravenous antibiotics and arrange a renal ultrasound scan during the current admission
Continue intravenous antibiotics and arrange a dimercaptosuccinic acid scan in 6 months as routine assessment
Switch to oral co-trimoxazole prophylaxis only and arrange outpatient renal ultrasound in 6 weeks' time
Continue intravenous antibiotics and arrange a micturating cystourethrogram during the current admission
Cease intravenous antibiotics, observe off treatment, and repeat urine culture in 48 hours from a fresh sample

stem:
A 9-year-old girl with known persistent asthma is in your paediatric resuscitation bay with severe acute asthma. Her mother says 'her chest is sucking in and she can hardly say a word'. She has had three back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium bromide 250 mcg added to each dose, and was given oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg 40 minutes ago. She has had a normal chest X-ray and there is no pneumothorax.

On examination she remains using accessory muscles with persistent subcostal recession and only marginally improved tachypnoea. Her air entry is fair throughout with persistent expiratory wheeze; the chest is not silent. She is GCS 15 but tired. Cardiac monitoring shows sinus tachycardia at 156. Her capillary blood gas shows pH 7.30 (7.35-7.45), pCO2 46 mmHg (35-45), bicarbonate 22 mmol/L (22-26). She has no history of intubation. Intravenous access is established and her potassium is 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 156, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 38, SpO2 91% on 6 L/min mask oxygen, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Sitting upright, tired, single words, accessory muscle use, persistent expiratory wheeze with fair air entry, no silent chest, GCS 15
data_table.Investigations: Capillary pH 7.30, pCO2 46 mmHg (35-45), bicarbonate 22 mmol/L (22-26), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), chest X-ray clear
data_table.Medications: Three back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg plus ipratropium 250 mcg; oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg 40 minutes ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg as a slow infusion over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring
Commence intravenous aminophylline loading dose 10 mg/kg over 1 hour and then a maintenance infusion
Add nebulised hypertonic saline 3% as a respiratory adjunct and continue continuous nebulised salbutamol
Intubate and commence mechanical ventilation with permissive hypercapnia and inhaled volatile anaesthesia
Commence non-invasive ventilation with bi-level positive airway pressure as the next escalation modality

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to your emergency department after eating a peanut-containing biscuit at a birthday party 20 minutes ago. His mother says 'his face puffed up, he came out in hives and now he's wheezing and saying he can't breathe properly'. He has had two prior reactions to peanuts treated with antihistamines without adrenaline. He has been previously well and is not on any regular medications.

On examination he has facial and periorbital angioedema, generalised urticaria, and audible wheeze with intercostal recession. He is alert but anxious. His weight is documented as 16 kg from a recent immunisation visit. Intravenous access has not yet been established. He has had no prior fluid bolus. Oxygen is being delivered by mask at 6 L/min. The ED nursing team is preparing intramuscular adrenaline at your direction. There is no inspiratory stridor at rest yet.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, BP 80/46 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 92% on 6 L/min mask oxygen, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert anxious, facial and periorbital angioedema, generalised urticaria, audible wheeze with intercostal recession, no stridor at rest
data_table.Investigations: Documented weight 16 kg, no IV access yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first dose of adrenaline?

options.text: Adrenaline 150 microgram (EpiPen Junior equivalent) intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh now
Adrenaline 160 microgram (10 microgram/kg) intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh now as a calculated dose
Adrenaline 300 microgram (EpiPen equivalent) intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh now
Adrenaline 16 microgram (1 microgram/kg) intravenously as a single bolus dose without an infusion
Adrenaline 1.6 milligram (100 microgram/kg) nebulised via a paediatric nebuliser mask immediately

stem: A 14-month-old boy with 3 days of profuse diarrhoea and vomiting is brought in by ambulance. He is drowsy. His weight is 9 kg, down from 10.5 kg a fortnight ago.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 186, BP 68/40, RR 44, temperature 37.2
data_table.Examination: Mottled, capillary refill 5 seconds, cool peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 4.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous sodium chloride 0.9 percent 20 mL/kg over 15 minutes
Nasogastric rehydration solution at 25 mL/kg each hour for 4 hours
Intravenous sodium chloride 0.9 percent with glucose at maintenance
Oral rehydration solution 5 mL by syringe every 5 minutes for an hour
Oral ondansetron 2 mg then a further supervised oral fluid trial

stem:
A 16-month-old Aboriginal boy is brought to your remote primary care clinic with 24 hours of fever to 39.0 °C and ear-pulling. His mother says 'he keeps grabbing at his right ear and crying when he lies down to sleep'. He has had no diarrhoea, no rash, and no respiratory distress. He is fully immunised. He attends a remote community kindergarten and has had three previous episodes of acute otitis media in the past 6 months.

On examination both tympanic membranes are bulging and erythematous, with loss of light reflex on the right. There is no perforation and no purulent discharge. The neck is supple, the throat is unremarkable, and the chest is clear. His hydration is satisfactory. He is otherwise alert and consoles in his mother's lap. The clinic has access to oral amoxicillin and intramuscular ceftriaxone but not a same-day audiology service. The community has high rates of chronic suppurative otitis media in older children.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 26, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 39.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Both tympanic membranes bulging and erythematous, loss of light reflex right, no perforation, no discharge, supple neck, clear chest
data_table.Investigations: None indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe high-dose oral amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day in two divided doses for 7 days and review in person at 48 hours
Adopt watchful waiting with regular paracetamol and review in 48 hours if symptoms persist or worsen
Administer a single intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg dose now as initial therapy and review in 48 hours
Prescribe oral amoxicillin with clavulanic acid 90 mg/kg/day amoxicillin component divided three times daily for 14 days
Refer urgently for tympanocentesis and culture of middle ear fluid before commencing any antibiotic therapy

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar on call. A 22-month-old girl is on the general paediatric ward 36 hours after a first dose of intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg for complete Kawasaki disease (8 days of fever, conjunctivitis, oral changes, peripheral oedema, polymorphous rash). The bedside nurse calls you because she has spiked a fever to 39.2 °C again 12 hours after the IVIG completed. Her CRP, which had fallen to 84 mg/L at the end of the infusion, is now 138 mg/L on a repeat measurement.

On examination she remains miserable, with persistent dry fissured lips and bilateral conjunctival injection. There is no new petechiae, no shock, and no new murmur. Her aspirin 80 mg/kg/day in four divided doses is ongoing. The baseline echocardiogram at 24 hours showed no coronary artery dilatation (Z-score plus 0.6 in the left main coronary, plus 0.4 in the right). Her family is from a Japanese background and her parents ask 'is there something stronger now?'. She has had no live vaccines in the last 4 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 154, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Miserable, persistent dry fissured lips, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, no shock, no new murmur, no new rash
data_table.Investigations: CRP 138 mg/L rising from 84 mg/L post-IVIG, albumin 27 g/L (35-50), echocardiogram coronary Z-score plus 0.6 LMCA plus 0.4 RCA at 24 hours
data_table.Medications: IVIG 2 g/kg completed 12 hours ago; aspirin 80 mg/kg/day divided four times daily ongoing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg as the next step in escalation for IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease
Administer intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse daily for 3 days as the second-line escalation step
Add intravenous infliximab 5 mg/kg single dose as the second-line escalation step ahead of further IVIG
Continue current therapy and observe for a further 48 hours before any decision to escalate treatment
Cease aspirin and commence anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin instead pending repeat echocardiogram

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called urgently to the ward. A 10-year-old girl was admitted 6 hours ago with new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus presenting in diabetic ketoacidosis (pH 7.05, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, glucose 32 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L). She has received 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride as a single bolus, then 0.9% sodium chloride at a 48-hour rehydration rate, plus a fixed-rate insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour. Her glucose is now 14 mmol/L and her pH has improved to 7.18.

The nurse says 'she's been a bit harder to rouse over the last 20 minutes and her headache is worse'. On examination her GCS has dropped from 15 to 13 (eyes open to voice, confused conversation). Her pulse is 64 (down from 122 on arrival), blood pressure is 142/88 mmHg (up from 102/60), and respiratory rate has slowed from 38 to 22. Pupils are 4 mm and equal, with sluggish reactions. The fontanelle is closed. There is no focal neurological deficit. Bedside glucose is now 12 mmol/L; ketones 4.1 mmol/L; bicarbonate 12 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 64 (was 122), BP 142/88 mmHg (was 102/60), RR 22 (was 38), SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: GCS 13 (eyes open to voice, confused), pupils 4 mm equal sluggish, no focal deficit, fontanelle closed
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 12 mmol/L, ketones 4.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (was 6)
data_table.Medications: Fixed-rate insulin infusion 0.05 units/kg/hour and 0.9% sodium chloride at 48-hour rehydration rate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous mannitol 1 g/kg over 20 minutes and reduce intravenous fluid rate by one-third immediately
Increase the intravenous fluid rate to compensate for ongoing osmotic diuresis and continue insulin at the present rate
Cease the insulin infusion entirely to allow biochemical stabilisation before any further osmotic therapy
Order an urgent computed tomography head scan before any intervention to confirm cerebral oedema or other cause
Administer intravenous dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single dose for presumed inflammatory cerebral oedema

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the postnatal ward. A 36-hour-old, term, exclusively breastfed boy has had two episodes of green vomiting in the last 4 hours. The midwife says 'his vomits have gone from milk-coloured to bright green and his tummy looks a bit bloated now'. He had been feeding well until this morning and had one meconium pass at 18 hours of life.

On examination he is alert but quiet, with a mildly distended abdomen and no palpable mass. The abdomen is soft without peritonism. Bowel sounds are present. Anus is patent on inspection. The remaining examination is unremarkable. Bedside finger-prick glucose is 4.4 mmol/L. The mother had normal antenatal scans including a 20-week morphology scan; there was no polyhydramnios. He has had no syndromic features identified. A nasogastric tube placed on your direction drains 25 mL of bilious fluid. He has had no further meconium since the first pass.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 152, BP 72/44 mmHg, RR 48, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert quiet, mildly distended soft abdomen, no peritonism, patent anus, no syndromic features
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.4 mmol/L; NGT drains 25 mL bilious fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent upper gastrointestinal contrast study to assess duodenojejunal flexure position and rule out volvulus
Reassure the team and observe with intravenous maintenance fluids while continuing breastfeeding on demand
Arrange supine and erect abdominal X-rays only and review again at 6 hours from the time of presentation
Arrange a barium enema as the first imaging modality to assess caecal position and possible obstruction
Stop oral feeding and start trial of probiotic for a presumed neonatal feeding intolerance with green vomits

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-month-old girl brought to a metropolitan emergency department by her mother and the mother's partner after a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting four minutes that resolved before arrival. She was previously well, immunisations are up to date, and she is exclusively breastfed.

On examination she is afebrile and alert with a normal cry. Anterior fontanelle is soft and flat. There is a 2 cm bluish bruise over the left cheek and a small bruise on the left pinna. Her mother explains the baby rolled off the change table this morning while she was answering the door, and the mother's partner is the primary daytime carer while father is on a fly-in fly-out roster. Coagulation profile, capillary glucose, ammonia and electrolytes are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 36/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused; left cheek bruise 2 cm, small left pinna bruise; anterior fontanelle soft; no other surface marks; tone normal
data_table.Investigations: BSL 4.6 mmol/L; sodium, urea, creatinine within normal limits; INR within normal limits; ammonia within normal limits

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Non contrast CT head and skeletal survey, then notify child protection services
Discharge home with safety net advice and paediatric outpatient follow up in two weeks
Outpatient EEG and developmental review through the local community paediatrician
Admit overnight for observation only, with discharge to the mother in the morning
Request a metabolic screen including plasma amino acids and urine organic acids

subtopic_detail: Follow-up echocardiography schedule after treated Kawasaki disease with normal initial imaging
stem: A 4-year-old girl received intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin for Kawasaki disease two days ago and has defervesced. Her parents ask you what heart monitoring she will need from here.

data_table.Examination: Well; no murmur; peeling of the fingertips
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiography at diagnosis showed normal coronary arteries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate cardiac follow-up plan?

options.text: Repeat echocardiography at two weeks and again at six to eight weeks
Repeat echocardiography at six months and then every two years
Repeat echocardiography only if cardiac symptoms develop in the years ahead
Repeat echocardiography tomorrow and then again at three months
No repeat echocardiography is needed as the first study was normal

stem:
You are the rural ED registrar at a regional hospital seeing a 22-month-old girl brought in 90 minutes after falling backwards off a kitchen chair onto a carpeted floor. The fall was witnessed by her father. There was no loss of consciousness. She vomited once at home and once in triage, then settled in her father's arms and accepted a bottle.

On arrival she is calm, smiles when distracted with bubbles, and her father states she is acting like herself. There is a 4 cm boggy haematoma over the right parietal scalp without overlying laceration. Anterior fontanelle is closed. Pupils are equal and reactive, tone is normal, and she tracks toys with both eyes. There is no palpable skull step. Glasgow coma score is 15.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, BP 94/58 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: GCS 15, calm in father's arms, accepts bottle; 4 cm boggy right parietal scalp haematoma; no palpable skull step; pupils equal and reactive
data_table.History: Fall from kitchen chair onto carpet, witnessed, no loss of consciousness, 2 episodes of vomiting, normal behaviour now

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate non contrast CT head and admit under the paediatric team
Discharge home immediately with written head injury advice for her father
Observe in the emergency department for 4 to 6 hours with neurological observations
Arrange a skull radiograph series to exclude a linear parietal fracture
Transfer urgently to a tertiary paediatric centre by retrieval team

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar caring for a 9-year-old girl admitted to the ward four hours ago with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes and diabetic ketoacidosis. She received a 10 mL/kg saline bolus on arrival, was started on 0.05 units/kg/hour intravenous insulin two hours ago, and is now on 0.45% saline plus 5% dextrose with potassium running at her calculated maintenance plus 48-hour deficit replacement rate.

Her mother calls you because the child has just complained of a new severe headache and has vomited once. On review she is drowsy, opens eyes only to voice and her speech is slurred. The bedside nurse reports the blood pressure has risen from 105/65 to 132/82 over the last 30 minutes and the heart rate has fallen from 122 to 88. Pupils are equal and reactive. Sodium has fallen from 138 to 131 since admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, BP 132/82 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Neurology: Drowsy, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5), pupils equal and reactive, no focal deficit
data_table.Investigations: BSL 14 mmol/L; sodium 131 mmol/L (135-145, was 138); pH 7.18 (was 7.05); ketones 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue the current fluid regimen at the same rate and reassess her neurology and pupils in 30 minutes
Administer mannitol 0.5 g/kg or hypertonic 3% saline 2.5 mL/kg and reduce IV fluid rate by one third
Increase the insulin infusion to 0.1 units/kg/hour and add a second saline bolus
Stop the insulin infusion entirely and check serum osmolality before any further action
Arrange an urgent non contrast CT head to confirm cerebral oedema before treatment

stem:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his grandmother after an episode at home four hours ago where he started coughing suddenly while eating peanuts on the couch and then settled. He has been intermittently coughing since and his grandmother says his breathing sounds noisier on one side.

On arrival he is alert and talking in full sentences. There is no audible stridor. Auscultation reveals reduced air entry and end-expiratory wheeze over the right lower zone with normal breath sounds on the left. There is no fever and no recent viral illness. He has never wheezed before and has no atopy. An inspiratory chest radiograph performed in the department is reported as showing no focal consolidation, no pneumothorax, equal lung volumes and no radio-opaque foreign body.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 30/min, SpO2 95% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Talking in full sentences; mild subcostal recession; reduced air entry plus end-expiratory wheeze over right lower zone; left chest clear; no stridor
data_table.Investigations: Inspiratory chest radiograph: no consolidation, no pneumothorax, equal lung volumes, no radio-opaque foreign body

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for urgent flexible bronchoscopy under sedation in the emergency department
Trial salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer and reassess auscultation in 20 minutes
Refer urgently to ENT or paediatric surgery for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia
Discharge home with safety net advice and outpatient paediatric review next week
Order a non contrast chest CT to identify the level of the aspirated foreign body

stem:
An 8-year-old known asthmatic boy presents to a metropolitan emergency department with worsening cough and shortness of breath for 12 hours after running outside this morning. He has had asthma since age 4 on twice-daily fluticasone 100 mcg and a salbutamol reliever as needed. He has used his blue puffer six times in the last two hours at home with no sustained improvement.

On arrival he speaks in short phrases, is sitting forward, and uses accessory muscles. Auscultation reveals widespread polyphonic wheeze with reduced air entry bilaterally. He receives three back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg plus ipratropium 250 mcg combinations over 30 minutes and oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg. After this he remains tachypnoeic with continued accessory muscle use and SpO2 92% on 4 L/min via nasal prongs; he is still speaking in short phrases only.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, RR 38/min, SpO2 92% on 4 L/min nasal prongs, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Sitting forward, accessory muscle use; widespread polyphonic wheeze, reduced air entry bilaterally; speaks in short phrases
data_table.Medications given: Three back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg plus ipratropium 250 mcg; oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes (max 2 g)
Add nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 to the next bronchodilator cycle
Increase the inhaled fluticasone dose to 250 mcg twice daily before discharge
Commence broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics for presumed bacterial chest infection
Switch from nasal prong oxygen to high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min

stem:
A 22-month-old boy is brought to your general practice clinic by his mother for a third episode of audible wheeze in the past 6 months. Each episode followed a runny nose by 24 to 48 hours and lasted 4 to 5 days. Between episodes he is completely well and runs around without breathlessness. He has had no nocturnal wheeze. There is no family history of asthma, eczema or hay fever, and he has had no admissions.

On examination today he is afebrile, talking in normal phrases for his age, and his work of breathing is normal. Auscultation reveals scattered end expiratory wheeze with normal air entry bilaterally. His mother has been giving 4 puffs of salbutamol via a small-volume spacer at the onset of each cold which she says reduces symptoms within 30 minutes. He has had no salbutamol use today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, BP 92/56 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Talking in normal phrases for age, no accessory muscle use; scattered end expiratory wheeze; normal air entry; afebrile
data_table.History: 3 episodes wheeze in 6 months, each cold-triggered, well between episodes; no nocturnal wheeze; no atopy; salbutamol responsive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence inhaled corticosteroid fluticasone 50 mcg twice daily as a daily preventer
Trial montelukast 4 mg orally each evening for 12 weeks then reassess
Continue salbutamol as needed via spacer and review again if symptoms change
Refer for skin prick allergen testing to common inhaled and food allergens
Prescribe an oral prednisolone course for use at the start of each viral episode

stem:
You are the neonatal registrar reviewing a 32 week, 1.4 kg male preterm infant now 12 days old who has had bloody stools and bilious aspirates for the last 18 hours. He had been tolerating expressed breast milk via gavage at 120 mL/kg/day until two days ago. He was started on broad spectrum antibiotics and bowel rest 12 hours ago and has had an umbilical arterial catheter inserted for serial gases.

Over the last 6 hours his platelet count has fallen from 145 to 62 x10^9/L and lactate has risen from 1.8 to 5.4 mmol/L. He is now intubated and on dopamine 10 mcg/kg/min for mean arterial pressure 28 mmHg. His abdomen is tense, discoloured and quiet to auscultation. The on-call radiographer reports the upright abdominal radiograph shows extensive pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas and a small amount of free intra-abdominal gas in the right upper quadrant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178/min, MAP 28 mmHg on dopamine, RR 60/min ventilated, SpO2 92% on 60% FiO2, temperature 35.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Tense discoloured abdomen with absent bowel sounds; mottled lower limbs; CRT 5 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L (140-220); platelets 62 x10^9/L (was 145); lactate 5.4 mmol/L (was 1.8); pH 7.18; base excess -12; CRP 142 mg/L
data_table.Imaging: Upright abdominal radiograph: extensive pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas, free gas in right upper quadrant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent paediatric surgical referral for laparotomy or peritoneal drain insertion
Continue medical management with bowel rest, antibiotics and inotropic support
Add intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg as adjunctive therapy for severe sepsis
Repeat the abdominal radiograph in 6 hours to confirm progression before referral
Switch enteral feeds to a hydrolysed amino acid formula via continuous nasogastric infusion

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional emergency department reviewing a 5-week-old boy brought in by his mother with 4 days of paroxysmal cough now associated with brief blue-around-the-lips episodes during feeds. He was born at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery; mother received her routine antenatal whooping cough booster at 18 weeks rather than the recommended 20 to 32 weeks window. He has not yet received any of his own scheduled vaccinations.

On examination between paroxysms he is alert and afebrile. During an observed paroxysm he goes briefly cyanotic with SpO2 dropping to 87% before recovering. Chest auscultation between episodes is clear. There are no inspiratory crepitations and no hepatosplenomegaly. White cell count is 28 x10^9/L with a lymphocyte predominance and a nasopharyngeal Bordetella pertussis PCR is positive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158/min, BP 88/54 mmHg, RR 44/min, SpO2 94% room air between paroxysms, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert between paroxysms; cyanotic during paroxysm with SpO2 87%; chest clear on auscultation; no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: WCC 28 x10^9/L (5-15) with lymphocyte predominance; nasopharyngeal Bordetella pertussis PCR positive; CXR no focal consolidation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for inpatient observation and commence oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 5 days
Treat only household contacts with azithromycin prophylaxis and discharge the infant home today
Admit for nebulised salbutamol with chest physiotherapy and reassess oxygenation hourly
Discharge home with safety net advice and arrange a paediatric clinic review within 48 hours
Admit and commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg six-hourly for presumed pneumonia

stem:
A 5-week-old first-born male is referred from a peripheral hospital with 7 days of forceful non-bilious vomiting after every feed. He has lost 280 g since his 4-week weigh-in. His mother reports he appears hungry immediately after vomiting and wants to feed again.

On examination he is sleepy, with sunken anterior fontanelle and dry mucous membranes. After a test feed visible peristalsis is observed crossing the upper abdomen left to right and a 2 cm olive-shaped mass is palpable just lateral to the right rectus border above the umbilicus. Capillary refill is 4 seconds. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.52, pCO2 52 mmHg, bicarbonate 36 mmol/L, chloride 88 mmol/L, potassium 3.0 mmol/L and an abdominal ultrasound has just confirmed pyloric muscle thickness 5 mm and pyloric channel length 19 mm.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168/min, BP 78/48 mmHg, RR 36/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Sleepy, sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes; visible upper abdominal peristalsis; palpable olive; CRT 4 seconds
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.52, pCO2 52, HCO3 36, Cl 88, K 3.0; abdominal ultrasound pyloric muscle 5 mm, channel 19 mm

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Order an upper gastrointestinal contrast study before commencing any fluid resuscitation
Resuscitate with 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus then maintenance with 0.9% saline and added potassium
Trial of small volume thickened formula via nasogastric tube before any further intervention
Commence intravenous erythromycin 3 mg/kg six-hourly as a prokinetic before any surgery
Proceed directly to laparoscopic Ramstedt pyloromyotomy in the next available theatre

stem:
A 16-month-old boy is brought to the general practice by his mother because preschool staff said he looks pale and is becoming a fussy eater. He was breastfed exclusively until 11 months and is now drinking around 1500 mL of cow's milk daily from a bottle. He refuses red meat and most vegetables but accepts crackers and yoghurt. Birth was uncomplicated and his immunisations are up to date.

On examination he is pale with no jaundice and no organomegaly. There is no lymphadenopathy and his developmental milestones are appropriate for age. There is no history of melaena and faecal occult blood testing is negative. Full blood count shows haemoglobin 78 g/L (105-135), mean corpuscular volume 58 fL (75-85), platelets 412 x10^9/L, white cell count 9.4 x10^9/L. Ferritin is 6 mcg/L (20-200), transferrin saturation 5%, CRP under 5.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, BP 92/55 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Pale, alert, no jaundice; no hepatosplenomegaly; no lymphadenopathy; developmental milestones appropriate
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78 g/L (105-135); MCV 58 fL (75-85); ferritin 6 mcg/L (20-200); transferrin saturation 5%; CRP under 5; FOBT negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Transfuse 10 mL/kg packed red cells before any oral iron supplementation is started
Switch to a soy-based formula and arrange follow-up full blood count in 4 weeks
Commence oral elemental iron 3 mg/kg once daily and counsel to limit cow's milk to 500 mL
Trial a multivitamin without iron and cease cow's milk completely for 6 weeks
Refer to day stay for intravenous ferric carboxymaltose infusion as a single dose

stem:
You are the general paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-year-old previously well girl referred by her general practitioner with widespread petechiae on the trunk and lower limbs noticed by her mother yesterday. She had a coryzal illness ten days ago which resolved without treatment. There has been no epistaxis, gum bleeding, melaena or haematuria, and her mother denies any minor trauma that could explain the bruising. She is up to date with vaccinations and is fully immunised against measles.

On examination she is afebrile and well perfused, running around the consulting room. There is no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly and no bone tenderness. She has scattered petechiae on the trunk and a 1 cm wet purpura on the lower lip but no other mucosal bleeding. The full blood count shows haemoglobin 122 g/L, white cell count 7.4 x10^9/L with normal differential and morphology, and platelets 11 x10^9/L; the blood film comment from the haematologist is 'normal red cell and leucocyte morphology, occasional giant platelets, no blasts'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102/min, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Active, well perfused; scattered petechiae trunk and lower limbs; 1 cm wet purpura lower lip; no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Hb 122 g/L, WCC 7.4 x10^9/L with normal differential, platelets 11 x10^9/L; film: normal red cell and leucocyte morphology, occasional giant platelets, no blasts

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for urgent bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy before any therapeutic decision
Oral prednisolone 4 mg/kg/day for 4 days then taper over 14 days as outpatient
Single dose intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg as inpatient with observation overnight
Outpatient observation with written bleeding advice and repeat platelet count in 1 week
Single bag of platelets 10 mL/kg now and proceed to bone marrow examination today

stem:
A 14-year-old girl is referred to the paediatric clinic from her general practitioner with three weeks of daily frontal headache that is worse on waking and worse on bending forward. She has also noticed transient grey-outs in both eyes lasting seconds when she stands up quickly. Her body mass index has risen from 27 to 31 kg/m2 over the last 12 months. She has been taking isotretinoin 30 mg daily for severe acne for four months and the combined oral contraceptive pill for three months for cycle control.

On examination her blood pressure is normal and she is afebrile. Visual acuity is 6/6 each eye. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral grade 2 papilloedema. Cranial nerve examination is otherwise normal. Non contrast magnetic resonance imaging shows partial empty sella, posterior globe flattening, prominent perioptic cerebrospinal fluid spaces and no mass lesion or venous sinus thrombosis. Lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position shows an opening pressure of 32 cmH2O with normal CSF cell count, glucose and protein.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally; bilateral grade 2 papilloedema on fundoscopy; cranial nerves otherwise intact
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: partial empty sella, posterior globe flattening, no mass, no venous sinus thrombosis; LP opening pressure 32 cmH2O, CSF cell count, glucose, protein within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Isotretinoin 30 mg daily for 4 months; combined oral contraceptive pill for 3 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: High dose intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse for 3 days then taper
Refer for ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion within 2 weeks for cerebrospinal fluid diversion
Refer urgently for optic nerve sheath fenestration to protect visual function
Sumatriptan 50 mg orally during attacks with propranolol 40 mg twice daily prophylaxis
Start oral acetazolamide 25 mg/kg/day in divided doses and discontinue isotretinoin

stem:
A 3-year-old girl with known homozygous sickle cell disease is brought to the emergency department by her parents, who recently migrated from West Africa, with 6 hours of progressive lethargy and a visibly distended abdomen. Her baseline haemoglobin is 80 g/L. She received penicillin V prophylaxis from diagnosis at 9 months and is fully immunised including pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccines.

On examination she is pale and drowsy but responsive to her name. Capillary refill is 4 seconds and her hands are cool to the wrists. The abdomen is distended and the spleen is palpable extending to the umbilicus. There is no focal abdominal tenderness, no jaundice, and the chest is clear on auscultation with no murmur. Haemoglobin is 38 g/L, reticulocytes 12% (baseline 8%), white cell count 16 x10^9/L, platelets 124 x10^9/L. Group and crossmatch is in progress.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 162/min, BP 78/40 mmHg, RR 36/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Pale, drowsy; CRT 4 seconds; abdomen distended with spleen palpable to umbilicus; chest clear; no jaundice
data_table.Investigations: Hb 38 g/L (baseline 80); reticulocytes 12% (baseline 8%); WCC 16 x10^9/L; platelets 124 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Urgent simple top-up transfusion of leucodepleted phenotyped red cells to a target haemoglobin
Continue penicillin prophylaxis only and observe overnight with serial haemoglobin checks
Refer urgently for emergency splenectomy to remove the sequestering reservoir
Commence hydroxycarbamide 15 mg/kg/day and oxygen at 6 L/min via non rebreather mask
Urgent exchange transfusion targeting haemoglobin S fraction under 30% and oxygen via mask

stem:
A 12-day-old female infant is brought to the emergency department by her parents with poor feeding and three episodes of forceful vomiting today. She is the first child of non-consanguineous parents and was discharged at day 3 with a normal newborn screen pending. Birth weight was 3.4 kg and she has now lost 12% of her birth weight.

On examination she is mottled, lethargic and minimally responsive to handling. Her anterior fontanelle is sunken and capillary refill is 5 seconds. There is unexpected mild clitoromegaly and posterior labial fusion noted today by the registrar; the clitoral length is at the upper limit of normal and the urethral opening sits within the clitoral shaft. There is no abdominal mass and the chest is clear. Capillary blood gas shows pH 7.22, base excess minus 12. Bedside sodium is 122 mmol/L, potassium 7.4 mmol/L, glucose 2.6 mmol/L and the on-call biochemist has rung to confirm the newborn screening 17-hydroxyprogesterone is markedly elevated.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 184/min, BP 58/32 mmHg, RR 64/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Mottled, lethargic; sunken fontanelle, CRT 5 seconds; mild clitoromegaly and posterior labial fusion
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.22, base excess -12; sodium 122 mmol/L; potassium 7.4 mmol/L; glucose 2.6 mmol/L; 17-hydroxyprogesterone markedly elevated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous insulin 0.05 units/kg/hour with dextrose infusion and urgent karyotype analysis
Intravenous hydrocortisone 25 mg stat plus 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg bolus with 10% dextrose maintenance
Empirical intravenous cefotaxime 50 mg/kg and urgent lumbar puncture for septic workup
Salbutamol 0.5 mL of 5 mg/mL nebulised solution with calcium gluconate 10% 0.5 mL/kg
Intravenous 10% dextrose 5 mL/kg bolus then oral fludrocortisone 100 mcg via nasogastric tube

stem:
You are the on-call neonatology registrar at a tertiary centre called to a 72-hour-old term male infant on the postnatal ward. He fed well for the first 36 hours and was discharge planned. Over the last 12 hours he has become progressively lethargic, has refused 3 consecutive feeds, vomited twice and now has irregular hyperventilation. He is the second child of consanguineous parents; the first child died at 5 days of age of presumed sepsis without a confirmed cause.

On examination he is encephalopathic with poor tone and absent suck. Heart rate is regular and the chest is clear; the abdomen is soft with no organomegaly. There is no rash and the anterior fontanelle is soft. Capillary glucose is 4.2 mmol/L. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.50, pCO2 22 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L with a normal anion gap. Sodium 138, potassium 4.0, lactate 2.0. Plasma ammonia returned 30 minutes ago at 580 micromol/L (under 50). LFTs and coagulation are within normal limits. Urinary ketones are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 156/min, BP 64/38 mmHg, RR 76/min irregular, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Encephalopathic with poor tone, absent suck; soft abdomen, no organomegaly; soft fontanelle
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.50, pCO2 22, HCO3 18, normal anion gap; glucose 4.2 mmol/L; lactate 2.0; ammonia 580 micromol/L (<50); LFTs and coagulation within normal limits; urinary ketones negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Therapeutic hyperventilation with intubation and intravenous mannitol 0.5 g/kg for cerebral oedema
Commence empirical intravenous cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin and obtain blood cultures
Cease all protein intake, commence intravenous 10% dextrose and arrange urgent haemodialysis transfer
Loading dose of phenobarbital 20 mg/kg for presumed neonatal seizures with maintenance therapy
Intravenous thiamine, pyridoxine and biotin trial alongside continued enteral feeds at half rate

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar overnight on a metropolitan general paediatric ward. A 7-week-old boy admitted with RSV-positive bronchiolitis has been on low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min for the past 2 hours. He was born at 36+5 weeks gestation and his mother reports he has been feeding poorly today with his last wet nappy 6 hours ago.

On reassessment he is now drowsy and pale with moderate to severe intercostal and subcostal recession and audible expiratory wheeze. Auscultation reveals widespread crackles bilaterally. SpO2 has stabilised at 91% on 1 L/min only with continued tactile stimulation between paroxysmal coughing episodes. He had one brief witnessed apnoea 15 minutes ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178/min, BP 76/48 mmHg, RR 68/min, SpO2 91% on nasal prong 1 L/min, temperature 37.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, pale; moderate to severe intercostal and subcostal recession; widespread crackles and wheeze bilaterally; one brief witnessed apnoea
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.28, pCO2 58 mmHg (35-45), HCO3 24 mmol/L (22-26), lactate 1.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); CXR hyperinflation, no focal consolidation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Commence high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min titrating FiO2 to SpO2 90-94%
Increase low-flow nasal prong oxygen to 4 L/min and review in 1 hour
Intubate and commence mechanical ventilation in the resuscitation bay now
Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg via face mask and reassess work of breathing
Nebulised hypertonic saline 3% 4 mL with monitoring of airway tolerance

stem:
You are the ED paediatric registrar at a tertiary children's hospital. A 5-year-old boy weighing 22 kg is brought in by his school teacher after eating a peanut at lunch. He developed generalised hives, lip swelling, a hoarse voice, and audible wheeze within 5 minutes. The teacher gave the school's EpiPen Jr (150 mcg adrenaline) at 7 minutes after onset; he is now 12 minutes from the original ingestion.

On arrival in resus he remains distressed with persistent wheeze, stridor, and a sense of impending doom. The hives have not faded. He has known peanut allergy with one previous mild reaction confined to urticaria. He has no other medical conditions.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158/min, BP 76/40 mmHg, RR 42/min, SpO2 90% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Distressed; widespread urticaria; lip swelling; stridor at rest; bilateral wheeze; capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 5.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.8); no other immediate investigations performed

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Repeat IM adrenaline 150 mcg (EpiPen Jr equivalent) into the anterolateral thigh
IM adrenaline 300 mcg (0.3 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral mid-thigh
IV adrenaline 100 mcg bolus while securing intravenous access
Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg plus IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg first
IM promethazine 25 mg plus oral cetirizine 10 mg to suppress histamine

subtopic_detail: Paediatric DKA fluid plan no bolus
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar at a tertiary hospital reviewing an 11-year-old girl, weight 35 kg, who is a new presentation of type 1 diabetes with diabetic ketoacidosis. Her mother reports 3 weeks of polyuria and polydipsia and 2 days of vomiting. On arrival she is mildly tachycardic but warm with capillary refill 2 seconds and a clear mental state.

Venous gas confirms a moderate ketoacidosis. There are no signs of shock and her conscious state remains preserved. She has had no prior insulin and no IV fluid has been commenced. The PICU registrar and consultant are aware and have asked you to prescribe the initial fluid plan according to the RCH paediatric DKA guideline.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, BP 105/68 mmHg, RR 28/min (deep), SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented; capillary refill 2 seconds; mucosae dry; mild tachypnoea; no peripheral cyanosis
data_table.Investigations: BSL 28.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.8); venous pH 7.10, HCO3 9 mmol/L (22-26); blood ketones 5.2 mmol/L; Na 134 mmol/L (135-145), K 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), corrected Na 138 mmol/L; weight 35 kg

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial fluid and insulin plan?

options.text: 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg bolus stat, then insulin 0.1 unit/kg/hour after the bolus
0.9% saline 10 mL/kg over 30 minutes, then commence insulin infusion immediately
Insulin 0.1 unit/kg/hour immediately followed by deficit replacement over 24 hours
Maintenance plus 5% deficit over 48 hours, no bolus, insulin 0.05 unit/kg/hour at 1 hour
Hartmann's bolus 20 mL/kg, then insulin 0.1 unit/kg/hour plus sodium bicarbonate

subtopic_detail: UTI imaging cascade for recurrent under 2 years
stem:
You are the general paediatrics registrar reviewing a 14-month-old girl referred by her GP after her second confirmed E coli urinary tract infection in 4 months. Both episodes were typical lower tract UTIs that responded clinically within 48 hours of oral cefalexin. Her antenatal renal ultrasound at 20 weeks was normal and she has had no hospital admissions.

She is well between episodes, growing along the 50th centile, and her examination today is unremarkable. Her urine culture from the most recent illness was 10^8 cfu/mL pure E coli, sensitive to cefalexin. Her family ask what investigation she now needs to look for a structural cause.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 110/min, BP 92/56 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Well; abdomen soft, non-tender; no flank fullness or scars; growth on 50th centile for weight and length
data_table.Investigations: Most recent urine: pure E coli 10^8 cfu/mL, sensitive to cefalexin; UEC and creatinine within normal limits; antenatal renal ultrasound normal at 20 weeks

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: DMSA renal cortical scan in 4 to 6 months to assess for cortical scarring
Micturating cystourethrogram urgently to exclude vesicoureteric reflux
Renal ultrasound during the current illness rather than after recovery
Combined DMSA scan plus MCUG to maximise diagnostic yield in this group
Renal ultrasound as an outpatient within 6 weeks of recovery

subtopic_detail: Sudden deterioration during treatment of acute asthma
stem: A 12-year-old boy being treated for acute severe asthma suddenly deteriorates during his third salbutamol nebuliser. He becomes agitated and his oxygen saturations fall despite a non-rebreather mask.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 170, RR 44, SpO2 84 percent, BP 82/50
data_table.Examination: Trachea deviated left, absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on the right

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Needle decompression of the right chest followed by a drain
Urgent portable chest radiograph before any further intervention
Intravenous magnesium sulfate and continuous nebulised salbutamol
Rapid sequence intubation with ketamine and positive pressure
Intravenous adrenaline infusion and a fluid bolus of 20 mL/kg

subtopic_detail: Septic workup in young infant under 3 months
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a tertiary ED reviewing a 5-week-old girl brought in by her parents with a 12 hour history of fever, poor feeding, and reduced activity. She was a term spontaneous vaginal delivery, GBS-unknown maternal status, and her mother had a urinary tract infection in late pregnancy. She has had no vaccines yet.

On examination she is lethargic and pale with a bulging anterior fontanelle and decreased tone. Capillary refill is 3 seconds and her extremities are cool. She has had no focal symptoms apart from one episode of vomiting after a small feed. Empirical antibiotics have not yet been given and the team has just sited an IV cannula and obtained blood cultures.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 188/min, BP 78/44 mmHg, RR 52/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, pale; bulging anterior fontanelle; reduced tone; capillary refill 3 seconds; cool peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Capillary BSL 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-7.8); blood cultures taken; FBC, UEC, CRP, lactate sent; LP not yet performed; venous gas pH 7.32, lactate 3.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate empirical antibiotic plan within the next hour?

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg alone after lumbar puncture is performed first in resus
IV cefotaxime 50 mg/kg plus IV amoxicillin 50 mg/kg within the hour, defer LP until stable
Urinalysis and blood cultures then await results before commencing antibiotics
IV gentamicin 7 mg/kg plus IV amoxicillin 50 mg/kg as sole empirical therapy
Discharge home on oral cefalexin with safety netting and review in 24 hours

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional ED reviewing an 18-month-old boy weighing 12 kg with 3 days of watery diarrhoea and 24 hours of vomiting. His mother reports he is drinking less and his last wet nappy was 6 hours ago. He has had no fever and no blood in the stool. He is fully vaccinated and otherwise well.
