On examination he is alert but listless with dry mucous membranes and capillary refill of 2.5 seconds. He has just vomited 5 mL of oral rehydration solution within 2 minutes of a small sip offered by his mother. His weight from last clinic visit 2 weeks ago was 12.6 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 144/min, BP 95/58 mmHg, RR 30/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert but listless; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 2.5 seconds; abdomen soft, non-tender; current weight 12 kg (previous 12.6 kg)
data_table.Investigations: Capillary BSL 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-7.8); UEC and ketones not yet performed; estimated dehydration 5% (mild-moderate)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management strategy?

options.text: 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg intravenous bolus then maintenance over 24 hours
Continued small sips of oral rehydration solution every 5 minutes and review in 1 hour
Single oral ondansetron 2 mg, then nasogastric ORS at 50 mL/kg over 4 hours
Loperamide 0.1 mg/kg orally plus continued oral rehydration solution and review
IV maintenance fluids alone without rehydration of the estimated deficit

subtopic_detail: Refractory paediatric septic shock inotrope escalation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a tertiary ED. A 6-month-old infant, weight 8 kg, has presented with rapidly progressive purpuric rash, fever, and reduced level of consciousness consistent with meningococcal sepsis. You have given IV ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg within 20 minutes of arrival and three sequential 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline boluses over 30 minutes (cumulative 60 mL/kg). The PICU registrar is on the phone and the retrieval team is 90 minutes away.

Despite the fluid resuscitation he remains mottled with capillary refill of 4 seconds, cool peripheries, and is now drowsy. The peripheral cannula remains patent. The intraosseous needle from the initial resuscitation is still in place in his left tibia. He has no known cardiac history and there is no clinical evidence of pulmonary oedema or hepatomegaly to suggest fluid overload.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 198/min, BP 60/32 mmHg, RR 50/min, SpO2 95% on 8 L/min mask, temperature 39.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy; widespread purpura; mottled, cool peripheries; capillary refill 4 seconds; chest clear; liver edge 1 cm below costal margin (unchanged from arrival)
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.21, lactate 6.5 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), HCO3 14 mmol/L (22-26), K 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 4.8 mmol/L; FBC and coags pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Fourth 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus over 15 minutes then reassess perfusion
Albumin 5% 20 mL/kg IV bolus as colloid replacement instead of further crystalloid
Whole blood transfusion 10 mL/kg empirically for possible occult haemorrhage
Peripheral adrenaline infusion 0.1 mcg/kg/min via intraosseous, intubate, request PICU
IV hydrocortisone 50 mg/m² stat for presumed adrenal insufficiency

subtopic_detail: Late-onset neonatal sepsis empirical antimicrobial choice
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional ED reviewing a 12-day-old term boy brought in lethargic and febrile by his parents. He was born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, mother GBS-negative, and was feeding well until 24 hours ago when intake halved. His parents report he has been increasingly hard to rouse, with a single brief episode of facial twitching this morning that lasted about 30 seconds.

On examination he is mottled with cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds, and a bulging anterior fontanelle. His tone is reduced and he has had no further seizure activity since arrival. Vesicles are not seen on the skin or mucous membranes. He has had no antibiotics, no IV fluids, and no blood cultures yet. The senior registrar from the children's hospital is on the phone preparing for retrieval.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 192/min, BP 62/34 mmHg, RR 56/min, SpO2 96% on 2 L nasal prong, temperature 38.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Mottled, cool peripheries; capillary refill 4 seconds; bulging anterior fontanelle; reduced tone; no vesicular rash
data_table.Investigations: Capillary BSL 2.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.8); venous pH 7.18, lactate 5.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); coags and LFTs pending; blood cultures not yet taken

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-hour management?

options.text: Lumbar puncture before any antibiotics to obtain accurate CSF microbiology
Withhold antibiotics until results of FBC, CRP, and blood culture are available
IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg as a single agent because Listeria risk falls after the first week
Resuscitate with 10 mL/kg crystalloid bolus and start IV amoxicillin alone
Resuscitate, defer LP, give IV cefotaxime plus amoxicillin plus aciclovir within the hour

stem:
An 11-month-old previously well boy is brought to the metropolitan emergency department with a 14 hour history of intermittent severe abdominal pain. The mother describes that he suddenly starts crying, draws his legs up to his tummy, then settles drowsily between episodes. He has had two non-bilious vomits and one dark slimy nappy this morning.

On examination he is quiet and pale between episodes but alert. The abdomen is soft with a long thin lump palpable in the right upper area; bowel sounds present. He has not had any recent gastroenteritis or weight loss, and there is no abdominal distension or guarding. Capillary refill is 2 seconds and peripheries are warm.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, palpable elongated mass right upper quadrant; no peritonism, no guarding, normal bowel sounds; nappy contains dark mucoid stool
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.36, lactate 1.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); FBC and electrolytes within normal limits; abdominal ultrasound shows target sign in right upper quadrant with ileocolic intussusception and no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Intravenous fluid resuscitation, paediatric surgical consultation, and image-guided air enema reduction by an interventional radiologist
Conservative bowel rest with intravenous fluids, nasogastric decompression, and clinical reassessment within the next 24 hours
Urgent open laparotomy and primary manual surgical reduction in the operating theatre overnight by the on-call paediatric surgical team
Outpatient paediatric gastroenterology referral for colonoscopy within the next 2 weeks for any further clinical evaluation
Trial of oral rehydration solution with reassessment of clinical status in the paediatric short stay unit after 4 hours

subtopic_detail: Pyloric stenosis - correcting electrolytes before surgery
stem:
A 5-week-old boy, born at term and previously thriving, is brought to the paediatric assessment unit with a 10 day history of progressively worsening vomiting after feeds. The mother describes vomiting as forceful, the milk shooting out across the cot, and the baby seems immediately hungry to feed again. The vomit has never contained any green colour.

His current weight is 7% below his weight at the 4 week health check. On examination he appears mildly dehydrated with sunken anterior fontanelle and dry mucous membranes. There is visible peristalsis across the upper abdomen; a small olive-like mass is palpable in the epigastrium during a test feed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 162/min, BP 82/50 mmHg, RR 38/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mildly dehydrated; visible peristaltic waves left to right across upper abdomen; firm olive-like mass palpable just lateral to right of epigastrium; normal nappy output today
data_table.Investigations: Na 132 mmol/L (135-145), K 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), Cl 88 mmol/L (98-107), HCO3 32 mmol/L (22-26), urea 7.5 mmol/L (2.5-7.0); pH 7.50; ultrasound pylorus 5 mm muscle thickness 18 mm length

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Transfer immediately to the operating theatre for pyloromyotomy within the next hour to relieve the obstruction
Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium replacement until chloride above 100 mmol/L and bicarbonate below 30 mmol/L, then surgery
Continue oral feeds with thickened formula at smaller volumes and review the response to feeding over the next 48 hours
Trial of oral erythromycin 10 mg/kg three times daily to improve gastric emptying and prevent need for surgery in this infant
Order an upper gastrointestinal contrast study to confirm diagnosis and exclude malrotation before any surgical intervention

subtopic_detail: Neonatal jaundice - phototherapy thresholds with negative coombs
stem:
A 5-day-old male infant born at 39+2 weeks via uncomplicated normal vaginal birth is reviewed in the neonatal home visit clinic at 108 hours of life. He is exclusively breastfed but feeding has been slow. The midwife reports him as visibly yellow to the mid-chest. His mother is blood group O Rhesus positive and the infant is A Rhesus positive.

On examination he is alert, well perfused, with normal tone and reflexes. There is no hepatosplenomegaly or bruising. Birth weight was 3450 g and current weight is 3210 g (7% loss). His direct antiglobulin test is negative and there are no spherocytes on film. A transcutaneous bilirubin reading of 320 micromol/L is confirmed by serum total bilirubin 332 micromol/L with conjugated fraction <5%.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, BP 72/45 mmHg, RR 44/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert and active; jaundice to mid-chest; no hepatosplenomegaly, bruising or cephalohaematoma; normal tone; weight 3210 g (7% below birth weight)
data_table.Investigations: Serum total bilirubin 332 micromol/L, conjugated 12 micromol/L; haemoglobin 165 g/L (140-200); reticulocyte count 3.0% (1-2); direct antiglobulin test negative; blood group A positive (mother O positive); peripheral film no spherocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure the parents that this represents physiological jaundice; encourage breastfeeding and arrange community midwife review in 48 hours
Replace all breastfeeds with formula for 48 hours and recheck serum bilirubin then with a view to restarting breastfeeding once it falls
Commence intensive phototherapy and recheck serum bilirubin in 4-6 hours with ongoing breastfeeding and lactation support
Arrange immediate exchange transfusion under neonatology supervision given the rapidly rising bilirubin level threatening kernicterus risk
Send thyroid function tests, urine culture, and G6PD assay before any treatment is started and await results overnight before intervening

subtopic_detail: Recurrent UTI in infant under 6 months - RCH imaging cascade
stem:
A 4-month-old previously well girl is reviewed in the paediatric clinic with her third confirmed urinary tract infection in 3 months. Each prior episode was suprapubic-aspirate-confirmed E. coli pyelonephritis treated with intravenous cefotaxime for 48 hours then oral co-trimoxazole to complete a 10 day course, with clinical defervescence by 36-48 hours each time.

She is exclusively breastfed, thriving on the 75th centile, with normal milestones and normal nappy output. Antenatal anomaly scan at 20 weeks was reported as normal. Her renal function and electrolytes have been within normal limits throughout. There is no family history of vesicoureteric reflux or renal disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, BP 88/52 mmHg, RR 32/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Well, thriving; soft non-tender abdomen; no palpable kidneys or bladder; nappy clear with no offensive odour
data_table.Investigations: Today's mid-stream-equivalent urine culture pending; urine dipstick at clinic positive nitrites and leucocytes; FBC, UEC, CRP within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next imaging investigation?

options.text: Micturating cystourethrogram during the current illness to identify and grade any vesicoureteric reflux for grading-based prophylaxis decisions
DMSA scintigraphy scan in 3 months to assess for cortical scarring as a screening test before considering reflux management options
CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder under sedation to assess anatomy and exclude stone disease as a recurrent UTI driver in this infant
Renal tract ultrasound during this current illness to assess anatomy, hydronephrosis, scarring proxies and bladder emptying as the first-line investigation
Repeat urine microscopy and culture monthly for 6 months without any imaging until a fourth episode is confirmed by laboratory testing on collected sample

subtopic_detail: Henoch Schonlein purpura with renal involvement
stem:
A 7-year-old boy is reviewed in the paediatric short-stay unit 5 days after developing a non-blanching rash on his buttocks, the back of his thighs and his shins. He has had bilateral ankle pain limiting his walking and complains of cramping tummy pains worse in the evenings. Today his mother noticed his urine has turned a dark cola-coloured shade.

He had a runny nose 10 days ago that has since resolved. On examination there is symmetrical palpable purpura on the buttocks, posterior thighs and shins, with mildly swollen tender ankles bilaterally. Abdomen is soft with mild diffuse tenderness, no peritonism. No oral lesions; no joint deformity. He had a primary varicella vaccination at age 1.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 118/76 mmHg, RR 20/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura on buttocks and lower limbs; symmetrical swollen tender ankles bilaterally; abdomen soft mildly tender, no guarding; no oral ulcers or scleritis
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis blood 3+, protein 2+; urine PCR 180 mg/mmol (<30); serum creatinine 38 micromol/L (estimated GFR 95 mL/min/1.73 m² by Schwartz); FBC, coagulation studies, electrolytes within normal limits; CRP 28 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day for 4 weeks now to prevent progression of nephritis and shorten the duration of arthritis pain symptoms
Methylprednisolone pulse 30 mg/kg intravenously daily for 3 days followed by oral taper and renal biopsy this admission to guide further care
Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg given as a single infusion over 12 hours for empirical immunomodulation of the cutaneous and renal disease activity
Reassurance with simple analgesia and discharge with GP review in 1 week, and re-presentation guidance for worsening symptoms or new features overall
Admit for blood pressure monitoring, daily urine protein creatinine ratio and serial creatinine over 7 days, with paediatric nephrology referral if proteinuria or hypertension persists

subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease - timing of IVIG within 10 days
stem:
A 3-year-old previously well boy is reviewed in the paediatric emergency department with day 6 of fever to 39.5 °C. He has had a polymorphous truncal rash for 4 days, bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate, cracked red lips and a strawberry tongue. There is a single right cervical lymph node measuring 2 cm, and his hands and feet became puffy yesterday with desquamation starting around his fingertips today.

He is irritable but consolable, drinking small volumes of fluids. There is no recent travel or sick contacts beyond his older sister with a cold. He completed all primary vaccinations on time. There is no history of immunodeficiency.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, BP 100/60 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 39.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Polymorphous truncal rash; bilateral non-exudative bulbar conjunctivitis; cracked red lips, strawberry tongue; right cervical node 2 cm; non-pitting oedema of hands and feet; peripheral desquamation
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.5 x10⁹/L (5.5-15.5), platelets 580 x10⁹/L (150-400), CRP 180 mg/L (<5), ESR 95 mm/h (<15), ALT 65 U/L (<40), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), urine analysis sterile pyuria 25 leucocytes/HPF

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg as a single infusion over 12 hours, plus aspirin 30-50 mg/kg/day in divided doses while febrile and a baseline echocardiogram
Aspirin 5 mg/kg daily monotherapy and reassessment for clinical response over the next 48 hours before any other treatment is added to the regimen now
Empirical intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg six-hourly and ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily for presumed staphylococcal or streptococcal scarlet-like illness today
Defer all definitive therapy until the echocardiogram is performed in the morning to confirm coronary involvement before any IVIG decision is made today
Discharge with parental advice on rash care, oral hydration support, paracetamol for fever, and paediatric outpatient follow-up review within the next week

stem:
A 2-year-old previously well girl is brought to a metropolitan emergency department by her parents after sudden onset fever to 39.5 °C and progressive lethargy over the past 6 hours. Her parents noticed two small purple spots appear on her legs in the last hour that did not fade when pressed with the side of a glass. She has had two episodes of vomiting.

She is drowsy but rousable to voice with weak cry. There is no neck stiffness. On examination peripheries are cool with capillary refill time 4 seconds. Two non-blanching petechiae 6 mm and 4 mm are present on her right shin and left thigh. There is no recent travel; her vaccinations are up to date including meningococcal B and meningococcal ACWY at appropriate ages.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168/min, BP 78/40 mmHg, RR 36/min, SpO2 95% room air, temperature 39.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, weak cry; cool peripheries, mottled; CRT 4 seconds; two non-blanching petechiae on lower limbs; no neck stiffness, fontanelle closed
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-6.5); intravenous access yet to be established; rapid bedside whole-blood lactate 4.5 mmol/L (<2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 50 mg/kg as a stat dose and arrange urgent transfer by paediatric retrieval to the nearest tertiary paediatric centre overnight
Establish IV or IO access, give IV ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg with blood cultures, commence 20 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9% bolus, and activate paediatric retrieval
Perform lumbar puncture immediately to obtain CSF microscopy and culture before any antibiotic is given so as not to compromise organism identification today
Administer dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg intravenously immediately before any antibiotic is given to reduce inflammatory complications and neurological sequelae from infection
Observe with continuous monitoring for the next 30 minutes while awaiting blood culture results before deciding on definitive antibiotic therapy and access strategy

subtopic_detail: Bacterial tracheitis - airway emergency after failed croup treatment
stem:
A 5-year-old girl who presented to the paediatric emergency department 36 hours ago with classic croup symptoms (barking cough, hoarse voice, mild stridor at rest) was treated with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and discharged after observation when her stridor settled. She represents today with worsening stridor at rest, high fever to 39 °C, and a toxic appearance. She received a second dose of dexamethasone and one nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 in the ambulance with minimal improvement.

On arrival she sits upright leaning forward and is noticeably distressed but cooperative. There is loud biphasic stridor at rest, marked tracheal tenderness to gentle palpation, and minimal drooling. Auscultation reveals transmitted upper airway sounds. There is no neck mass.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158/min, BP 105/65 mmHg, RR 42/min, SpO2 91% room air, temperature 39.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Toxic appearance; biphasic stridor at rest; tracheal tenderness on palpation; mild tracheal tug; minimal oral secretions; chest auscultation transmitted sounds only
data_table.Investigations: Blood cultures sent; FBC WCC 22 x10⁹/L (5.5-15.5), CRP 220 mg/L (<5); no imaging yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 and second dose of oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg with ongoing observation in the paediatric resuscitation bay for response
Obtain a lateral neck X-ray to confirm the diagnosis and exclude epiglottitis before any decision on airway intervention is made in the next hour today
Urgent ENT and anaesthetic-led airway evaluation in operating theatre under inhalational induction with intubation, then IV flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg six-hourly plus IV cefotaxime
Trial of high-flow heliox 70:30 mixture and high-flow nasal cannula in the paediatric ward bay with reassessment of work of breathing over the next hour while awaiting bloods
Empirical IV amoxicillin alone targeting Haemophilus influenzae as the most likely organism, with reassessment of airway pending response to antibiotic treatment over the next 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Foreign body aspiration - rigid bronchoscopy under GA
stem:
An 18-month-old boy is brought to the paediatric emergency department after a sudden coughing fit while eating peanuts at his older brother's birthday party 6 hours ago. He recovered quickly with a few coughs but has had a persistent mild cough and intermittent wheeze for the past 4 hours. His parents report he ate a handful of nuts before the choking episode.

He is alert, smiling and not in respiratory distress at rest. On auscultation there are decreased breath sounds and expiratory wheeze localised to the right side. The left side has normal vesicular breath sounds. There is no stridor and no cyanosis. He has no fever and no past respiratory history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124/min, BP 100/65 mmHg, RR 32/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Comfortable at rest; decreased breath sounds and expiratory wheeze right side; left lung normal vesicular sounds; no stridor, no cyanosis; no chest wall asymmetry
data_table.Investigations: Inspiratory and expiratory chest X-ray shows hyperinflation of right lung on expiratory film with mediastinal shift to left; no radiopaque foreign body visible

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Trial of nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg via face mask, observe respiratory response over the next 60 minutes and discharge if symptoms resolve with parental advice
Postural drainage and supervised chest physiotherapy regimen to dislodge the foreign body, with reassessment of breath sounds and air entry afterwards on serial examination
Flexible bronchoscopy under conscious sedation in the radiology suite to visualise and assess airway anatomy before any decision on operative removal is made
Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia in operating theatre with ENT and anaesthetic teams for both confirmation and definitive removal of the foreign body today
Discharge home with parental education on red-flag respiratory symptoms and arrange a planned outpatient paediatric review within 48 hours to reassess clinical status

subtopic_detail: Testicular torsion - direct to theatre without imaging delay
stem:
A 14-year-old boy is brought to the metropolitan emergency department by his father with a 5 hour history of sudden severe left scrotal pain that woke him from sleep at 2 am. The pain is constant and rated 9 out of 10. He has had two episodes of vomiting. There is no history of trauma, no recent unprotected sexual activity, and no urinary symptoms.

On examination he is in severe distress lying still. The left hemiscrotum is swollen, exquisitely tender, with the testis riding high and lying transversely. The left cremasteric reflex is absent. The right testis is normal in position and lie with a normal cremasteric reflex. There is no urethral discharge.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 110/min, BP 130/78 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Left hemiscrotum swollen, exquisitely tender; testis high-riding and transverse; absent left cremasteric reflex; right testis normal lie and position with intact cremasteric reflex; no urethral discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis clear; no nitrites, no leucocytes, no blood; FBC and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Urgent colour Doppler ultrasound of the scrotum to assess testicular blood flow before any surgical decision is made on operative management of this presentation
Procedural sedation in emergency department with manual detorsion attempt by rotating testis outward (book opening direction) and surgical exploration only if pain does not resolve immediately
Empirical IV cefotaxime 50 mg/kg and supportive analgesia for presumed acute epididymo-orchitis with reassessment in 4 hours for response to antimicrobial therapy
Discharge home with analgesia and urgent next-day outpatient urology clinic review for further assessment and definitive imaging in the morning at the earliest opportunity
Direct transfer to the operating theatre for scrotal exploration, manual detorsion and bilateral orchidopexy under general anaesthesia by the on-call urologist without further investigations

subtopic_detail: Convulsive status epilepticus - second dose of benzodiazepine
stem:
A 4-year-old previously well boy is brought to the metropolitan emergency department by paramedics after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure that began at school 12 minutes ago. Paramedics gave a single dose of buccal midazolam 5 mg en route 6 minutes ago without effect. He continues to seize on arrival.

He has no prior history of seizures. He has been febrile with a 24 hour history of viral upper respiratory tract symptoms. There is no head trauma, no toxic exposure, and no relevant family history. No peripheral intravenous access has yet been established. The on-call paediatric registrar is at bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 162/min, BP 105/68 mmHg, RR 30/min via bag-valve-mask 100% oxygen, SpO2 96% with oxygen, temperature 39.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Continuous generalised tonic-clonic activity; pupils equal and reactive; jaw not relaxed; airway patent with manoeuvres; no purpura, no rash, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.2 mmol/L (3.5-6.5); ECG sinus tachycardia rate 162; no other investigations yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Intramuscular midazolam 0.15 mg/kg now, while preparing IV or IO access and second-line agent if seizure continues beyond 15 minutes from onset
Phenytoin 20 mg/kg intravenously over 20 minutes once IV access is obtained as the second-line definitive agent for ongoing convulsive seizure activity in this child
Levetiracetam 40 mg/kg intravenously as a single rapid bolus over 5 minutes immediately, without further benzodiazepine, given the seizure has continued past first benzo dose now
Rapid sequence intubation with thiopentone 5 mg/kg now and admission to paediatric intensive care for thiopentone infusion and continuous EEG monitoring with neurology input
Urgent CT head before further pharmacological intervention to exclude an acute structural cause for status epilepticus such as bleed or space-occupying lesion or hydrocephalus

stem:
A 2-year-old girl presents to the metropolitan emergency department with septic shock and a 12 hour history of fever, lethargy and reduced wet nappies. She has cool mottled peripheries with delayed capillary refill, is drowsy and minimally responsive. Two attempts at peripheral venous cannulation by the paediatric emergency registrar over the past 75 seconds have failed; both attempts targeted antecubital fossae.

The paediatric retrieval team has been called and is 30 minutes away. The team is preparing for further peripheral attempts. Empirical antibiotics are drawn up and ready. The mother is at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 188/min, BP 65/40 mmHg, RR 50/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 39.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 12; cool mottled peripheries; capillary refill >5 seconds; respiratory rate elevated with shallow effort; no rash or purpura
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.5 mmol/L (3.5-6.5); rapid bedside lactate 5.5 mmol/L (<2.0); blood cultures yet to be obtained because peripheral access failed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for vascular access?

options.text: Continue peripheral intravenous cannulation attempts for up to 5 more minutes by the most experienced operator available before considering alternative access strategies
Insert intraosseous needle into proximal tibia 1-2 cm below tibial tuberosity on medial flat surface, commence resuscitation including fluid bolus 20 mL/kg and IV antibiotics now
Wait for paediatric anaesthetist or retrieval team to insert ultrasound-guided central venous catheter once they arrive on site within the next 30 minutes for definitive resuscitation access
Perform venous cut-down to the long saphenous vein at the ankle by paediatric surgical registrar in the next 10 minutes to achieve large-bore access for ongoing resuscitation
Administer subcutaneous fluids via the hyaluronidase-assisted hypodermoclysis technique into both thighs while continuing peripheral attempts for next ten minutes with senior clinician

subtopic_detail: Toxic shock syndrome - clindamycin and source control
stem:
A 14-year-old girl presents to the paediatric emergency department on day 4 of menstruation with fever to 40 °C, diffuse erythematous rash that looks like sunburn, watery diarrhoea and one episode of vomiting over the past 24 hours. She is confused and unable to give a coherent history. She is using high-absorbency tampons.

On examination she is in shock with cool peripheries and capillary refill 4 seconds. The rash is a diffuse blanching erythroderma over the trunk and limbs without target lesions. There is non-purulent conjunctival injection and a strawberry tongue. A tampon is in situ on examination. No surgical wound, no skin abscess. Vaccinations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140/min, BP 75/40 mmHg, RR 30/min, SpO2 95% room air, temperature 40.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Confused, GCS 13; diffuse blanching erythroderma; conjunctival injection; strawberry tongue; tampon in situ; cool peripheries CRT 4 seconds; no abscess or wound
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18 x10⁹/L (4-11), platelets 130 x10⁹/L (150-400), Na 130 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 180 micromol/L (45-90), CK 880 U/L (<200), ALT 95 U/L (<40), INR 1.4 (0.9-1.2), lactate 4.5 mmol/L (<2.0); blood cultures sent

lead_in: After IV access, 20 mL/kg sodium chloride bolus, and PICU activation, what is the most appropriate antimicrobial and source control strategy?

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 15 mg/kg six-hourly monotherapy with tampon removal at presentation and supportive intensive care management of fluid resuscitation and inotropes
Intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg daily and metronidazole 12.5 mg/kg eight-hourly without tampon removal, escalation only if antibiotic response is poor over the first 24 hours
Intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg six-hourly plus clindamycin 15 mg/kg eight-hourly, immediate tampon removal as source control, and consider IVIG 1-2 g/kg if shock is refractory
Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg six-hourly as broad-spectrum monotherapy with delayed tampon removal once shock has been adequately stabilised over the first 4 hours of care
Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily plus intravenous gentamicin 7 mg/kg daily for empirical sepsis cover pending blood culture and microbiology susceptibility results overnight

subtopic_detail: Exertional heatstroke - cold water immersion target
stem:
A 16-year-old male competitive runner collapses 9 km into a 10 km charity run on a 38 °C ambient temperature day. Paramedics arrive within 8 minutes and find him confused, ataxic, with hot dry red skin and a tympanic core temperature of 41.2 °C. There is no history of seizure, drug use, or psychiatric medication. He has no significant medical history.

On arrival to the paediatric emergency department he is confused (GCS 13), unable to stand, with profound hyperthermia. He is hypotensive and tachycardic. He has not had any oral fluids since the start of the race 90 minutes ago and last urinated 4 hours ago before the start.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140/min, BP 95/55 mmHg, RR 32/min, SpO2 99% room air, tympanic temperature 41.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Confused GCS 13; hot dry red skin; no rash, no neck stiffness; ataxic gait; muscles tender to palpation; no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Na 148 mmol/L (135-145), K 5.5 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 200 micromol/L (45-90), CK 8000 U/L (<200), lactate 6.2 mmol/L (<2.0), pH 7.30, HCO3 16 mmol/L (22-26); urinalysis 3+ blood, no red cells on microscopy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate cooling strategy?

options.text: Tepid sponging and oral cold fluids in resus bay with active cooling fan only, antipyretic paracetamol 1 g orally, monitor over the next hour for response to passive cooling measures
Paracetamol 1 g orally and evaporative cooling with continuous fanning of misted skin alone in resus bay aiming to cool gradually over the next 60 minutes with reassessment
Endovascular cooling catheter insertion via right femoral vein in resus bay with target temperature 36 °C over the next 60 minutes under continuous arterial line monitoring of core
Immediate cold water immersion target core temperature of 39 °C achieved within 30 minutes, with continuous rectal probe core temperature monitoring throughout the cooling intervention period
Whole body application of ice packs to neck axillae and groin without water immersion, with continuous rectal probe monitoring of core temperature to a target of 36 °C over 60 minutes

subtopic_detail: Tracheo-oesophageal fistula recognition at first feed
stem:
A newborn boy at 12 hours of life, born at 39 weeks via uncomplicated normal vaginal birth to a primigravida mother, develops frothy white secretions from the mouth and brief desaturation to 85% during his first attempted breastfeed in the postnatal ward. He coughed, spluttered, and recovered to baseline saturations on room air within 90 seconds without intervention. He has been spitting up small amounts of clear fluid between feeds since birth.

Antenatal anomaly scan at 20 weeks was reported as polyhydramnios with amniotic fluid index 26 cm; no other anomaly was visualised. Family history is non-contributory. On examination he is alert and pink on room air. The abdomen is scaphoid. There is no facial or limb anomaly. Cardiac examination is normal with no murmur.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, BP 70/40 mmHg, RR 50/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, pink on air; frothy oral secretions reaccumulating; scaphoid abdomen; no facial dysmorphism; symmetric chest movements; no cardiac murmur; anus patent
data_table.Investigations: Routine antenatal serology negative; no postnatal investigations yet performed; no vertebral or limb anomaly on cursory examination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Trial of paced bottle feeds with thickened formula and reassessment of feeding tolerance over the next 24 hours in the postnatal ward with lactation consultant support and review
Discharge with home apnoea monitor and lactation support with paediatric outpatient review within 7 days for ongoing reassessment of feeding and breathing in the home environment
Echocardiogram only as the priority investigation today, as cardiac anomalies are common in this cohort, before any consideration of further alimentary tract investigations or surgical referral
Barium swallow study under fluoroscopy this morning to dynamically assess swallowing mechanics and detect any tracheal communication before paediatric surgical referral is finalised today
Pass a 10 French orogastric tube to estimate distance to coiling or resistance, then obtain a plain chest and abdominal X-ray to assess tube position and gas pattern, and refer to paediatric surgery

stem:
A 5-month-old boy is admitted to a regional paediatric ward with 3 days of coryza followed by 24 hours of laboured breathing and reduced feeding. He is taking about 50% of usual milk volumes and has wet nappies 4 hourly. He was born at 38 weeks gestation with no perinatal complications and has no chronic conditions.

On arrival he is alert with moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, widespread fine inspiratory crackles, and scattered wheeze. Nasopharyngeal aspirate returns positive for respiratory syncytial virus. He has been on room air for the first 4 hours, with SpO2 fluctuating between 88% and 91%. Low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min has been running for the past 2 hours and SpO2 is now persistently 89%-90% with ongoing moderate work of breathing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168/min, BP 88/52 mmHg, RR 62/min, SpO2 90% on 1 L/min nasal prong, temperature 37.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, no head bobbing, no apnoeas; bilateral crackles and wheeze; capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.34, pCO2 48 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, lactate 1.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); nasopharyngeal aspirate RSV positive; chest x-ray hyperinflation only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Commence high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with heated humidified oxygen titrated to maintain SpO2 at 90% or above
Increase low-flow nasal prong oxygen from 1 L/min to 4 L/min through the standard nasal prongs and continue monitoring in the ward
Continue low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min and reassess work of breathing and saturations again in another 2 hours
Administer a 5 mg salbutamol nebuliser and reassess respiratory effort and oxygen requirement 20 minutes after the dose has finished
Switch directly to bilevel positive airway pressure via tight-fitting face mask in the high dependency area for ongoing respiratory support

stem:
A 13-month-old girl is brought to a paediatric emergency department 15 minutes after a single bite of a peanut butter sandwich at home. The parents report rapid onset of facial swelling, widespread red blotchy rash on the trunk, persistent harsh barking cough, and one episode of vomiting on the way to hospital. She has known egg and dairy allergy but no previous reaction to peanut.

In the resuscitation cubicle she is alert but distressed with audible inspiratory stridor and bilateral wheeze. A cot weight is unavailable but a recent weighing card states 11 kg. Intravenous access has not yet been established. The nurse has the paediatric anaphylaxis tray open and is asking which adrenaline dose to draw up.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 172/min, BP 78/40 mmHg, RR 48/min, SpO2 93% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Lip and periorbital oedema, urticarial rash trunk and limbs; inspiratory stridor with bilateral wheeze; capillary refill 3 seconds; not yet cannulated
data_table.Investigations: Bedside investigations deferred pending resuscitation; weight on weighing card 11 kg (no current cot weight)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate single best initial adrenaline dose and route?

options.text: Adrenaline 110 micrograms (0.11 mg of 1:1000) intramuscular into the anterolateral mid-thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if no response
Adrenaline 50 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1:10 000) slow intravenous bolus over 5 minutes after rapid IV cannulation has been established
Adrenaline 300 micrograms (0.30 mg of 1:1000) intramuscular into the anterolateral mid-thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if no response
Adrenaline 150 micrograms (0.15 mg of 1:1000) intramuscular into the anterolateral mid-thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if no response
Adrenaline 5 mg nebulised (5 mL of 1:1000) via face mask immediately to treat the upper airway oedema and the audible stridor

stem:
A 22-month-old boy is brought to a metropolitan emergency department with 36 hours of profuse non-bloody diarrhoea and 24 hours of vomiting up to 6 times daily. His older brother had similar symptoms last week. Parents report he is taking small sips of water but vomiting most of them.

He is alert but irritable on assessment. He weighs 12 kg today; the family Red Book records 12.7 kg three weeks ago. Eyes appear sunken, mouth is dry, capillary refill is 2 to 3 seconds, peripheries are warm. He has had no wet nappy for 6 hours. A first dose of oral ondansetron 2 mg was given on triage 30 minutes ago and he has just vomited again. He has no abdominal distension, no peritonism, no bilious vomit, and no blood in the stool.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 142/min, BP 92/60 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, soft non-tender abdomen, no organomegaly; capillary refill 2-3 seconds; weight loss 5.5%
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.34, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, lactate 2.1 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); urea and electrolytes within normal limits; venous glucose 4.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Encourage small frequent oral sips of clear fluids at home and review with the general practitioner in the next 24 to 48 hours for clinical reassessment
Insert an intravenous cannula and administer a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus over the next 30 minutes followed by maintenance intravenous fluids
Insert a nasogastric tube and commence oral rehydration solution at 25 mL/kg over the first hour followed by ongoing maintenance plus deficit
Repeat ondansetron 4 mg orally and reassess oral fluid tolerance again in 30 minutes before considering any further intervention or escalation
Send urgent stool sample for microscopy culture sensitivity and rotavirus PCR before commencing any active rehydration to confirm the underlying cause

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease in an infant
stem:
A 7-month-old girl is reviewed on day 7 of a febrile illness in a regional paediatric ward. Persistent daily fevers to 39.5 °C have not responded to paracetamol or ibuprofen; oral amoxicillin started by the GP on day 3 has made no difference. She has been miserable, off feeds, and her mother reports erythema of the hands which has now begun to peel around the fingertips.

On examination she has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, a faint perineal rash, and a single 1.5 cm cervical lymph node. Lips are red but not fissured. There is no oropharyngeal exudate. Three of the five classical Kawasaki criteria are present. Inflammatory markers are markedly elevated and a transaminitis is noted; urine has sterile pyuria. A focused echocardiogram has been arranged and is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158/min, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 36/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival injection bilateral non-exudative, single 1.5 cm cervical node, perineal rash, peeling fingertips; no joint swelling; mild hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: CRP 145 mg/L (<5), ESR 78 mm/h, WCC 18.4 x10^9/L with neutrophilia, platelets 612 x10^9/L, ALT 96 U/L (<35); urine microscopy 80 x10^6/L leucocytes with negative culture; albumin 28 g/L (35-50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Wait for completion of the echocardiogram and only commence treatment if coronary artery z-score is greater than 2.5 on the formal report
Continue supportive care alone and reassess clinically in 48 hours given that classical criteria for Kawasaki disease are not yet fully met
Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours together with high-dose aspirin pending the formal echocardiogram report
Switch oral amoxicillin to intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily for empirical cover of an unidentified bacterial focus before any other intervention
Commence a 3-day course of intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg/day as primary therapy and review the response after the third pulse

stem:
A 5-year-old boy with newly diagnosed B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukaemia presents to a metropolitan paediatric emergency department on day 10 of induction chemotherapy. The mother brings him in because of a single fever to 38.6 °C tympanic and a brief shaking chill. He has a tunnelled central venous line in place that looks clean and is non-tender.

He appears tired but alert, with capillary refill of 2 seconds and warm peripheries. There is no oral mucositis, no abdominal tenderness, no perianal tenderness, and no focal infective findings on examination. The leukaemia treatment team has been notified. Blood cultures have been drawn from both line lumens and a peripheral site. Empirical antibiotic choice is being prepared in the resuscitation cubicle.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, BP 102/60 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Central line site clean and non-tender, no oral mucositis, soft abdomen, no perianal tenderness, no skin lesions
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophil count 0.3 x10^9/L, platelets 42 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 92 g/L; CRP 65 mg/L; venous lactate 1.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); chest x-ray clear; urine microscopy bland; blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical intravenous antibiotic regimen for this child?

options.text: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg per dose every 6 hours as monotherapy after blood cultures have been drawn from line and peripheral sites
Intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily plus oral amoxicillin twice daily for empirical streptococcal and gram-negative cover until cultures are reported
Intravenous vancomycin 15 mg/kg every 6 hours and intravenous gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg once daily without any beta-lactam pending final blood culture results
Intravenous meropenem 20 mg/kg every 8 hours immediately as empirical broad-spectrum cover and add filgrastim 5 mcg/kg subcutaneously on the day of admission
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily combined with oral ciprofloxacin discharge home with daily outpatient haematology phone review

subtopic_detail: Hypercyanotic spell in tetralogy of Fallot
stem:
A 10-month-old girl with known unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after a brief episode at home of inconsolable crying, deepening lip colour, and limpness. She has previously had two milder spells which resolved as her mother brought her knees to her chest. The cardiology team is aware and a primary repair is planned for next month.

In the resuscitation bay she is irritable but rousable. SpO2 has been 72% to 78% on room air for the last 10 minutes despite knee-to-chest positioning by the parent and 8 L/min facemask oxygen. She has a barely audible right upper sternal edge systolic murmur. Peripheries are cool and dusky. Capillary refill is 4 seconds centrally. Intravenous access has been established. Cardiology has been called and is en route.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 184/min, BP 78/44 mmHg, RR 56/min, SpO2 76% on 8 L/min mask, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Central cyanosis, knees drawn up to chest, soft systolic ejection murmur (previously grade 3, now grade 1), cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.18, lactate 5.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), bicarbonate 14 mmol/L; haemoglobin 168 g/L; venous glucose 5.2 mmol/L; bedside echo deferred to inpatient team

lead_in: After positioning, oxygen, and intravenous fluid bolus, what is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion at 0.05 micrograms/kg/min to keep the ductus arteriosus open and improve oxygenated pulmonary blood flow at this age
Intravenous adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg push as inotropic support given the cool peripheries and the prolonged centralised capillary refill time of 4 seconds
Intravenous morphine 0.1 mg/kg by slow injection to reduce hyperpnoea and break the spiral of right ventricular outflow tract spasm and cyanosis
Intravenous furosemide 1 mg/kg to offload the right ventricle and reduce pulmonary congestion before the cardiology team arrives at the bedside
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg as an immediate buffer for the metabolic acidosis demonstrated on the bedside venous blood gas analysis

stem:
A 4-week-old boy is reviewed at a paediatric outpatient clinic for severe constipation since birth. The mother reports he did not pass any stool until day 3 of life when a paediatric resident performed a digital examination at the maternity ward, which produced a forceful explosion of meconium. Since then he opens his bowels only every 4 to 5 days with marked straining, and only after a glycerine suppository.

He is bottle fed with standard formula and is on the 25th centile for weight (down from the 50th at birth). The abdomen is mildly distended without visible bowel loops. There is no inguinal hernia and the perianal area looks normal. A focused examination shows a tight anus with an explosive release of gas and watery stool after the examining finger is removed. Plain abdominal x-ray shows dilated bowel loops with absent rectal gas.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140/min, BP 78/48 mmHg, RR 38/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Mild abdominal distension, soft non-tender abdomen, tight anus with explosive release of gas and stool on rectal examination; weight 25th centile, length 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Plain abdominal x-ray dilated proximal bowel with reduced rectal gas; haemoglobin 132 g/L, electrolytes within normal limits; thyroid stimulating hormone 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); coeliac serology not yet sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the underlying diagnosis?

options.text: Trial of macrogol osmotic laxative for 4 weeks at maintenance dose and review the response in clinic before considering invasive testing or referral
Suction rectal biopsy at the appropriate level above the dentate line obtained at a paediatric surgical centre for histopathology
Sweat chloride test conducted on at least two occasions to exclude cystic fibrosis as the underlying cause for the meconium plug and constipation
Anorectal manometry to demonstrate the absence of the rectoanal inhibitory reflex via balloon distension under conscious sedation by paediatric gastroenterology
Barium enema with full bowel preparation to look for the transition zone on imaging and confirm the diagnosis before progressing to definitive surgical management

subtopic_detail: Hyperammonaemia presentation in late-onset urea cycle disorder
stem:
A 2-year-old boy is transferred from a regional emergency department after 12 hours of vomiting and progressive drowsiness. His family had a high-protein BBQ dinner the night before symptoms began. He was previously well except for two unexplained encephalopathic episodes at 9 and 14 months that were attributed to viral gastroenteritis. An older male sibling died unexpectedly at 18 months overseas; cause of death is not documented.

On arrival he opens eyes only to painful stimuli and has hyperventilation without obvious respiratory distress. There is no fever, neck stiffness, or focal neurology. Initial investigations done at the referring hospital show normal sodium, glucose, lactate, ketones, ammonia not measured. A repeat venous blood gas in your department shows respiratory alkalosis. Plasma ammonia returns markedly elevated; lactate is normal; the rest of the metabolic screen is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, BP 108/68 mmHg, RR 36/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.2 °C
data_table.Examination: GCS E2 V2 M4 (8/15), pupils equal and reactive, no focal deficit, no rash, no organomegaly, no signs of trauma
data_table.Investigations: Plasma ammonia 480 micromol/L (<50), arterial blood gas pH 7.52 pCO2 28 mmHg HCO3 22 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), glucose 5.4 mmol/L, urine ketones negative, sodium 138 mmol/L, anion gap normal; CT brain no acute findings

lead_in: Beyond intubation and intensive care transfer, what is the single most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous dextrose 10% at 1.5 times maintenance rate plus intralipid 20% infusion and stop all enteral protein intake while awaiting metabolic team review
Give intravenous mannitol 0.5 g/kg over 20 minutes to manage incipient cerebral oedema and continue conservative metabolic management with regular ammonia rechecks
Administer intravenous sodium benzoate 250 mg/kg load followed by sodium phenylbutyrate 250 mg/kg over 90 minutes and reassess ammonia level in 2 hours
Initiate urgent extracorporeal continuous renal replacement therapy via central access at a tertiary centre to remove ammonia mechanically and rapidly
Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg and aciclovir 20 mg/kg pending the lumbar puncture and CSF analysis to exclude a viral or bacterial cause of encephalopathy

stem:
An 18-month-old boy presents to the emergency department at 02:00 with a barking cough that began two days ago following coryza. Overnight he woke with noisy breathing audible from his cot. He has had no fevers above 38.0 degrees Celsius and is taking sips of water.

On arrival you hear inspiratory stridor at rest while he sits calmly on his mother's lap, with mild intercostal recession. He speaks in short sentences and is not drooling. Vital signs are within normal limits for age. There is no urticaria, no preceding choking episode, and immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits for age
data_table.Examination: inspiratory stridor at rest, mild intercostal recession, calm and well perfused, no drooling, oropharynx unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: clinical diagnosis, no imaging or bloods performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate corticosteroid management?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose now
Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single dose now
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with cardiac monitoring
Inhaled salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer with face mask now
Discharge home with paracetamol and humidified air advice

subtopic_detail: First febrile UTI imaging cascade in toddlers (RCH)
stem:
A 14-month-old girl presents with two days of fever to 39.2 degrees Celsius and reduced feeding. There is no rash, no respiratory symptoms, and no clear focus on examination. A clean-catch midstream urine sample collected with a maternal-assist technique grows greater than 10^8 colony-forming-units per litre of pure Escherichia coli, sensitive to trimethoprim and cefalexin.

She defervesces within 36 hours of starting oral trimethoprim and is feeding normally by review at 48 hours. Her antenatal scans were normal, she is fully immunised, and her growth tracks the 50th centile. There is no history of constipation, no abdominal mass, and no family history of vesicoureteric reflux.

data_table.Vital signs: afebrile at review, otherwise within normal limits
data_table.Examination: well perfused, no abdominal mass, normal external genitalia, no spinal anomaly
data_table.Investigations: MSU pure growth >10^8 CFU/L E. coli (sensitive to trimethoprim and cefalexin), renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging recommendation?

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound during the acute illness, before discharge
No routine imaging; arrange clinical review and treat any recurrence promptly
DMSA scan at 4 to 6 months to assess for renal cortical scarring
Micturating cystourethrogram to exclude vesicoureteric reflux
Outpatient renal ultrasound within 6 weeks of completing antibiotics

subtopic_detail: Investigation and antibiotic use in bronchiolitis
stem: A 6-month-old boy admitted with respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis is on day 3 of illness. He is febrile, is feeding two thirds of normal and is maintaining his saturations in room air.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 150, RR 52, SpO2 93 percent in room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recession, widespread crackles and wheeze, alert

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue supportive care without radiography or antibiotic therapy
Arrange a chest radiograph and start intravenous benzylpenicillin
Arrange a chest radiograph and start oral amoxicillin for 5 days
Send blood cultures and start intravenous ceftriaxone empirically
Start oral azithromycin and arrange a chest radiograph in the morning

subtopic_detail: Henoch-Schonlein purpura with renal warning features
stem:
A 7-year-old girl presents to the paediatric emergency department with a one-week history of palpable purpura over the buttocks and shins, intermittent crampy abdominal pain, and bilateral ankle swelling. Her parents report her urine has been a darker colour than usual for the past 48 hours. She had a viral upper respiratory infection 10 days earlier and is otherwise well.

On examination she is alert with pulse 96, blood pressure 132 by 88 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 100 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. There is no rash above the waist and joints are not actively inflamed. Urinalysis shows protein 3+ and blood 3+. Serum creatinine is 92 micromol/L (35-65), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), and renal tract ultrasound is structurally normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 132/88, RR 18, SpO2 100% room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: palpable purpura buttocks and shins, bilateral ankle oedema, abdomen soft, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: urinalysis protein 3+ blood 3+; creatinine 92 micromol/L (35-65); albumin 28 g/L (35-50); renal ultrasound structurally normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Symptomatic care with simple analgesia and primary-care review in one week
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg for two weeks with outpatient paediatric review
Commence amoxicillin pending blood cultures and admit for observation
Admit for blood-pressure management and urgent paediatric nephrology referral for biopsy
Send antinuclear antibody and ANCA panel and review when results return

subtopic_detail: Pre-transfer benzylpenicillin in suspected meningococcal sepsis
stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to a rural emergency department by his parents after waking unwell with fever, irritability, and a rash that began 90 minutes before arrival. The parents describe him as 'floppy' and unwilling to be put down.

On examination he is mottled, with pulse 180, blood pressure 72 by 40 mmHg, respiratory rate 44, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill at the sternum is 5 seconds. There are non-blanching purple spots over the lower limbs and trunk, expanding under observation. He does not have neck stiffness and is rousable but drowsy. Intravenous access has failed twice. The nearest paediatric retrieval team estimates 75 minutes to arrival.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 180, BP 72/40, RR 44, SpO2 95% room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: mottled, CRT 5 sec, non-blanching purpuric rash expanding under observation, drowsy but rousable
data_table.Investigations: no peripheral IV access after two attempts; venous lactate from initial draw 6.2 mmol/L (<2.0)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next action while preparing intraosseous access?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics until blood cultures can be obtained via the IO line
Give intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg before any antibiotic dose
Give intramuscular benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg into the lateral thigh now
Defer all antibiotics until paediatric retrieval team arrival in 75 minutes
Attempt a third peripheral cannula for fluid resuscitation before any antibiotic

subtopic_detail: Fluid resuscitation in paediatric DKA with shock
stem:
A 9-year-old girl with no past medical history is brought in by ambulance with two weeks of polyuria and polydipsia followed by 24 hours of vomiting and abdominal pain. The paramedics report she has become progressively more drowsy in the past hour.

In the resuscitation bay she has pulse 144, blood pressure 86 by 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 with Kussmaul pattern, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill at the sternum is 4 seconds and peripheries are cool. GCS is 13 (E3 V4 M6). Bedside blood glucose is 32 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), beta-hydroxybutyrate is 5.8 mmol/L (<0.6), venous pH 7.05 and bicarbonate 6 mmol/L (22-32). She weighs 28 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 144, BP 86/48, RR 38 with Kussmaul breathing, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: drowsy GCS 13, cool peripheries, CRT 4 sec at sternum, dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: BSL 32 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.8 mmol/L (<0.6), pH 7.05, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L (22-32), Na 132, K 5.1, weight 28 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid bolus?

options.text: Insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/h commenced immediately with no fluid bolus
20 mL/kg of 0.9 percent sodium chloride over 5 to 10 minutes, then reassess
20 mL/kg of compound sodium lactate over 5 to 10 minutes, then reassess
10 mL/kg of 0.9 percent sodium chloride over 30 minutes, then reassess
Sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 60 minutes to correct severe acidosis

subtopic_detail: Classical galactosaemia in the septic neonate
stem:
A 9-day-old infant born at term to consanguineous parents is admitted with 24 hours of poor feeding, lethargy, and progressive jaundice. Antenatal screening was unremarkable and the newborn screening sample was sent on day 3 but results are not yet back.

On examination he is jaundiced, hypotonic, with pulse 180, respiratory rate 60, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 38.1 degrees Celsius. The liver is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin. Red-reflex examination at the cot reveals reduced reflex bilaterally with a grey haze.

Investigations: conjugated bilirubin 80 micromol/L (<5), ALT 220 U/L (<40), INR 2.1 (0.8-1.2), bedside glucose 1.8 mmol/L (3.0-6.0), blood culture preliminary growth of Gram-negative rods (later confirmed Escherichia coli), urine reducing substances strongly positive.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 180, RR 60, SpO2 95% room air, temperature 38.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: jaundiced, hypotonic, hepatomegaly 4 cm, bilateral reduced red reflex with grey haze
data_table.Investigations: conjugated bilirubin 80 micromol/L (<5), ALT 220 U/L (<40), INR 2.1 (0.8-1.2), glucose 1.8 mmol/L (3.0-6.0), blood culture Gram-negative rods (E. coli), urine reducing substances positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate combination of actions?

options.text: IV cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin, continue expressed breast milk feeds
IV cefotaxime plus amoxicillin and switch to hydrolysed-protein cow's milk formula
Continue routine feeds and await newborn screening results before changing formula
Phototherapy and IV cefotaxime, defer feed change pending GALT enzyme result
Stop feeds, IV dextrose-saline plus cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin, switch to soy formula

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after eating a peanut butter sandwich at a birthday party. His parents say his lips swelled, he developed a widespread itchy rash, and he started coughing and saying his throat felt funny on the drive in. He has a known peanut allergy and carries an EpiPen Jr at preschool, but it was not used at the party.

On arrival he is tachypnoeic with audible wheeze and is anxious but answering questions. There is no stridor and no drooling. His weight on the resus chart is 18 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 86/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 /min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: diffuse urticaria over trunk and face, periorbital and lip swelling, bilateral expiratory wheeze, chest moving symmetrically, no stridor
data_table.Investigations: clinical diagnosis, no bloods drawn yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate adrenaline dose and route?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 150 micrograms (0.15 mL of 1 in 1000) into the anterolateral thigh
Intramuscular adrenaline 300 micrograms (0.3 mL of 1 in 1000) into the anterolateral thigh
Intravenous adrenaline 18 micrograms (1.8 mL of 1 in 100 000) as a slow bolus
Subcutaneous adrenaline 180 micrograms (0.18 mL of 1 in 1000) at 10 micrograms per kg
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 via face mask with high-flow oxygen

stem:
A 3-year-old girl is brought to a regional emergency department with three days of fever and one day of lethargy and reduced oral intake. Her parents say she has been wetting fewer nappies and is harder to rouse this afternoon.

She responds to voice but is mottled to the knees. Capillary refill is 4 seconds centrally. Her weight is 14 kg. Peripheral access is being attempted; the paediatric registrar is at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 78/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 40 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: mottled peripheries, prolonged central capillary refill, dry mucous membranes, no rash, soft abdomen, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: venous gas lactate 4.2 mmol/L; FBC, UEC, blood cultures pending

lead_in: After IV access is obtained, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Take blood cultures then give IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg, then a 20 mL/kg saline bolus
Give a 20 mL/kg saline bolus, then blood cultures, then IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg
Start a peripheral adrenaline infusion at 0.05 micrograms per kg per minute now
Give IV hydrocortisone 2 mg/kg as the priority before antibiotics or fluids
Give a 10 mL/kg saline bolus over 10 minutes and reassess before any antibiotic

stem: A 9-month-old breastfed girl has had 2 days of watery diarrhoea and occasional vomiting. She is alert, playful and has had 5 wet nappies today. Her mother asks what she should be feeding her.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, RR 28, temperature 37.3
data_table.Examination: Moist mucous membranes, capillary refill 2 seconds, weight unchanged

lead_in: What is the most appropriate feeding advice?

options.text: Continue breastfeeding as normal and offer her usual solid foods
Stop breastfeeding for 24 hours and give rehydration solution only
Continue breastfeeding but withhold all solid food for 48 hours
Change to a lactose free formula and reintroduce solids in 3 days
Offer diluted apple juice and dry toast until the diarrhoea settles

stem:
A 5-week-old boy is brought to the emergency department in the late evening with a rectal temperature of 38.4 degrees Celsius measured at home and confirmed on arrival. He was born at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery, breastfed, and previously well. He has had reduced feeds today and one episode of vomiting; the bottle volumes have dropped from 90 mL to 50 mL over three feeds.

He is alert in the cot but his cry is high-pitched when handled. The anterior fontanelle is soft and flat. There is no rash. The urine dipstick from a clean catch is negative for leukocytes and nitrites. A chest film is clear. He has received his 6-week immunisations 36 hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 76/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 56 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: high-pitched cry, soft fontanelle, no neck stiffness possible to assess in a 5-week-old, peripheries warm, no purpura
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 14.8 x10^9/L, CRP 22 mg/L (less than 5), urine dipstick negative, chest film clear, blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Procalcitonin level and discharge if below 0.5 micrograms per litre
Reassure that post-immunisation fever within 48 hours requires no further workup
Catheter urine specimen for culture and discharge home with safety netting
Lumbar puncture for CSF cell count, protein, glucose, gram stain, culture, and HSV PCR
Cranial ultrasound through the anterior fontanelle to exclude intracranial infection

stem:
A 9-month-old boy is brought in by his mother with episodes where he suddenly starts screaming, draws his legs up toward his tummy, and looks pale; between episodes he is settled and breastfeeds normally. The episodes started 14 hours ago and are now every 20 minutes. He passed a smear of dark mucousy stool with a streak of blood in his nappy two hours ago.

On examination during a quiet phase, his abdomen is soft. There is a vague fullness in the right upper quadrant. He is alert and well perfused with normal capillary refill. There is no peritonism and no abdominal distension.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 142 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: intermittent inconsolable distress with leg drawing, vague RUQ fullness between episodes, soft abdomen, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: ultrasound abdomen: target lesion in the right upper quadrant with a 3 cm diameter; no free fluid; no pneumoperitoneum on supine abdominal film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Trial of conservative management with bowel rest and observation for 24 hours
Immediate laparotomy for manual reduction by the paediatric surgical team
IV access and pneumatic reduction under fluoroscopy by paediatric radiology
Repeat ultrasound in 6 hours to confirm the lesion before any intervention
Barium contrast enema for combined diagnosis and hydrostatic reduction

stem:
A 4-year-old previously well girl is brought to her general practitioner with widespread bruising and a petechial rash on her shins and palate that her mother first noticed three days ago after a viral illness two weeks before. She has had no nosebleeds, no menorrhagia obviously not applicable, no haematuria, and is eating and playing normally. Her parents are anxious about cancer.

On examination she is well perfused. There is no hepatosplenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, and no joint swelling. Bruising is scattered without a distribution suggesting trauma. Mucosal bleeding is limited to a few petechiae on the soft palate.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits for age
data_table.Examination: scattered cutaneous bruising, palatal petechiae, no hepatosplenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, no bony tenderness
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 122 g/L (110 to 140); WCC 7.6 x10^9/L with normal differential; platelets 14 x10^9/L (150 to 400); film: isolated thrombocytopenia, no blasts, normal red cells

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine before any management decision
IV immunoglobulin 0.8 g/kg as a single dose with paracetamol pre-medication
Oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg per day for 14 days followed by a taper
Watchful waiting with safety advice, no medication, and clinic review in one week
Platelet transfusion 10 mL/kg to raise the count above 50 x10^9/L

stem:
A 5-week-old infant born at 37 weeks presents to the emergency department with 3 days of coryza, worsening work of breathing, and feeding at about a third of normal volume. The parents report fewer wet nappies in the last 12 hours and a quiet, less interactive baby.

On arrival he is alert but irritable with audible wheeze and moderate subcostal and intercostal recessions. There is no apnoea witnessed in the cubicle. Bedside viral PCR is positive for RSV. Chest x-ray shows hyperinflation only.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 78/46 mmHg, respiratory rate 70 /min, SpO2 88% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert but irritable, subcostal and intercostal recessions, audible wheeze with widespread fine crackles, capillary refill 2 seconds, anterior fontanelle slightly sunken
data_table.Investigations: RSV PCR positive, chest x-ray hyperinflated lungs with no focal consolidation, venous blood gas pH 7.34 pCO2 48 mmHg HCO3 24 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial respiratory support?

options.text: Commence low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min and titrate to maintain SpO2 at or above 90 percent
Commence high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with FiO2 titrated to SpO2 92 to 94 percent
Administer nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with ipratropium bromide 250 micrograms and reassess in 20 minutes
Give nebulised 3 percent hypertonic saline 4 mL and reassess respiratory effort in 1 hour
Give oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg once daily for 3 days and observe in short-stay unit

subtopic_detail: Severe asthma exacerbation refractory to inhaled therapy
stem:
An 8-year-old girl with a background of moderate persistent asthma on daily fluticasone presents to the emergency department with progressive shortness of breath despite three salbutamol pMDI doses at home over the last hour. Her mother says she has needed her reliever six times today.

After triage she has been given continuous nebulised salbutamol 0.5 percent for 1 hour, nebulised ipratropium 250 micrograms three doses, and oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg. After 60 minutes she remains tachypnoeic, can only speak in short phrases, and SpO2 has improved from 86 to 91 percent on 6 L/min oxygen by mask. She is alert and cooperative. There are no features of impending respiratory arrest.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 /min, SpO2 91% on 6 L/min via face mask, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: tripoding, marked subcostal and intercostal recessions, prolonged expiratory phase with bilateral wheeze, no silent chest, able to speak in 3-word phrases
data_table.Investigations: venous blood gas pH 7.32 pCO2 46 mmHg HCO3 23 mmol/L (24-32), peak flow not assessable, chest x-ray hyperinflation with no pneumothorax

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous aminophylline 5 mg/kg loading dose over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring
Intravenous salbutamol 5 micrograms/kg bolus over 5 minutes followed by infusion at 1 microgram/kg/min
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) infusion over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring
Intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg of 1 in 1000 into the anterolateral thigh
Intubate and commence pressure-controlled ventilation with permissive hypercapnia

subtopic_detail: RCH UTI imaging cascade after first typical UTI
stem:
An 18-month-old previously well girl is reviewed in the paediatric outpatient clinic two weeks after her first ever urinary tract infection. The infection was treated with 7 days of trimethoprim. She had fever to 38.6 degrees Celsius for 48 hours, responded clinically by hour 36 of antibiotics, and was systemically well at discharge from the short-stay unit.

MSU at presentation grew Escherichia coli sensitive to trimethoprim. Her antenatal renal ultrasound at 20 weeks was normal. She has had a healthy growth trajectory and is fully toilet trained. Examination today is normal.

data_table.Examination: growing along the 50th centile for weight and height, abdomen soft and non-tender, no flank tenderness, no palpable bladder, external genitalia normal
data_table.Investigations: MSU at presentation grew E coli with sensitivities to trimethoprim and cefalexin, no current symptoms or repeat MSU performed, prior antenatal anomaly scan reported normal kidneys bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange a micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) within 4 to 6 weeks to screen for vesicoureteric reflux of any grade
Arrange a renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks to screen for structural anomalies and post-infective changes
Arrange a dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) scan in 4 to 6 months to look for cortical defects and renal scarring
Reassure the family that no further investigation is required and provide written advice on prompt re-presentation if recurrent symptoms develop
Commence prophylactic trimethoprim 2 mg/kg nocte for 6 months until paediatric nephrology review at that time

subtopic_detail: Suspected airway foreign body diagnostic pathway
stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his grandmother. While he was eating cashew nuts at lunch he had a sudden episode of coughing and choking. He recovered within a few minutes but has had a persistent dry cough and intermittent wheeze ever since, for about 4 hours.

He is currently calm, breathing comfortably, and feeding sips of water without distress. Inspection shows no stridor or drooling. Auscultation reveals decreased air entry on the right with localised wheeze on that side. The grandmother says he was choking on a whole nut, not a piece, and that no one performed back blows or any manoeuvres.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 122 /min, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert and playful, no stridor or drooling, reduced air entry on right with monophonic wheeze on right, no recessions, no fever
data_table.Investigations: inspiratory and expiratory chest x-ray shows air trapping on the right with mediastinal shift to the left on expiration, no opacity visible

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Trial inhaled salbutamol via spacer for 1 hour and review with a repeat chest x-ray before deciding on referral
Arrange computed tomography of the chest with low-dose protocol prior to making a definitive surgical referral
Urgent referral to ENT or paediatric surgery for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia in theatre
Perform five back blows followed by five chest thrusts to attempt to dislodge the suspected foreign body
Admit for ward observation overnight with a repeat chest x-ray in 12 hours before deciding on intervention

stem:
A 9-month-old boy presents with 12 hours of episodic distress described by his parents as starting suddenly, drawing his knees up, and screaming, then settling for 15 minutes before the next episode. The last episode included a single dark red jelly-like stool. Between episodes he is pale and quiet.

In the emergency department abdominal examination during a quiet phase reveals a long thin lump in the right upper part of his tummy. Bedside ultrasound shows a target sign in the right upper quadrant. Paediatric surgery and interventional radiology are on site. Two attempts at pneumatic reduction are now complete; the second attempt confirmed only partial reduction of the intussuscipiens with persisting ileocolic invagination.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 156 /min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: settled between episodes, mildly pale, soft abdomen with palpable elongated mass in right upper quadrant, no peritonism, well-perfused peripheries
