data_table.Investigations: ultrasound target sign in right upper quadrant, full blood count haemoglobin 112 g/L (110-140) white cells 11.4 x10^9/L (4-12), venous lactate 1.6 mmol/L (under 2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and re-image at 12 hours before deciding on theatre
Attempt a third pneumatic reduction under deeper sedation after a 1-hour rest
Transition to hydrostatic saline reduction under ultrasound guidance as a salvage attempt
Admit for observation with serial abdominal examination and repeat ultrasound in 6 hours
Proceed to theatre for laparotomy with manual reduction and bowel viability assessment

stem:
A 6-week-old breastfed boy is admitted with a one-week history of progressive forceful vomiting that shoots out after feeds, with no green or yellow colour reported by his mother. He is feeding eagerly but losing weight. The general practitioner found a palpable upper abdominal lump during a feed yesterday. Bedside ultrasound performed in the emergency department this morning showed pyloric muscle thickness 4.5 mm and pyloric channel length 19 mm.

He is mildly dehydrated with reduced skin turgor and a sunken anterior fontanelle. Paediatric surgery has reviewed the patient and listed him for pyloromyotomy. The surgical team is asking whether they can proceed this afternoon or whether you would like to delay until tomorrow.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 162 /min, blood pressure 78/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: mildly dehydrated, sunken fontanelle, palpable olive-shaped mass in the upper abdomen, abdomen otherwise soft, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 2.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), chloride 88 mmol/L (95-110), bicarbonate 34 mmol/L (22-32), urea 9.2 mmol/L (2.0-7.0), pH 7.52 base excess +9 mmol/L, ultrasound confirms pyloric stenosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management before pyloromyotomy?

options.text: Commence oral electrolyte rehydration solution while maintaining nil-by-mouth status overnight for next-day theatre
Proceed directly to theatre this afternoon and correct any residual electrolyte disturbances during anaesthesia
Insert a nasogastric tube on free drainage and operate within 4 hours regardless of current biochemistry result
Correct the hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with intravenous fluid resuscitation before theatre
Commence ranitidine 1 mg/kg intravenously for gastric acid suppression and proceed to theatre this evening

stem:
A 4-year-old girl is brought to the general practice clinic with 8 months of stool withholding, infrequent painful bowel motions every 5 to 7 days, and recent daily soiling of small amounts of liquid stool into her underwear. Her mother says her tummy is always full and hard. She is otherwise well, eats a varied diet, and is on the 50th centile for height and weight.

Examination shows an alert child with a non-tender, distended abdomen and a palpable faecal mass in the left iliac fossa. Anal inspection is normal with no fissure and no sacral pit. There are no red flags for organic disease (no failure to thrive, no delayed first stool in the newborn period, no green vomiting, no neurological signs). Her current management is occasional lactulose with limited adherence.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 100/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: soft non-tender abdomen with palpable left iliac fossa faecal mass, normal anal inspection, no sacral dimple or tuft of hair, normal lower limb tone and reflexes
data_table.Investigations: clinical diagnosis, no imaging or bloods required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue lactulose at the current dose and emphasise dietary fibre and fluid intake at follow-up in 4 weeks' time
Disimpaction with macrogol 3350 with electrolytes at an escalating regimen over 3 to 7 days then daily maintenance
Administer a daily phosphate enema for 3 days in clinic to clear the impaction before commencing maintenance therapy
Commence senna 2.5 mL nocte as a stimulant laxative for 4 weeks and review symptoms at the end of that course
Refer for urgent paediatric gastroenterology review and arrange an abdominal x-ray to confirm faecal impaction

stem:
A 7-year-old boy presents to the paediatric outpatient clinic for review 1 week after discharge with a diagnosis of Henoch-Schonlein purpura. He had palpable purpura over the buttocks and extensor surfaces of the lower legs, bilateral ankle pain that has resolved, and 3 days of cramping tummy pain that came in waves that settled with simple analgesia. He never had macroscopic haematuria.

At admission his urinalysis showed trace blood and no proteinuria, his blood pressure was at the 50th centile, and his renal function was normal. Today he is well. His mother asks how often you need to check his urine and blood pressure from here.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 100/64 mmHg (50th centile for age and height), respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: fading non-blanching purpura on buttocks and lower legs, no joint swelling, no abdominal tenderness, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: urinalysis trace blood no protein, urine albumin creatinine ratio less than 2 mg/mmol, creatinine 38 micromol/L (paediatric range), blood pressure on growth chart at 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate renal follow-up plan?

options.text: Renal ultrasound at 3 months and at 6 months as the primary screening tool for evolving nephritis or scarring
Repeat urinalysis only if macroscopic haematuria, peripheral oedema or hypertension develop in the next 6 months
Weekly urinalysis and blood pressure measurement for 2 months then monthly until 6 months from initial onset
Daily urinalysis for 6 weeks at home using parent-performed dipstick testing with weekly clinic blood pressure
Refer for percutaneous renal biopsy now to define histological prognosis before any further surveillance plan

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki recognition and IVIG timing
stem:
An 11-month-old boy is admitted with 9 days of fever to 39 to 40 degrees Celsius. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, perineal desquamation, and a single right cervical lymph node 1.8 cm in diameter. He has no rash, no oral mucosal changes, and no extremity changes. He has been investigated for sepsis with negative urine, blood, and respiratory virus cultures.

C-reactive protein is 142 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/hour, platelets 612 x 10^9/L, albumin 28 g/L, ALT 78 U/L, and urine has sterile pyuria. The paediatric cardiology echocardiogram performed today shows a left anterior descending coronary artery z-score of 2.6 with perivascular brightness.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 158 /min, blood pressure 94/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, perineal desquamation, single tender right cervical lymph node 1.8 cm, no rash, no oral changes, no extremity oedema
data_table.Investigations: CRP 142 mg/L (under 5), ESR 78 mm/hour (under 15), platelets 612 x 10^9/L (150-450), albumin 28 g/L (35-45), ALT 78 U/L (under 40), urine sterile pyuria, echocardiogram LAD z-score 2.6 with perivascular brightness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue observation with daily inflammatory markers and repeat echocardiogram in 1 week
Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours with high-dose aspirin therapy
Commence intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg daily for 3 days as primary therapy without IVIG
Start infliximab 5 mg/kg as primary therapy in view of the high CRP and coronary z-score
Commence broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and re-image at 48 hours before deciding on therapy

stem:
A 3-year-old girl is referred from her general practitioner with a 4-day history of bruising and a petechial rash. She had a viral upper respiratory illness 2 weeks ago. She is otherwise well, eating and drinking normally, and active at preschool. Examination shows scattered petechiae over the trunk and limbs and a few small bruises on her shins; there are no wet purpura, no mucosal bleeding, and no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy.

Full blood count shows isolated thrombocytopenia at 18 x 10^9/L with normal haemoglobin and white cell count. Blood film confirms isolated thrombocytopenia with normal red cells and white cells; there are no blasts. She has no family history of bleeding disorders and is up to date with immunisations. The haematology registrar has reviewed and confirmed the working diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 102 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: well child, scattered petechiae over trunk and limbs, small bruises on shins, no wet purpura, no mucosal bleeding, no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 122 g/L (110-140), white cells 7.8 x10^9/L (4-12), platelets 18 x10^9/L (150-450), blood film isolated thrombocytopenia with normal red and white cells and no blasts

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Give a platelet transfusion targeting a platelet count above 50 x10^9/L to provide short-term haemostatic cover
Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 0.8 g/kg as a single dose to raise the platelet count rapidly within hours
Commence oral prednisolone 4 mg/kg/day for 4 days followed by a stepwise taper over the next 1 to 2 weeks
Observation with written advice on bleeding precautions and arrange weekly platelet count for the next 4 weeks
Refer for urgent bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy to exclude an underlying haematological malignancy

subtopic_detail: New T1DM without DKA - initiation approach
stem:
A 9-year-old boy is referred by his general practitioner with 4 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and 3 kg weight loss. A clinic capillary blood glucose was 22 mmol/L. He is alert, ambulating, and tolerating oral fluids. The general practitioner sent him to the emergency department after capillary ketones returned 0.6 mmol/L.

In the emergency department his repeat capillary blood glucose is 19 mmol/L, capillary ketones are 0.5 mmol/L, and venous blood gas shows pH 7.36 and bicarbonate 23 mmol/L. He is haemodynamically stable, mucous membranes are moist, and abdominal examination is normal. The on-call paediatric endocrinology consultant has reviewed and confirmed this is new-onset Type 1 diabetes mellitus without diabetic ketoacidosis.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert, moist mucous membranes, abdomen soft and non-tender, normal mental state, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: capillary blood glucose 19 mmol/L (under 7 fasting), capillary ketones 0.5 mmol/L (under 0.6), venous pH 7.36 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 23 mmol/L (22-32), sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial insulin regimen?

options.text: Discharge for outpatient initiation of insulin by the community diabetes team in the next 24 to 48 hours
Intravenous fluid bolus 10 mL/kg of 0.9 percent saline followed by an insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour
Twice-daily premixed insulin 30/70 with breakfast and dinner as a simpler starter regimen for the family
Oral metformin 500 mg twice daily as initial therapy and arrange outpatient endocrinology review in 1 week
Subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin (long-acting once daily plus rapid-acting with meals) with diabetes education

stem:
A 12-day-old phenotypically female infant is brought to the emergency department by her parents with 2 days of poor feeding and vomiting and a noticeable change in alertness this morning. She was born at term, weight 3.4 kg, and discharged on day 2. The newborn screen result is not yet back.

In the resus bay she is lethargic with mottled peripheries and prolonged capillary refill. Her parents describe ambiguous-appearing external genitalia (described in their words as a small lump with what looks like a urinary opening underneath). Bedside glucose is 2.4 mmol/L and capillary blood gas shows pH 7.22, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L, sodium 122 mmol/L, potassium 6.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 188 /min, blood pressure 58/32 mmHg, respiratory rate 50 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: lethargic, mottled, capillary refill 4 seconds, sunken fontanelle, virilised external genitalia with phallic enlargement and partial fusion of labial folds, no palpable gonads, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 6.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 2.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), bicarbonate 14 mmol/L (22-32), pH 7.22 (7.35-7.45), 17-hydroxyprogesterone sent urgently

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 25 mg bolus then 0.9 percent saline with 10 percent dextrose 10 mL/kg and admit to PICU
Intravenous dexamethasone 0.1 mg/kg bolus and arrange transfer to paediatric intensive care once stabilised
Intravenous calcium gluconate 0.5 mL/kg of 10 percent over 10 minutes for the hyperkalaemia then reassess plan
Intravenous fludrocortisone 0.1 mg single dose and 0.9 percent saline 20 mL/kg bolus then reassess perfusion
Send urgent karyotype, serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone and urinary steroid profile before any therapeutic decision

stem:
An 11-year-old girl with new-onset Type 1 diabetes is on the paediatric ward 6 hours into treatment for severe diabetic ketoacidosis. She has received 0.9 percent saline 10 mL/kg over 60 minutes, followed by maintenance plus deficit fluids over 48 hours, and an insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour. Initial venous pH was 7.05.

The nurse calls you because the patient has developed a headache that started 30 minutes ago, has become irritable, and her heart rate has fallen from 124 to 78 /min while her blood pressure has risen from 102/64 to 138/86 mmHg. She is rousable but slow to respond. The team has just checked a venous blood gas which shows pH 7.18 and glucose 14 mmol/L. The on-call consultant is en route.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), pupils equal and reactive, no focal neurology, well perfused, weight 42 kg
data_table.Investigations: venous pH 7.18 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 14 mmol/L (22-32), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 14 mmol/L (3.5-7.0 fasting), ketones 3.2 mmol/L (under 0.6)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Add 5 percent dextrose to the maintenance fluid because the glucose has fallen to 14 mmol/L
Increase intravenous fluid rate by 50 percent to address presumed worsening dehydration
Stop the insulin infusion and arrange urgent computed tomography of the head before further therapy
Give intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg to reduce cerebral oedema and continue current fluids
Reduce intravenous fluid rate by one-third and give intravenous 3 percent hypertonic saline 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with 6 hours of fever, vomiting, and a rapidly spreading rash. His parents say he was well at school yesterday. On the way in he became unusually drowsy.

In the resus bay he is mottled with cold peripheries, capillary refill 5 seconds, and a non-blanching purpuric rash over his trunk and legs which is visibly spreading. He is rousable but irritable. The team has obtained intraosseous access. Bedside glucose is 4.2 mmol/L. The on-call anaesthetist has been called.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 178 /min, blood pressure 78/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: mottled, cold peripheries, capillary refill 5 seconds, non-blanching purpuric rash over trunk and limbs, drowsy but rousable, GCS 12, neck supple, no photophobia documented
data_table.Investigations: intraosseous access established, blood cultures and full blood count drawn, lactate 4.8 mmol/L (under 2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Defer antibiotic administration and perform a lumbar puncture immediately for CSF cell count and microscopy
Administer intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg through the intraosseous line with 20 mL/kg saline bolus and defer LP
Administer benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg intramuscularly through the deltoid prior to attempting intravenous access
Administer intravenous adrenaline 1 microgram/kg bolus to raise the blood pressure before any antibiotic dose
Administer intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg before the first dose of empirical antibiotic for meningitis

stem:
A 19-day-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents who measured an axillary temperature of 38.2 degrees Celsius this evening. He has been feeding less in the last 12 hours and seems quieter than usual. He was born at term by uncomplicated vaginal delivery; mother had no maternal GBS swab documented in the discharge summary, and there was prolonged rupture of membranes at 19 hours.

In triage he is alert but quiet, with normal capillary refill, anterior fontanelle flat, and no rash. Fully exposed examination is unremarkable. The most senior available decision-maker is the paediatric registrar on call.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 156 /min, blood pressure 78/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 48 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert but quiet, flat anterior fontanelle, no rash, no respiratory distress, abdomen soft, no focal source on full exposed examination
data_table.Investigations: venous blood gas pH 7.36 lactate 1.4 mmol/L, capillary blood glucose 4.8 mmol/L, urinalysis pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a full septic workup including lumbar puncture and commence intravenous ceftriaxone empirically
Perform a full septic workup including lumbar puncture and commence intravenous amoxicillin plus cefotaxime empirically
Perform a full septic workup excluding lumbar puncture and observe on the ward for 24 hours before deciding on antibiotics
Take blood and urine cultures only and commence oral cefalexin once the urine result is back
Apply paracetamol and observe for 4 hours; if temperature settles, discharge with safety-net advice

stem:
A 6-year-old boy with a known peanut allergy was given intramuscular adrenaline 300 micrograms by his mother 30 minutes ago after he developed widespread urticaria and stridor at a friend's house following biscuit ingestion. In the ambulance he received a second IM adrenaline 300 micrograms because his stridor recurred 12 minutes after the first dose.

On arrival in the emergency department he is alert, asymptomatic, with no rash, no stridor, no wheeze, and normal vital signs. His parents ask whether he can be discharged now that he looks well. He has had three previous mild anaphylactic episodes and has an ASCIA action plan; he weighs 22 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 102 /min, blood pressure 104/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert and active, skin clear with no urticaria, oropharynx clear, chest auscultation clear, no abdominal tenderness, normal mental state
data_table.Investigations: clinical diagnosis, no further investigations indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge now with a clear written action plan and a replacement adrenaline autoinjector to take home
Observe in the emergency department for at least 4 hours from the last adrenaline dose before discharge planning
Admit to the paediatric ward for 24 hours of observation regardless of the symptom-free interval
Discharge with a 3-day course of oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg to prevent a biphasic reaction
Discharge with oral antihistamine cetirizine 5 mg twice daily for 5 days and review by general practitioner

stem:
A 7-day-old term boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents who say he stopped feeding well 12 hours ago and is now floppy and cold. He was born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery with no antenatal concerns; the discharge ward midwife discharged him on day 2 with no echocardiogram performed.

In the resus bay he is grey, lethargic, and tachypnoeic. Pre-ductal SpO2 on the right hand is 96 percent and post-ductal SpO2 on the foot is 84 percent. Femoral pulses are not palpable while brachial pulses are present. Four-limb blood pressures show right upper limb 92/58 mmHg and right lower limb 56/34 mmHg.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 184 /min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg right arm and 56/34 mmHg right leg, respiratory rate 64 /min, SpO2 96% right hand and 84% right foot, temperature 36.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: grey lethargic infant, capillary refill 4 seconds, absent femoral pulses bilaterally, brachial pulses present, tachypnoea with mild recessions, harsh systolic murmur left infraclavicular area
data_table.Investigations: venous blood gas pH 7.18 lactate 5.4 mmol/L, sodium 137 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 6.8 mmol/L, creatinine 64 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intravenous furosemide 1 mg/kg for the tachypnoea attributed to congestive heart failure secondary
Give 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus and reassess perfusion before initiating any other targeted intervention
Intubate and commence inotropes with a peripheral adrenaline infusion before organising interhospital transfer
Administer intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg empirically for presumed late-onset neonatal bacterial sepsis cover
Commence intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion 5 nanograms/kg/min and prepare for retrieval to a cardiac centre

stem:
A 7-year-old boy was rescued from a house fire 2 hours ago. He has full-thickness circumferential burns to the right forearm and partial-thickness burns to the trunk, totalling 18 percent body surface area. He was intubated at scene for inhalational injury and is now in the resuscitation bay. He has received the calculated first 8 hours of resuscitation fluid per the AU paediatric burn formula.

You are reassessing the right upper limb. Distal capillary refill is 5 seconds, the radial pulse is just palpable on Doppler, and the hand is cool. The forearm compartments feel firm. The patient is sedated and intubated, ventilated with no airway pressure alarms.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 122 /min, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min ventilated, SpO2 98% on FiO2 0.4, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: right forearm circumferential full-thickness burn with leathery eschar, distal capillary refill 5 seconds, Doppler-only radial pulse, hand cool, forearm compartments firm, partial-thickness trunk burns
data_table.Investigations: intubated and sedated, urine output 0.8 mL/kg/hour, lactate 2.4 mmol/L (under 2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange transfer to a paediatric burns centre for theatre-based fasciotomy under general anaesthesia
Elevate the limb above heart level and reassess in 1 hour before deciding on intervention
Increase the fluid resuscitation rate by 25 percent to improve distal perfusion via central pressure
Perform urgent escharotomy of the right upper limb at the bedside to restore distal perfusion
Apply silver sulfadiazine dressing and arrange repeat assessment in 4 hours

stem:
A 7-month-old non-mobile infant is brought to the emergency department by her father with a swollen, painful right thigh that he noticed after picking her up from her cot this morning. He says she may have rolled awkwardly. The infant cries with movement of the right leg. X-ray of the right femur shows a spiral fracture of the mid-shaft.

The infant is fully immunised, growing along the 25th centile, and on review of the parent-held record she has been seen for two previous emergency department attendances in the last 4 months: one for a frenulum tear and one for a bruise on her cheek. The father attends alone and is reluctant to provide a clear narrative about the cot event. Mother is not contactable.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 126 /min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: tender right mid-thigh with swelling, otherwise well-grown infant, no other obvious external injury on full exposed examination, no torn frenulum currently visible
data_table.Investigations: right femur x-ray spiral mid-shaft fracture, full blood count haemoglobin 110 g/L (105-135) platelets 282 x10^9/L (150-450), coagulation profile within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Admit and arrange skeletal survey, ophthalmology review, hospital child protection team and statutory notification
Apply a long-leg cast under procedural sedation in the emergency department and discharge with GP follow-up in 1 week
Send a urinary catecholamine sample to exclude phaeochromocytoma as a cause of fragile vessels and apparent bruising
Refer to orthopaedics for elective fracture clinic follow-up and arrange outpatient social work review within 2 weeks
Request a haematology consultation to exclude osteogenesis imperfecta as a unifying diagnosis before notification

stem:
A 5-day-old breastfed term boy is brought to the paediatric assessment unit by his parents because they noticed yellow skin spreading down to his thighs since yesterday. He was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, weight 3.6 kg at birth and 3.4 kg today (less than 10 percent weight loss). Mother's blood group is O Rh-positive, infant's blood group is A Rh-positive, and the direct antiglobulin test (DAT) is positive.

The infant is alert, feeding 6 to 7 times in 24 hours, with adequate wet and dirty nappies. There is no hepatosplenomegaly and no petechiae. Serum bilirubin at 120 hours of age is 340 micromol/L (unconjugated component 332 micromol/L, conjugated 8 micromol/L). The treatment chart for this gestation and age placed the phototherapy line at 310 micromol/L and the exchange transfusion line at 430 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 138 /min, blood pressure 70/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 42 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert and feeding, jaundice extending to thighs (zone 4), no hepatosplenomegaly, no petechiae, normal tone and reflexes
data_table.Investigations: total serum bilirubin 340 micromol/L at 120 hours (phototherapy threshold 310, exchange transfusion threshold 430), unconjugated 332 micromol/L, conjugated 8 micromol/L, DAT positive (ABO incompatibility), full blood count haemoglobin 158 g/L (140-220 newborn) reticulocytes 4.8 percent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease breastfeeding for 48 hours and substitute infant formula to reduce serum bilirubin levels more rapidly
Arrange urgent double-volume exchange transfusion because the direct antiglobulin test is positive for ABO incompatibility
Commence intensive phototherapy and repeat serum bilirubin in 6 hours; continue breastfeeding with supplementation
Discharge with home phototherapy biliblanket and review by community paediatrician in the next 24 to 48 hours
Reassure the family that the jaundice is physiological and rebook for repeat serum bilirubin in 48 hours time

subtopic_detail: Type 1 diabetes sick day rules - intercurrent illness
stem:
A 13-year-old girl with established Type 1 diabetes (basal-bolus regimen, insulin glargine 18 units nocte and insulin aspart with meals) is brought to the paediatric short-stay unit by her father. She has had vomiting and fever from gastroenteritis for 24 hours. Her father has been omitting her basal insulin because she has not been eating, and he asks whether to continue this approach.

She is alert, mildly dehydrated, tolerating sips, with no abdominal tenderness. Her capillary blood glucose is 16.2 mmol/L and capillary ketones are 1.8 mmol/L. Venous gas shows pH 7.35 and bicarbonate 21 mmol/L. She has not been able to eat solid food but is keeping down water and electrolyte drinks.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 102 /min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert, mildly dehydrated, capillary refill 2 seconds, mucous membranes slightly dry, abdomen soft and non-tender, no Kussmaul respiration
data_table.Investigations: capillary blood glucose 16.2 mmol/L, capillary ketones 1.8 mmol/L (under 0.6), venous pH 7.35 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 21 mmol/L (22-32), sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her insulin regimen?

options.text: Discharge home with antiemetic ondansetron and advice to omit her insulin until she is eating normal meals again
Withhold both basal and bolus insulin while she is not eating and restart once she is tolerating solid food again
Reduce her basal insulin glargine to half dose because of the reduced oral intake and review again in 12 hours
Switch her to an intravenous insulin infusion regardless of acid-base status to ensure reliable insulin delivery
Continue usual basal insulin glargine, give rapid-acting aspart correction doses for ketones, substitute carbohydrate fluids

stem:
A 13-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with 3 hours of severe right-sided scrotal pain that began at school. The pain came on suddenly while he was sitting in class. He has vomited once. He has no urinary symptoms, no fever, and no preceding illness. There is no history of trauma.

On examination the right testis is high-riding and lies in a horizontal axis. There is marked tenderness on palpation. The cremasteric reflex is absent on the right. The left testis is normal. The urinary tract is otherwise normal. The on-call paediatric surgical registrar is contactable and in the hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 124/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: right testis high-riding with horizontal lie, marked tenderness, absent cremasteric reflex on right, left testis normal, no scrotal erythema
data_table.Investigations: urinalysis no leucocytes no nitrites, full blood count haemoglobin 138 g/L white cells 9.4 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent scrotal ultrasound with colour Doppler before deciding on surgical exploration
Urgent referral to paediatric surgery for scrotal exploration and orchidopexy
Commence oral cefalexin 500 mg twice daily for empirical epididymo-orchitis and review in 24 hours
Attempt manual detorsion at the bedside and admit for surgical orchidopexy in the morning
Administer simple analgesia and discharge with general practitioner review in 1 to 2 days

subtopic_detail: Stopping antiplatelet therapy after Kawasaki disease when follow-up echocardiography is normal
stem: A 5-year-old girl attends the cardiology clinic seven weeks after treatment for Kawasaki disease. She has taken aspirin 4 mg/kg once daily since discharge and has been entirely well.

data_table.Examination: Well grown; normal cardiovascular examination
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiography today shows normal coronary arteries; ESR 8 mm/h, platelets 290 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing management?

options.text: Cease aspirin and arrange general practitioner review as needed
Continue aspirin 4 mg/kg daily indefinitely and review each year
Continue aspirin and restrict her from competitive sport for a year
Cease aspirin and start clopidogrel 1 mg/kg once daily instead
Continue aspirin until a repeat echocardiogram at twelve months

stem:
A 3-year-old previously well girl is brought to a regional emergency department with three days of fever to 39.6 degrees, a wet cough, and the parents say she is breathing fast and has stopped drinking from her cup. She has had no vomiting and her last wet nappy was four hours ago.

On examination she is alert but tachypnoeic with mild subcostal recession. Auscultation reveals reduced breath sounds and bronchial breathing at the right base with crackles audible into the mid zone. The left chest is clear. Capillary return is two seconds and mucous membranes are moist. There is no stridor or wheeze, and no rash. She is immunised on schedule including 13-valent pneumococcal and Haemophilus vaccines.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 142, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 48, SpO2 92 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: chest radiograph confirms right lower lobe consolidation without effusion, point-of-care blood gas within normal limits, capillary glucose 4.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit, commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg every six hours, and supplemental oxygen titrated to SpO2 92 percent
Discharge home on oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg three times daily for five days with general practice review at 48 hours
Admit and commence intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily as monotherapy for empirical broad spectrum cover
Admit and commence intravenous azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily as monotherapy targeting atypical bacterial pathogens
Admit on intravenous fluids alone and withhold antibiotics pending respiratory viral PCR and procalcitonin results

stem:
A 9-month-old infant is brought to a tertiary emergency department with a 14 hour history of episodic distress. The parents describe him going pale and pulling his legs up, screaming for 90 seconds, then becoming floppy and quiet between episodes. He has now had two soft jelly-like dark red stools in his nappy and refused his last two feeds.

On examination he is pale but rouseable. The abdomen is soft with a faintly palpable long thin lump in the right upper quadrant. Bowel sounds are present. There are no peritonitic signs and no abdominal distension. Capillary return is two seconds. He has had no recent gastroenteritis or upper respiratory infection. There is no Henoch-Schonlein purpura rash.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 144, blood pressure 88/52, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: venous blood gas pH 7.36 base excess negative 2, lactate 1.8 mmol/L, point-of-care abdominal ultrasound shows a target sign in the right upper quadrant with no free fluid and preserved bowel wall echogenicity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge after a normal abdominal radiograph with paracetamol and family safety netting about red flag symptoms
Arrange immediate laparotomy with paediatric surgery without prior attempt at radiological reduction by air enema
Resuscitate with 20 mL/kg saline, place a nasogastric tube on drainage, and arrange image guided air enema reduction
Admit for 24 hours nil by mouth with maintenance intravenous fluids and reassessment by surgical team in the morning
Commence intravenous metronidazole and gentamicin and proceed to immediate diagnostic laparoscopy regardless of imaging

stem:
A 7-week-old infant is brought to a metropolitan emergency department because the mother noticed bruising on his right cheek and a swollen left thigh. The family attended a community drop-in immunisation clinic earlier the same day and the nurse there raised concerns. There is no reported trauma. The mother is 19, the partner she lives with is not the biological father, and the social history records financial stress and recent eviction.

On examination the infant is alert and feeding well. There is a 2 cm purple bruise on the right zygoma and a 4 cm fusiform swelling over the mid left thigh with reluctance to weight-bear when held vertically. Fundi are clear. There is no rash, no birthmarks, and the fontanelle is soft. The remainder of the systemic examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Investigations: skeletal survey not yet performed, full blood count and coagulation studies within normal limits, capillary glucose 4.6 mmol/L, urinalysis sterile, paediatric early warning score zero

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with general practitioner review in 48 hours and a safety net to return if any new bruising appears
Reassure that bruising is common at this age, request iron studies, and arrange community paediatrician review
Request coagulation screen and platelet function tests before deciding whether to notify the child protection authority
Admit, notify statutory child protection, request skeletal survey, retinal examination, head imaging, and social work
Discuss the bruising openly with the mother and notify child protection only if she fails to give a plausible account

stem:
A previously well 22-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department after his parents found him pale and unresponsive in his cot at 6 am. He vomited twice the previous evening and went to bed without his usual milk. Paramedics measured a capillary glucose of 1.6 mmol/L and gave 2 mL/kg of 10 percent dextrose with rapid recovery of consciousness. He has had no previous similar episodes and is on the 25th centile for weight.

On examination he is now alert and playful. There is no hepatomegaly, no Cushingoid features, no hyperpigmentation, and no midline defects. Tone, reflexes, and cranial nerves are normal. The parents say he refused dinner because of the gastroenteritis but the older sister recovered without low sugars. Vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Investigations: critical sample drawn at glucose 1.6 mmol/L: ketones (3-hydroxybutyrate) 4.2 mmol/L, free fatty acids 2.6 mmol/L, insulin <2 mU/L, C-peptide <0.1 nmol/L, cortisol 612 nmol/L, growth hormone 18 mcg/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L, ammonia 38 micromol/L (10-50), urine organic acids and acylcarnitine profile pending

lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Medium chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency presenting at this age
Congenital hyperinsulinism due to a sulfonylurea receptor (KATP channel) mutation
Idiopathic ketotic hypoglycaemia of childhood with appropriate counter-regulation
Glycogen storage disease type 1 (von Gierke) with subclinical hepatomegaly
Adrenal insufficiency with subclinical cortisol deficiency exacerbated by vomiting

stem:
A 9-year-old girl presents to a tertiary paediatric emergency department with two weeks of fatigue, polyuria, and nocturnal wetting, and one day of vomiting. The mother says she has lost weight despite eating more, and today she looked drowsy. There is no recent overseas travel and no family history of diabetes.

On examination she is drowsy but rouseable, breathing deeply, with dry mucous membranes and capillary return three seconds. There is no abdominal tenderness, no rash, and no signs of cerebral oedema. Pulse rate 132, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 36, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees. Her actual body weight on arrival is 28 kg. A point-of-care capillary blood gas confirms a severe metabolic acidosis with hyperglycaemia and high ketones.

data_table.Investigations: venous pH 7.06, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, base excess negative 22, glucose 28 mmol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.8 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145) corrected sodium 138, potassium 4.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 9.2 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, urinalysis 4+ glucose 4+ ketones

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid plan in the first hour?

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg saline bolus over 15 minutes then commence intravenous insulin infusion immediately at 0.1 units/kg/hour
Replace the calculated fluid deficit over six hours alongside maintenance fluids to correct dehydration rapidly
Commence intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately without preceding fluid bolus resuscitation
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 60 minutes to correct severe acidaemia before any other intervention
Give a 10 mL/kg saline bolus over 30 to 60 minutes, withhold insulin for the first hour, and reassess perfusion at one hour

stem:
A 24-day-old term infant is brought to the emergency department with a temperature recorded at home of 38.4 degrees and one day of poor feeding. He was born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, exclusively breastfed, and gained weight at the maternal child health nurse review three days ago. There has been no rash, no vomiting, and the mother had no fevers or rash in pregnancy. The maternal Group B Streptococcus swab at 36 weeks was negative.

On examination he is alert but reduced in spontaneous movement. The anterior fontanelle is soft. There is no rash, no bulging fontanelle, no clinical jaundice, and capillary return is two seconds. The chest is clear, the abdomen is soft without organomegaly, and the umbilical stump is dry. Vital signs are within normal limits except temperature 38.2 degrees.

data_table.Investigations: venous blood gas pH 7.36 lactate 2.0 mmol/L, capillary glucose 3.6 mmol/L, urinalysis nitrites negative leucocytes negative, paired blood cultures and urine sent, chest radiograph clear, viral respiratory panel pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Observe in short stay, repeat temperature in two hours, and discharge with general practice review if cultures negative
Admit, perform lumbar puncture, take blood and urine cultures, and start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin
Admit, take blood and urine cultures, start intravenous flucloxacillin and gentamicin, and defer the lumbar puncture
Admit, perform lumbar puncture, take blood and urine cultures, and start intravenous cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin
Send respiratory virus polymerase chain reaction panel and discharge if positive for any seasonal respiratory virus

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is referred from a regional emergency department on day 12 of a quotidian fever spiking to 40 degrees once daily, with a salmon-coloured rash that comes and goes with the temperature. He has had two doses of IVIG and high-dose aspirin at his local hospital under a presumptive diagnosis of incomplete Kawasaki disease, but his fevers have not resolved.

On arrival to the tertiary centre he is irritable, pale, with hepatosplenomegaly and a non-tender right knee effusion. A baseline echocardiogram from day 7 was reported as normal coronary arteries. There is no conjunctival injection, no oral changes, no peripheral oedema, and no cervical lymphadenopathy now. The salmon rash appears during a temperature spike during the assessment and fades as the fever settles two hours later.

data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 88 g/L (110-145), platelets 142 x10^9/L falling from 612 a week ago, white cells 24.6 x10^9/L (5-15) neutrophils 19.8, ferritin 18400 mcg/L (15-150), triglycerides 4.8 mmol/L (<2.3), fibrinogen 1.4 g/L (1.5-4), AST 412 U/L, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), CRP 96 mg/L, ESR 12 mm/hr disproportionately low for CRP, D-dimer 8.6 mg/L

lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Immunoglobulin resistant complete Kawasaki disease needing second dose immunoglobulin and infliximab
Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis complicated by macrophage activation syndrome
Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia with diffuse bone marrow infiltration and cytokine release
Visceral leishmaniasis complicated by secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
Periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, and adenitis syndrome decompensation

stem:
A 22-month-old boy is brought to a regional emergency department at 2 a.m. by his parents who describe a barking cough and a hoarse cry starting earlier the previous evening and worsening overnight.

On examination he has audible inspiratory stridor at rest with mild intercostal recession but no tracheal tug and no nasal flaring. Air entry is symmetrical with no wheeze. He looks tired but engages with his parents and drinks half a cup of water in front of you. There is no drooling, no toxic appearance, and no history of a choking episode. Vaccinations including Haemophilus influenzae type b are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 140, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 36, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer a single oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg dose and observe in the department with clinical reassessment after thirty minutes
Administer a single oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg dose and arrange immediate paediatric intensive care review by phone
Administer nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 and admit for a minimum four hour observation period after the dose
Discharge home on oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for three days with general practice review the next morning
Arrange urgent retrieval to a tertiary centre for elective intubation and direct laryngoscopy in theatre

stem:
An 18-month-old girl is brought to a metropolitan emergency department with 24 hours of watery diarrhoea up to ten times and three episodes of non-bilious vomiting. Her parents have offered sips of oral rehydration solution at home but she has refused most of it and only had one wet nappy in the last six hours.

On examination she is mildly drowsy but rouseable. Mucous membranes are tacky, eyes are slightly sunken, and capillary return is between two and three seconds peripherally. There is no abdominal distension, no peritonism, and no rash. She weighs 11 kg. There is no recent overseas travel, no antibiotic exposure, and no household member with similar symptoms beyond expected viral gastroenteritis circulating at her childcare.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 138, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees
data_table.Investigations: venous blood gas within normal limits, capillary glucose 4.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Insert two large bore intravenous cannulae and commence a 20 mL/kg bolus of 0.9 percent saline over fifteen minutes followed by maintenance
Discharge home on small frequent oral rehydration solution sips with safety netting advice and review by general practitioner within 24 hours
Administer a single 2 mg dose of oral ondansetron wafer and insert a nasogastric tube for rapid enteral rehydration over four hours
Commence oral loperamide 0.1 mg/kg three times daily and continue oral rehydration solution as tolerated at home
Send stool for multiplex polymerase chain reaction and commence empirical oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily for five days

subtopic_detail: Anaphylaxis adrenaline dose by weight band
stem:
A 4-year-old girl is brought urgently to a metropolitan emergency department after eating a cashew biscuit at a birthday party. Within ten minutes her parents noticed lip swelling and a hoarse cry, and ambulance was called when she became wheezy and floppy in their arms en route.

On examination she is pale and lethargic with widespread urticaria and lip and tongue swelling. There is audible expiratory wheeze, mild intercostal recession, and a hoarse voice. Capillary return is three seconds and pulses are weak. She has no known prior reactions and no asthma diagnosis. Weight is documented as 16 kg from a clinic visit last week. There is no other ingestion and no recent infection. Intramuscular adrenaline has not yet been administered.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 168, blood pressure 78/40, respiratory rate 40, SpO2 91 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate adrenaline dose?

options.text: Administer intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms per kilogram of 1:10000 solution into the deltoid muscle and repeat after five minutes
Administer intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms of 1:1000 solution into the anterolateral thigh and repeat after ten minutes if needed
Administer intravenous adrenaline 1 microgram per kilogram of 1:10000 solution over one minute and titrate an infusion as required
Administer subcutaneous adrenaline 300 micrograms of 1:1000 solution into the deltoid muscle and review response after five minutes
Administer intramuscular adrenaline 150 micrograms of 1:1000 solution into the anterolateral thigh and repeat after five minutes if needed

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing measles from Kawasaki disease in a child with prolonged fever, conjunctivitis and rash
stem: An unimmunised 3-year-old girl returned from Indonesia nine days ago. She has had five days of fever with cough and coryza, and a rash that began on her face and has spread downwards.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.3, HR 140, RR 34, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis; white spots on the buccal mucosa; confluent maculopapular rash
data_table.Investigations: CRP 38 mg/L, platelets 190 x10^9/L, white cells 3.8 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Isolate her, swab the nasopharynx for viral PCR and notify public health
Admit her now for intravenous immunoglobulin with high-dose oral aspirin therapy
Arrange urgent echocardiography and admit her under paediatric cardiology
Start intravenous ceftriaxone and arrange a lumbar puncture on the ward
Discharge her with antipyretic advice and review by her family doctor

stem:
A 21-day-old term boy is brought to a metropolitan emergency department after his mother noticed he felt warm and was harder to wake for feeds during the night. He was born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 39 weeks with maternal group B streptococcal swab negative at 36 weeks and no rupture of membranes risk factors.

On examination he is mottled and sleepy but rouseable with vigorous handling. He is poorly perfused with capillary return of four seconds. Fontanelle is soft. There is no rash, no respiratory distress, and no focal source of infection. His mother has no history of genital herpes and no febrile illness in the third trimester. The mother is not on any antibiotics and breastfeeds exclusively.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 184, blood pressure 64/38, respiratory rate 56, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: venous gas pH 7.28 base excess negative 6, lactate 3.8 mmol/L, capillary glucose 3.2 mmol/L, urinalysis pending, point-of-care viral swab pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Take blood cultures, urine sample, and cerebrospinal fluid, then start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin with a 20 mL/kg saline bolus
Take urine and blood cultures only, defer lumbar puncture, and start oral amoxicillin pending culture results in twenty four hours
Observe in the short stay unit with regular paracetamol and four hourly reviews to assess whether the temperature settles
Take blood culture, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid then start intravenous cefotaxime, benzylpenicillin, and aciclovir with a 20 mL/kg saline bolus
Take blood cultures and urine then start intravenous ceftriaxone as monotherapy with a 10 mL/kg dextrose bolus to correct hypoglycaemia

stem:
A 5-week-old first-born boy is brought to a regional paediatric outpatient clinic with a four day history of forceful vomiting after every feed. The mother says the milk comes out in an arch and he is hungry again straight afterwards. His weight today is 4.0 kg compared with 4.3 kg at his two week check.

On examination he is alert but mildly dehydrated with sunken fontanelle and dry lips. Abdomen is soft with no palpable mass after careful palpation post-feed. Bowel sounds are present. There is no jaundice and no abdominal distension. There has been no bile-stained vomit, no haematemesis, and no diarrhoea. The mother is not on any medications and there is no family history of pyloric stenosis. He passes pale yellow urine in front of you.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 152, blood pressure 84/50, respiratory rate 38, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: venous gas pH 7.50 bicarbonate 32 mmol/L (22-28), sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), chloride 94 mmol/L (95-110), capillary glucose 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent abdominal ultrasound to measure pylorus dimensions and admit for intravenous rehydration with correction of electrolytes
Trial of thickened oral feeds for 48 hours and review in clinic if vomiting persists or weight gain remains poor
Send urgent upper gastrointestinal contrast study to look for malrotation with volvulus and book the operating theatre
Commence oral omeprazole 1 mg/kg daily for suspected reflux oesophagitis and provide reassurance to the mother
Refer for surgical pyloromyotomy directly without imaging and start a slow intravenous infusion of 0.9 percent saline overnight

subtopic_detail: Severe DKA initial fluid and insulin timing
stem:
A 7-year-old boy is brought to a regional emergency department by his mother after three days of polydipsia, polyuria, and weight loss followed by twelve hours of vomiting and progressive lethargy. He has no prior diagnosis of diabetes. He has no headache and no focal neurology.

On examination he is mildly drowsy but rouseable with eyes-open-to-voice and engages in short sentences. Mucous membranes are dry, capillary return is three seconds, and respirations are deep and slow. Pulse rate 144, blood pressure 98/58, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees, weight 22 kg. Capillary glucose is 28 mmol/L. The retrieval team will arrive in 60 minutes for transfer to the tertiary paediatric centre.

data_table.Investigations: venous blood gas pH 7.06, bicarbonate 7 mmol/L (22-28), base excess negative 22, sodium 134 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 9.2 mmol/L (2.5-7.8), creatinine 88 micromol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.2 mmol/L, GCS 14 (E3 V5 M6)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate fluid and insulin plan over the first hour?

options.text: Administer 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline as a rapid bolus over fifteen minutes and start intravenous insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately after the bolus
Administer 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline over thirty minutes, defer insulin until one hour after fluids commence, and arrange immediate paediatric retrieval
Administer maintenance 0.9 percent saline at 0.5 mL/kg/hour and commence intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg to correct severe acidosis
Administer 20 mL/kg Hartmann's solution as a rapid bolus and commence intravenous insulin 0.05 units/kg/hour with added potassium 40 mmol/L
Administer subcutaneous insulin 0.3 units/kg as a stat dose and offer oral rehydration with 10 mL/kg over the next sixty minutes

stem:
A 9-year-old girl (28 kg) presents to a regional ED with a severe asthma exacerbation that has not responded to back-to-back salbutamol and ipratropium nebulisers over the past 30 minutes, oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg 25 minutes ago, and a stat dose of intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg given 10 minutes ago. The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG suggests proceeding to IV salbutamol or aminophylline next; the Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory algorithm lists IV salbutamol as preferred. Both guidelines explicitly note that aminophylline retains an indication when IV salbutamol is unavailable or not tolerated.

She has known atopic asthma on inhaled budesonide 200 mcg BD with a salbutamol reliever, last admitted 8 months ago for an exacerbation without ICU. She has had no recent steroid course. She does not have congenital long QT syndrome and her ECG today shows sinus tachycardia at 158 bpm with normal QTc (392 ms).

The regional hospital does not stock IV salbutamol; the pharmacy can have it from a tertiary centre in 90 minutes. IV aminophylline is stocked. The retrieval service has been activated and the transfer team will arrive in approximately 75 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158 bpm, BP 105/68 mmHg, RR 42 with marked accessory muscle use, SpO2 88% on 8 L/min via Hudson mask, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Silent chest in upper zones bilaterally; able to speak in single words; alert; no cyanosis
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pH 7.27, pCO2 52 mmHg, lactate 4.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.0); ECG sinus tachycardia, QTc 392 ms; electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management while awaiting the retrieval team?

options.text: Commence intravenous aminophylline loading dose 10 mg/kg over 60 minutes (capped at 500 mg) followed by maintenance infusion 1 mg/kg/hour, with continuous cardiac monitoring and serum theophylline level at 2 hours
Commence intravenous salbutamol loading dose 15 mcg/kg over 10 minutes followed by infusion 1 to 5 mcg/kg/min, with continuous cardiac monitoring and electrolytes every 2 hours
Repeat the intravenous magnesium sulfate bolus at 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes with continuous BP monitoring and a held dose if systolic falls below 90 mmHg
Proceed to rapid sequence induction and intubation with ketamine 1 to 2 mg/kg and rocuronium 1 mg/kg, planning low tidal volume mandatory ventilation pending retrieval team arrival
Commence non-invasive bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) 12 over 5 cmH2O with FiO2 titrated to SpO2 of 94 to 98 percent, while awaiting retrieval
